My Educational Mechanical Examples Series This model is one of my educational mechanical mechanism examples on 80mm x 80mm base plates. You can find all models of the series in this collection => [Mechanical Mechanism Examples] The present model This is an educational model of a Hart's A-frame, which is one of the exact straight-line linkages. Brief Description The approximate straight-line mechanisms introduced so far — Watt's linkage, the Chebyshev linkage, and the Grasshopper linkage — are all based on four-bar linkages. The coupler point need not lie at a joint between two links; it may sit at the midpoint of a link or on its extension. Even so, these simple linkages confine the coupler point to a path that is only approximately straight — and they do so without any linear guide or prismatic pair. A four-bar linkage, however, cannot trace an exactly straight line. Hart's A-frame achieves exact straight-line motion by raising the number of links to six. Five of them move; the sixth is the base plate itself, which serves as the hidden ground link. Laid out as the capital letter A, each slanted side is built from a long link and a short link half its length, joined end to end, and the two short links meet at the apex. The lower end of each long link is pinned to the base plate, and these two fixed pivots are spaced apart by twice the length of the crossbar. The crossbar — the horizontal stroke of the A — joins the two long links at the points that divide them in a 3:1 ratio, with the longer portion toward the fixed pivot. Only these two lower pivots are anchored; every other joint is free to move. Under this arrangement the apex of the A, which is the coupler point, is constrained to travel along a perfectly straight line: the vertical line engraved on the base plate, which is the perpendicular bisector of the two fixed pivots. Move the coupler point by hand and you can feel it being held to this line. As you play with the model, though, you will find that this is not the only path open to the coupler point: the motion branches at the midpoint between the two pivots. There, the coupler point can leave the straight line for a second, skewed path that traces a distorted triangle, also engraved on the plate. Pushing on the coupler point alone will not carry it past the corners of that triangle; there you must also control how the links fold in order to pass through. To keep the motion well-behaved, confine the coupler point to either the upper or the lower half of the straight line, or guide it through the midpoint so that it does not slip onto the other branch. Reference https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart%27s_inversors Related Models Case This model is compatible with the case included in my first set . Printing Use the models named ???-printable.stl for printing . The models named ???-assembled.stl are provided just to show how they should be assembled. Use well-dried PETG to have better dimensional accuracy. Use 0.1 mm or 0.08 mm layer height to have smoother surfaces. Use slow printing speed for overhangs. Select “Random” seam position to have smoother rotation. Randomly distributed seam should be easily worn out after some wearing.Printing Sanding and Filing Note that, in this model, the rotation of the bases for bearings is intentionally made not too smooth. Sometimes, the gears suffer from the stringing effect and/or elephant foot effect, resulting in a too tight fit to the shafts (they are designed with a 0.15 mm radial clearance). If you see rough surface on the shafts due to stringing, sand off the roughness with a small piece of sand paper. If you feel the gears do not rotate smoothly due to an elephant effect, widen the hole slightly by using a thin round bar file. Without those issues, the parts should rotate very smoothly with minimal friction. Assembly Secure the links onto the shafts with the retaining rings. Additionally, I added a version of the engine with the lettering integrated directly into the body In “alternate Parts” profile. However, for the scaled-down versions, I recommend using the fully 3D-printed, bearingless configuration. At smaller scales, the printed bearing system generally rotates more smoothly because it produces less friction than a standard 608ZZ bearing. A traditional bearing may still work well if a high-quality, low-friction bearing is used. Sections Story & Background Engine Info Printing Tips & My Modifications Assembly Instructions Final Notes 1) Story & Background This model was originally designed for a special MTU event in the DFW area — a tribute to the engineers and technicians who work on and around one of the most advanced jet engines flying today. It was built for a friend who works there, and for the incredible team around them. Building this model meant diving deep into the real engineering behind the LEAP-1B, and coming out the other side with an even deeper respect for what CFM International has achieved. It was a labor of love from first sketch to final print, and sharing it with the maker community feels like the right next step. 2) Engine Info The CFM International LEAP-1B is the exclusive powerplant for the Boeing 737 MAX , designed and produced by CFM International — a 50/50 joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines , established in 1974. It represents a massive leap forward in efficiency and sustainability over its predecessor, the CFM56. MTU & the LEAP-1B This model was created for an MTU event — and MTU's connection to this engine runs deep. MTU Aero Engines is directly involved in MRO (Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul) services for both the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B, helping keep this massive global fleet airworthy and operational. 3) Printing Tips & Modifications I made targeted modifications on a per-component basis rather than applying global settings — for example, on the engine body I adjusted print speeds for better surface quality and used support enforcers and blockers on specific areas to avoid unnecessary supports elsewhere. If you use your own print profile, you will still get a good result. However, if you have a Bambu A1 like mine, you'll get the best results using my specific print profile. Since the A1 is a Cartesian (bed-slinger) printer , outer surface quality can sometimes suffer — my speed adjustments help mitigate this, though it may not be perfect. Alternate Parts & Customization I have also uploaded an alternate parts profile for those who want additional options or a cleaner look. This includes: Clean engine variant — a version free of decals for a sleek, minimal finish Alternate display stands — additional stand styles as shown in the figures below Blank logo plates — fully blank plates that you can customize by importing SVGs directly in Bambu Studio or your preferred CAD software Bearing Options The shaft supports are designed to accommodate several bearing configurations. Choose whichever works best for you: Option Specs Notes Bambu-sourced bearing (6000ZZ) ID/OD/W: 10 × 26 × 8 mm Recommended Common Amazon bearing ID/OD/W: 8 × 22 × 7 mm Easy to source 3D printed bearing — Works, but not ideal Custom / your own bearing — Blank shaft support included Bearingless option Surprisingly works well A blank shaft support is included if you'd like to fit your own bearing or design a custom solution. All alternate parts and bearing profiles are included in the alternate parts profile attached to this upload. If you use a bearing, the shafts are pressure fit where the blade shaft diameter is 12 mm. Nozzle recommendation: I have uploaded multiple print profiles ( 0.2mm and 0.4mm). A 0.2mm nozzle will give you the best results for the lettering and logo details. 4) Assembly Instructions Step 1 — Fan Core Sub-Assembly (Shaft + Flywheel + Fan Support) Start by assembling the three core components: the blade support shaft , the flywheel , and the fan holder . Orient the shaft correctly — the flat side faces a specific direction as shown in the photo. ⚠️ If installed backwards, the fan blades will not seat in the correct position. Apply a small amount of glue into the alignment hole only — do not over-apply. Applying glue here (rather than on the shaft body) prevents glue from migrating to the shaft collar, which must remain free to spin. The completed fan core must be able to rotate freely — confirm this before the glue sets. Step 2 — Install Fan Core into Engine Body Apply glue to the designated glue area on the engine body interior as shown in the photo. Insert the fan core sub-assembly into the body. Align the notches on the shaft holder with the corresponding notches inside the engine body — this is critical for correct positioning. description: Help students pause, breathe, and reset with this simple Box Breathing Pause Card from 3DprintEDU. This 3D printable calm corner tool gives children a tactile path to follow with their finger while practising a simple breathing routine. Students can trace the square, moving from corner to corner as they breathe in, hold, breathe out, and pause. description: 5-Speed Manual Gearbox with Reverse This is a fully functional, highly detailed 5-speed manual transmission model (plus Reverse) designed for educational demonstration, engineering enthusiasts, or anyone who loves mechanical design. Every major internal component of a real manual transmission is represented here, including the input shaft, counter shaft, main output shaft, synchronizer hubs, synchronizer rings, sliding sleeves, and a reverse idler gear. The multi-colored gear assembly makes it incredibly easy to visualize how shifting gears changes the drive ratios from the input shaft to the output shaft. Parts & Components List All components are designed to print at 100% scale (1:1) for a perfect mechanical fit. The model is organized into the following components: Shafts: INPUTSHAFT (Input Shaft) Counter (Counter Shaft) Shaft (Main Shaft) Output Gears: 26 34 38 44 44 reverse Synchronizer Assembly: HUB GEAR 17 14 (Synchronizer Hub) HUB GEAR 20 17 (Synchronizer Hub) SLEAVE GEAR (Synchronizer Sleeve) SYNC RING (Synchronizer Rings) Reverse Mechanism: IDLEAR GEAR V2 (Reverse Idler Gear) Display Stand & Hardware: Stand Part 1 & Stand Part 2 Stand Holder Part 1 & Stand Holder Part 2 14mm bolt & Pin SNAP RING & SNAP TO IDLER SHAFT Assembly & Printing Tips Color Coding: For the best visual effect, consider printing the matching gear sets on the main shaft and counter shaft in distinct colors (as shown in the project photos) to easily identify each speed. Tolerances: This is a mechanical model with interlocking parts. Ensure your printer's flow rate and X/Y tolerances are well-calibrated so the gears spin smoothly and the synchronizer sleeves slide without binding. Post-Processing: A small amount of plastic-safe lubricant (like silicone grease) on the shafts and gear teeth can drastically improve the smoothness of the manual shifting action.

Overview This basketball kinetic sculpture has linkages that cause the ball to always be centered in the exact same position. It is a basketball-themed version of the models you can find in the collection here: https://makerworld.com/en/collections/29606948-fixed-center-kinetic-sculptures All of the parts in all of the models in the collection are compatible with each other. Due to each hinge axis passing through the center, no matter how each link is moved, it will cause the entire structure to articulate around a stationary center. It features a print-in-place and thread-together design that requires no glue or additional hardware. It requires no supports and is extremely fascinating and satisfying. The base can also be filled with sand or other materials to provide a more premium feel. For printing Standard setting can be used for printing. Except for the ball, no parts require supports or an AMS. Two versions of the ball are available. One that requires an AMS or dual nozzle and one that requires the seams to be pressed or glued into place. For the print profiles, there is one with all parts on separate plates with both types of balls in the profile and two that have all the parts on a single plate (one includes the funnel and the other does not). All materials should work; however, for the ball to stay more centered, avoid flexible materials like TPU. Features The model prints in three or five pieces: the base, the print-in-place linkages, and the ball that requires AMS or the ball that does not and the two seam pieces. Additionally, a funnel can be printed to more easily fill the base with sand or another material. The hole for filling the base is the same hole that the linkage structure threads into. The entire structure is about 95 mm in diameter and about 105 mm tall. All of these parts are completely compatible with the other models in this collection. https://makerworld.com/en/collections/29606948-fixed-center-kinetic-sculptures Assembly Assembling this model is very simple. Optionally, the funnel can be threaded into the hole in the base and the base filled. After the funnel is removed, the linkage structure can be threaded into that same hole until it stops. The location of where the threads stop should position the linkage structure properly. If the no-AMS ball is printed, the seam pieces need to be placed in place (they will likely require some glue). Lastly, the ball can be threaded onto the rod at the center of the ring. The links may be slightly stiff and not want to move after printing, but with some slight pressure, the links can be broken free. Other Versions with Themes This is a basketball-themed version of the models you can find in the collection here: https://makerworld.com/en/collections/29606948-fixed-center-kinetic-sculptures I currently plan on making more variations of this model with other specific themes. These may include but not be limited to: A space theme with the ball being a planet or the moon. A version themed around a different sport such as baseball, tennis, golf, volleyball, or American football. A moving object-themed version that could be a motorcycle, racecar, airplane, or rocket. An outdoor activity-themed version that could have a surfboard, skateboard, or fishing bobber or lure. A larger version that had a light using the led light kit. There are many possible versions that I could create. Let me know which ones you want to see, and let me know of any other ideas that you have. description: OpenPrintSense - 3D Printed BLE Flex Sensor Glove OpenPrintSense is an open-source project that combines 3D printing, hardware, and software to create a wearable finger tracking system. The key innovation is a fully 3D-printed flex sensor that uses conductive TPU filament - as the sensor bends, its electrical resistance changes, allowing precise measurement of finger flexion. Data is transmitted wirelessly via BLE to an Android smartphone. How It Works: The 3D-printed sensor combines flexible TPU with conductive filament. When you bend your finger: The conductive filament stretches This increases the electrical resistance The microcontroller reads the resistance change via analog input The bend angle is calculated and sent to the app Use Cases: 🎮 Gesture-based game controllers 🤖 Robot hand control 🏥 Rehabilitation therapy tracking 🎵 Musical instrument interfaces 📊 Motion capture for research Electronics: Microcontroller: Seeed XIAO nRF52840 Sense Power: USB-C or 3.7V LiPo battery Wires: For connecting sensor to microcontroller 3D Printing Materials: Flexible Base: Bambu Lab TPU 90A - Flexible structure Conductive Element: Recreus FilaFlex Conductive - Variable resistance sensing Read the GitHub for more information on assembly and functionality: https://github.com/PaBu04/OpenPrintSense

model_name: Wind Turbine Project | Functional Simple Turbine
description: This is a heavily modified and fully functional remix of the excellent "Basic Wind Turbine" by kjt270000 . This remix transforms the original core concept into a practical, power-generating system designed specifically for apartment balconies and off-grid experimentation. This project includes completely redesigned mounting hardware, weatherproofing additions, structural reinforcements, and a complete perfboard electronics enclosure to harness the wind and charge an 18650 lithium-ion battery. 🛠️ What's New in this Remix? Two Optimized Sizes Medium Version: Retains the 24mm motor from the original model. Ideal for standard winds and smaller spaces. Large Version: Upgraded to house a 32mm motor, significantly increasing power generation potential for easier battery charging. Balcony-Ready Mounting System The mounting system has been completely engineered from scratch to easily clamp onto a typical balcony barrier. The Mast: Designed to use a standard 32mm (external diameter) PVC pipe with a 2.5mm wall thickness as the main tower. Free Rotation Yaw: To ensure the turbine can freely track wind direction (yaw) without friction, the design incorporates a standard bearing (27mm External Diameter / 15.5mm Internal Diameter) at the pivot point. Structural & Weatherproofing Upgrades Motor Cover: Added a top cover for the motor housing to improve weather resistance. (Note: While it provides splash and light rain protection, leaving the turbine out in heavy, continuous rain is still not encouraged). Tail Support: A new stabilizing brace was added to the tail section. This prevents the tail from sagging or bending under its own weight over time due to the natural layer orientation of FDM printing. Smart Cable Management On both versions, the main pivot body features a specific internal routing path. The cables run straight from the motor, inside the PVC pipe, and out the bottom. This prevents the wires from wrapping around the mast as the turbine rotates. ⚡ Electronics Overview (No Custom PCB Required!) Hardware Components List Core Modules & Power 1x 18650 Lithium-Ion Battery (3.7V, unprotected cell is fine since the circuit has protection) 1x 18650 Single Cell Battery Holder 1x TP4056 Lithium Battery Charging Module (Ensure you get the version with the built-in protection circuit—it has OUT+ and OUT- pads in addition to B+ and B-). 2x MT3608 DC-DC Step-Up Boost Converter Modules (Often marked as HW-045). Basic Electronic Components 4x Rectifier Diodes (1N4007 are standard, but 1N5819 Schottky diodes are highly recommended here for better efficiency and lower voltage drop). 1x Electrolytic Capacitor (Values around 470µF to 1000µF, rated for at least 16V or 25V). 1x Perfboard / Prototype PCB (Standard dot-matrix board, cut to fit your 3D printed enclosure). Miscellaneous Hookup wire (22-24 AWG stranded wire is ideal for flexibility) Solder How It Works (The Circuit Logic) Input & Rectification: The wind turbine motor generates erratic, fluctuating voltage (and possibly AC depending on the motor). The four diodes act as a Bridge Rectifier , ensuring the electricity flows in the right direction regardless of which way the wind spins the turbine. The Capacitor smooths out this rippling voltage. Boosting to Charge: The turbine might not always generate the 5V needed to charge the battery. The first MT3608 boost converter takes the smoothed voltage and steps it up to a steady 5V. Battery Management: The 5V feeds into the TP4056 module , which safely charges the 18650 battery and protects it from over-charging and over-discharging. Output Power: The 18650 battery outputs around 3.7V. The second MT3608 boost converter takes this battery voltage and steps it up to a stable 5V (or 12V, depending on what you are trying to power with the turbine). Step-by-Step Assembly Guide Important Pre-step: Before soldering the MT3608 modules into the final circuit, connect a temporary power source to their inputs, hook a multimeter to their outputs, and turn the little brass screw on the blue potentiometer until they output exactly your desired voltages (e.g., 5V for the first one). Step 1: The Rectifier Circuit (Power Input) Solder the 4 diodes onto the perfboard in a bridge rectifier configuration. Connect the two wires coming from your wind turbine motor to the AC input sides of the diode bridge. Solder the electrolytic capacitor across the positive and negative outputs of the diode bridge. Note: Capacitors have polarity; ensure the negative stripe side connects to the negative trace. Step 2: Voltage Stabilization (First Boost Converter) Connect the Positive output of the capacitor to the VIN+ on the first MT3608 module. Connect the Negative output of the capacitor to the VIN- on the first MT3608 module. Tune this module to output exactly 5V. Step 3: The Charging Circuit Connect the VOUT+ of the first MT3608 to the IN+ (or standard positive input pad) of the TP4056 module. Connect the VOUT- of the first MT3608 to the IN- of the TP4056 module. Solder the positive (red) wire from the 18650 battery holder to the B+ pad on the TP4056. Solder the negative (black) wire from the battery holder to the B- pad on the TP4056. Step 4: Output Power (Second Boost Converter) Connect the OUT+ pad from the TP4056 to the VIN+ pad of the second MT3608 module. Connect the OUT- pad from the TP4056 to the VIN- pad of the second MT3608 module. Adjust the potentiometer on this second MT3608 to your final desired output voltage (e.g., 5V for charging a phone, 12V for LED strips). Solder your final output wires to the VOUT+ and VOUT- pads of the second MT3608. Enjoy building, and may the wind be in your favor!

🧊 The ultimate customizable 3D shape generator! Need physical geometry manipulatives for a math class? Looking to create custom building blocks for your kids, or test out your printer's dimensional accuracy? This fully parametric OpenSCAD generator instantly creates 13 different mathematically perfect 3D solid shapes at any dimension you require. Membership Educational manipulatives and custom building blocks are great tools for schools and parents. While this basic geometric generator is freely available, joining my Commercial Membership for only €4.99/mo gives you full commercial rights to sell physical prints of this model, AND unlocks commercial rights to ALL my other premium generators! ⚙️ Customizer features: 13 classic volumes: Instantly render a cube, cuboid, cylinder, sphere, cone, truncated cone, torus, triangular prism, hexagonal prism, square pyramid, triangular pyramid, capsule, or ellipsoid. Mass batch generation: Select All Shapes Grid from the dropdown to instantly generate a perfectly spaced classroom layout of all 13 shapes on your build plate at once! Make it hollow: Enable Make_Hollow and specify a wall thickness. This automatically hollows out the top of the shape, turning it into an open cup or container. This is perfect for teaching volume in math class by filling them with water or sand! Infinite sizing: Enter your exact X, Y, and Z dimensions to stretch and scale the shapes dynamically. 🧠 Behind the design (For makers & moderators) To provide the absolute fastest rendering performance, this model uses dynamic parameter mapping. Instead of importing separate complex meshes, the algorithm manipulates the core OpenSCAD primitive functions. For example, prisms and pyramids are mathematically generated by taking a standard cylinder and dynamically overriding its face resolution ($fn) to 3, 4, or 6, instantly turning it into a sharp geometric solid. The Make_Hollow function utilizes a smart boolean difference, dynamically duplicating the chosen shape, shrinking it precisely by the user-defined wall thickness, and subtracting it from the original solid exactly at the top plane. 🖨️ Print settings: Material: PLA is perfect for educational blocks. Layer height: 0.20mm works beautifully. If you are printing the sphere or ellipsoid, 0.16mm will make the top curves much smoother. Supports: Mostly none. However, if you print the sphere or torus, adding standard snug supports under the bottom overhang is highly recommended to prevent print failure. Infill: 10% to 15% (Lightning or Gyroid) is plenty for solid shapes. ❤️ Share your prints! I love seeing your classroom setups and creative uses for these shapes. Please upload a photo of your make! It is a globe-themed version of the models you can find in the collection here: https://makerworld.com/en/collections/29606948-fixed-center-kinetic-sculptures All of the parts in all of the models in the collection are compatible with each other. Due to each hinge axis passing through the center, no matter how each link is moved, it will cause the entire structure to articulate around a stationary center. It features a print-in-place and thread-together design that requires no glue or additional hardware. It requires no supports and is extremely fascinating and satisfying. The base can also be filled with sand or other materials to provide a more premium feel. For printing Standard setting can be used for printing. No parts require supports. For the print profiles, there is one with all parts on separate plates and two that have all the parts on a single plate (one includes the funnel and the other does not). All materials should work; however, for the ball to stay more centered, avoid flexible materials like TPU. Features The model prints in three pieces: the base, the print-in-place linkages, and the globe. Additionally, a funnel can be printed to more easily fill the base with sand or another material. The hole for filling the base is the same hole that the linkage structure threads into. The entire structure is about 95 mm in diameter and about 105 mm tall. All of these parts are completely compatible with the other models in this collection. https://makerworld.com/en/collections/29606948-fixed-center-kinetic-sculptures Assembly Assembling this model is very simple. Optionally, the funnel can be threaded into the hole in the base and the base filled. After the funnel is removed, the linkage structure can be threaded into that same hole until it stops. The location of where the threads stop should position the linkage structure properly. Lastly, the globe can be threaded onto the rod at the center of the ring. The links may be slightly stiff and not want to move after printing, but with some slight pressure, the links can be broken free. My Educational Mechanical Examples Series This model is one of my educational mechanical mechanism examples on 80mm x 80mm base plates. You can find all models of the series in this collection => [Mechanical Mechanism Examples] The present model This is an educational model of self-centering chuck. Brief Description A self-centering chuck is a device often used with a lathe . A lathe is a machine tool that rotates a workpiece and presses a cutting tool against it to remove material, producing shapes that are symmetric about the axis of rotation. During turning, a workpiece often has to be re-clamped from a different side, and each time this is done the rotational center of the workpiece must be made to coincide exactly with the rotational center of the lathe. A self-centering chuck moves several jaws — arranged symmetrically around the lathe's axis — inward or outward together without breaking that symmetry, continuously varying the radius of the circle traced by their gripping faces. Because the jaws remain symmetric, a rotationally symmetric workpiece held in a self-centering chuck settles naturally with its own axis aligned to the lathe's axis, requiring no fine adjustment. The self-centering chuck shown here has three jaws, whose positions are set by a ring into which an Archimedean spiral is cut. An Archimedean spiral is a spiral whose adjacent turns are spaced a constant distance apart. When the ring turns at a constant rate, the point where the spiral crosses a given radius travels along that radius at a constant speed. The underside of each jaw carries a straight rack that meshes with this spiral, so as the ring turns and the crossing point moves, the jaw — whose motion is constrained to the radial direction — is carried along the radius by that motion. On the plane through the middle of a jaw, the mechanism is this simple, but the finite width of the rack teeth makes the story a little more complex. As the figure below shows, each rack tooth has to curve to follow the spiral. The curvature of an Archimedean spiral is not constant — it is tighter on the inside and gentler on the outside — so as a jaw travels along the radius, the curvature of the spiral tooth it meshes with changes as well. To keep the rack teeth from interfering at any position the jaw can reach, each tooth is shaped for the worst case: its inner edge is cut to the largest radius of curvature that occurs over the tooth's range of travel, and its outer edge to the smallest. This makes the valley between teeth wide and deep enough everywhere to clear the spiral ridge without interference. To keep all three jaws at the same distance from the center, the rack on each jaw is offset in phase by one third of a tooth pitch, as shown in the figure above. Only when the jaws are fitted in the correct order do the three jaws sit at equal distances from the center. In the photograph above, each jaw is stepped, growing thicker toward the center, as the left figure below. A jaw of this kind is called an inside-diameter (ID) step jaw. It is designed for two modes of use: gripping a workpiece placed between the three jaws by closing the jaws onto its outer surface, and supporting a hollow workpiece from within, by inserting the raised central step into the bore and opening the jaws against the inside of the hole. Both modes were demonstrated in the youtube video above. The model also includes, as optional parts, an outside-diameter (OD) step jaw, which instead grows thicker toward the outside (central figure), and a flat jaw with no steps (right figure). The OD step jaw is used to hold a workpiece whose diameter is too large to be gripped by the central part of the jaws. A working chuck on a lathe hides all of its mechanical detail inside a steel body; here, laid open, the spiral and the racks show plainly how symmetry is turned into motion. Related model In the model of Groove Cam , the follower motion was limited along an arc by the swinging arm. In the present model, the teeth on the bottom surface of the jaws can be regarded as followers running in the Archimedean spiral groove. There, the followers' motion is limited along straight lines by the linear guide, instead of arcs. The model of Archimedean spiral gear, included in "Educational Gear Examples 2" shows a combination of Archimedean spiral with a pinion gear, instead of rack. Case This model is compatible with the case included in my first set . Printing Use the models named ???-printable.stl for printing . The models named ???-assembled.stl are provided just to show how they should be assembled. Use well-dried PETG to have better dimensional accuracy. Use 0.1 mm or 0.08 mm layer height to have smoother surfaces. Use slow printing speed for overhangs. Select “Random” seam position to have smoother rotation. Randomly distributed seam should be easily worn out after some wearing.Printing Sanding and Filing Note that, in this model, the rotation of the bases for bearings is intentionally made not too smooth. Sometimes, the gears suffer from the stringing effect and/or elephant foot effect, resulting in a too tight fit to the shafts (they are designed with a 0.15 mm radial clearance). If you see rough surface on the shafts due to stringing, sand off the roughness with a small piece of sand paper. If you feel the gears do not rotate smoothly due to an elephant effect, widen the hole slightly by using a thin round bar file. Without those issues, the parts should rotate very smoothly with minimal friction. Assembly Place the knob on the shaft and secure it with the retaining ring. Place the ring gear. Push the legs of the linear guide into the holes on the base plate. They will snap into place. While turning the ring gear counter-clockwise, slide the jaws into the linear guides one by one to make them mate with the spiral, referring to the number of dimples on the jaws. The one with single dimple should be the first, one with two dimples the second, and one with three dimples the last. Since three jaws have their teeth at different phases, if they are placed with wrong order, they will not be at same distance from the center. The order of insertion is what matters — any jaw can go into any guide, as long as the single-, double-, and triple-dimple jaws are inserted in that order. To replace the jaws to those of different type, turn the ring gear clockwise fully until the jaws come out from the linear guide. Then slide the replacing jaws in following the step 4. Find them in this collection: https://makerworld.com/collections/15048577-my-educational-mechanism-models Happy printing! My Educational Mechanical Examples Series This model is one of my educational mechanical mechanism examples on 80mm x 80mm base plates. You can find all models of the series in this collection => [Mechanical Mechanism Examples] The present model Here are variety of generalized elliptical gears. Brief Description Non-circular gears meshing condition In this series, a few kinds of non-circular gears have been already introduced. In general, two non-circular gears can mesh only when their reference curves can have rolling contact with each other without slipping while the gears rotate. This condition can be decomposed into two mathematical conditions: As the contact point moves along each reference curve by the same arc length Δ L , in opposite rotational directions on each gear, the radius measured from the center of rotation increases by Δ r on one curve if and only if it decreases by Δ r on the other. Satisfying this condition allows the two gears, with fixed centers of rotation, to maintain contact and roll against each other without slipping. The total perimeters of the two reference curves must be in an integer ratio to each other. Satisfying this condition allows the contact point, after completing one full circuit, to return to the same phase relationship and continue meshing correctly beyond a single rotation. For the model “Non-circular Gear” shown above, the shape of one gear was first fixed as an eccentric ellipse. The shape of the mating gear was then found by solving a differential equation so as to satisfy condition 1, and finally the distance between the two centers of rotation was adjusted so that the perimeter ratio became 1:1. The model "Non-circular gears 2" followed a similar procedure. Here, the shape of the square-based gear was first assumed to be a square of side 4 a with its corners filleted by radius a . In addition to condition 1, a perimeter ratio of 4:3 was imposed, and from these two requirements the shape of the mating triangular gear and the distance between the centers of rotation were determined. The design of the Scroll Gear, by contrast, was much simpler. The curve used here, known as the logarithmic spiral, has the property that its radius increases at a constant rate per unit arc length along the curve. Because of this property, no differential equation needs to be solved: the logarithmic spiral is geometrically guaranteed to mesh correctly with a copy of itself. Ellipse Gear Like the logarithmic spiral, the ellipse is a curve that is guaranteed to roll against a copy of itself without slipping, with its focus serving as the center of rotation. Why is this guaranteed? An ellipse is known to be drawn by looping a string around two pins and tracing it out with a pencil held inside the loop, keeping the string taut, all the way around. If the distance between the pins is 2 c and the total length of the loop is 2( a + c ), then the semi-major axis of the ellipse is a , and the semi-minor axis is b = √( a ²− c ²). The positions of the pins are called the foci of the ellipse. With this in mind, it is easy to see from the animation below why an ellipse can roll against a copy of itself without slipping. The two red lines inside the fixed ellipse at the center represent the string running from each pin to the tip of the pencil. The combined length of the two red lines is always equal to 2 a . If we mirror the ellipse across its tangent line at the pencil's position, the mirrored ellipse is the second ellipse, which rolls around the fixed one. Notice that, as the two ellipses roll without slipping, the distance between their corresponding foci is always kept equal to 2 a . The Ellipse Gear model was built using two such ellipses as its reference curves. The two pivots fixed to the base plate are the two foci that serve as the fixed centers of rotation for the two ellipses. The other focus of each ellipse is not fixed, and instead moves as the gear rotates. A movable bar is attached on top of the gears to demonstrate that the distance between these two moving foci is also kept equal to 2 a . We encourage you to try removing this bar and confirm that the two gears still rotate together smoothly and stably on their own. Oval Gear Flow Meter The oval gear flow meter closely resembles the "Circumferential Piston Gear" included in the “External Pumps” model, already introduced earlier in this series, but its purpose is exactly the opposite of a pump's. Whereas a pump converts rotational motion into fluid flow, a flow meter works by converting fluid flow into rotational motion. In this model, as liquid flows in through one of the two ports, the oval gears are pushed into rotation by the resulting pressure difference. This rotation can then drive a counter connected to the gears, allowing the total volume of fluid that has passed through the meter, using nothing but the flow of the fluid itself, with no external power source required. Now, have you noticed that the two oval gears used in this flow meter rotate in a way quite different from the ellipse gear seen above? The ellipse gear rotated about its focus, whereas this oval gear rotates about its geometric center — that is, the shape's center of symmetry. So does an ellipse also roll against a copy of itself when its center of rotation is placed at the midpoint between its two foci, instead of at a focus? That turns out not to be the case. In fact, this oval-shaped gear is not an ellipse in the usual sense described above. It merely resembles one in shape. As we saw earlier, an ellipse can roll against a copy of itself when its center of rotation is placed at a focus, but if the center of rotation is instead placed at the midpoint between the two foci, the two curves can no longer roll against each other without slipping. Oval vs Ellipse To make the difference between the ellipse gear and the oval gear clear, this model combines both types together. The two gears on top are ellipse gears, rotating about their foci as pivots. The two gears on the bottom are the oval gears seen earlier, rotating about the geometric center of the shape as the pivot. Because the instantaneous speed ratio at each of the three meshing points varies continuously as the gears turn, and these variations compound across all three, the resulting variation in the overall speed ratio becomes extremely pronounced. If the gear at the bottom right is turned at a constant speed, the gear at the top left stays pointing downward and remains almost stationary for most of the time, then spins rapidly through a full rotation in the instant the bottom-right gear passes through its sideways orientation. In this model, the fact that two differently shaped gears — an ellipse and an oval — can roll against each other is no coincidence. In fact, this oval curve can be regarded as a relative of the ellipse, and belongs to a family of shapes called the higher-order ellipse . Higher-Order Ellipse Gear This curve, which we'll call a higher-order ellipse , extends the oval shape seen above into a more general family of shapes, each characterized by a number of "corners," n . From this point of view, the oval above can be thought of as a 2-cornered version, and the ordinary ellipse as a 1-cornered version. This higher-order ellipse is obtained by taking the polar equation of an ellipse, r ( θ ) = b ² / ( a − c cos θ ) and inserting n inside the cosine term: r ( θ ) = b' ² / ( a' − c cos( nθ ) ) (where a is the semi-major axis, b is the semi-minor axis, and c is half the distance between the foci). To make this curve mesh with the original ellipse, a ' and b ' are not simply set equal to a and b . Instead, they are chosen so that: the difference between the semi-major and semi-minor axes stays the same: a' − b' = a − b the total perimeter becomes n times that of the original ellipse Any two curves from this family of higher-order ellipses can then be freely combined and made to mesh with each other. Confirming why this meshing works requires a fairly involved calculation, but the outline is as follows: by first mapping the original ellipse onto the dashed circle shown below, and then mapping that circle onto the higher-order ellipse, one can verify that the two curves satisfy the condition stated at the beginning of this article — namely, that the radius changes by the same amount per unit arc length on both curves. What makes the higher-order ellipse particularly interesting is that, like the logarithmic spiral, it yields curves that roll against each other without slipping, without ever needing to solve a differential equation. The same curve can also be used to design internal gears, or planetary gear systems. On MakerWorld, many popular non-circular planetary gear systems with triangular or square-shaped satellite gears appear to have been designed using curves from this same family. If you see rough surface on the shafts due to stringing, sand off the roughness with a small piece of sand paper. If you feel the gears do not rotate smoothly due to an elephant effect, widen the hole slightly by using a thin round bar file. Without those issues, the parts should rotate very smoothly with minimal friction. Assembly Just secure the gears and the bar onto the shafts with the retaining rings. A minimalist hand-driven planetarium that turns the six classical planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn — at astronomically accurate relative speeds. 10 cm wide, 5 cm tall. A desk piece that models the solar system (as it was known in the 1700s!). Why only 6 planets? I came across a gear train for a planetarium that was designed by Scottish astronomer James Ferguson in the mid-1700s. At the time, Uranus and Neptune had not been discovered. His design used a single stacked gear to drive 6 planets, and I thought it was cool! In order to print it however, I had to include a dedicated connector gear for Jupiter-Saturn, as the teeth would have been too small to be printed. Description of the model can be found page 300 here . Parts Required Requires 7 ball bearings with these diameters: Sun = 12 mm Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars = 6 mm Jupiter, Saturn = 8 mm I included spheres for printing, but I think marbles or ball bearings would look much better. You can get all you need for approx €10 on ali express . I used a copper ball for Earth just to add distinction. description: My Social Battery — a tactile “how charged do I feel?” slider for kids Slide the lightning bolt and click through five stages — from flat-battery exhausted to fully charged — to show, at a glance, how much social/emotional energy you’ve got left. It’s a friendly, fidget-satisfying self-regulation and communication aid shaped like an AA battery. Built for kids 4–11 , and great for SEND / AAC / visual-support classrooms and calm corners — but honestly it’s for anyone who’s ever run out of “people battery.” Why you’ll like it A proper click. A print-tuned ratchet gives a crisp tick between stages and a firmer “settle” at each of the five homes — and it clicks exactly the same force in both directions (a symmetric twin-arm spring, not a one-sided one). Chunky lightning-bolt handle — rounded and wide, sized to survive a five-year-old, easy for little fingers to grab. Five emoji faces on removable colour panels: 😵 exhausted → 🙁 low → 😐 okay → 🙂 good → 😀 fully charged. Swap the panels toollessly — they snap in and pop out, so you can re-theme it (a 6-panel feelings set is on the way). Wall-mount or hand-hold — two rear keyholes or a Command-Strip on the flat back. Print settings Material: PLA. Stiff/standard PLA gives the crispest click (the spring is tuned for it). Nozzle / layers: 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layers. ~15 % infill is plenty. Supports: Tree supports for the Body only (they release much more cleanly than normal supports). Everything else prints support-free. Orientation (as exported): Part Orientation Supports Body front face up tree supports (for the channel roof / pockets) Slider flat (as exported) none — the spring must print flat so it flexes in-plane Grip (bolt) flat, bolt-face on the bed none Back cover flat none Panels ×5 flat none Two-colour panels: print each panel in its stage colour and swap to black at the face layer (Z ≈ 2.0 mm) so the embossed emoji prints black. On an AMS this is automatic; otherwise it’s a single manual filament change. Colours (suggested): Panel 1 red · 2 orange · 3 yellow · 4 light green · 5 dark green; body white/grey; bolt gold/yellow. Assembly (a couple of minutes, one drop of glue) The grip is a separate part because it’s far too wide to thread through the front slot. Drop the Slider into the body channel from the back — the square post pokes out through the front slot. From the front, press the Grip onto the post ( a drop of super-glue = a permanent, kid-proof bond). Press the Back cover into its rebate from behind until the sprung tabs snap home (firm tug to service later). description: Styracosaurus Skull A detailed display model of the spectacular skull of Styracosaurus , one of the most distinctive horned dinosaurs of the Late Cretaceous. Styracosaurus was a ceratopsian dinosaur closely related to Triceratops, but instead of the familiar three-horn arrangement, it carried a huge nasal horn and an incredible array of long spikes projecting from the back of its frill. It lived around 75 million years ago in what is now North America. This model is designed as a manageable display piece while still being large enough for all of those characteristic horns and frill details to really stand out. Dimensions Approximately: 250 mm tall 246 mm wide 140 mm front to back Removable Display Stand The skull comes with a removable display stand , allowing it to sit upright as a freestanding display piece. The stand is supplied on the second build plate , so you can also print the skull by itself if you have another display method in mind. Printing Despite the rather intimidating collection of horns, this is a fairly straightforward print. Support removal is easy, and the remaining support contact points clean up nicely with a sharp scalpel or hobby blade . Take your time around the smaller details and the finished model should require very little additional work before going on display. A great project for dinosaur fans, fossil collectors, classrooms, museums, palaeontology displays or anyone who simply wants an unusually spiky dinosaur skull sitting on their shelf. description: Membership 🚀 Turn Plastic into Profit with P3D Design! Want to sell high-margin products on your shop? By joining P3D Commercial Standard, you get full rights to sell physical 3D prints of my entire library of engineering upgrades and functional workshop fixtures. All models are designed in Autodesk Inventor and optimized for flawless printing on Bambu Lab. Cover your costs with just a few sales and keep your printers running 24/7! (Physical prints with your own photos only; no STL sharing). 2.5 D Plaster Molds Dino🦖🎨 Turn your 3D printer into a never-ending factory for creative toys! Are you looking for a great weekend activity to keep your kids entertained for hours? This project perfectly combines 3D printing technology with classic hands-on crafting. Anyone who has tried letting kids paint a standard 3D printed model (made of PLA or PETG) with watercolours or tempera knows it’s a struggle – the paint slides off the plastic surface, runs, and doesn't cover well. Plaster casts made from these TPU molds are a complete game-changer. Plaster has the perfect absorbency, so colors stick flawlessly, dry instantly, and look incredibly vibrant. You only need to print these flexible molds once, and you can cast plaster dinosaurs for your kids every single weekend, over and over again. 💡 Why TPU 95A? These molds are designed specifically for printing with TPU 95A flexible filament. Thanks to the unique compliance of this material, you don't have to worry about complex mold-release draft angles during modeling. The model is designed with an optimal wall thickness of 1.5 mm , which provides the perfect balance: the mold keeps its geometry perfectly and doesn't bulge under the weight of liquid plaster, yet it remains flexible enough that you can incredibly easily peel it off the hardened cast like a banana skin. No getting stuck, no broken details. 🛠️ Recommended Print Settings: Material: TPU 95A (e.g., Bambu TPU). Wall Thickness / Perimeters: 3 walls (crucial for maintaining the mold's stability). Infill: 10%. Note: Print directly from the rear spool holder of your printer, do NOT use the AMS , as flexible materials tend to get tangled and stuck in it! For a perfectly smooth inner surface, make sure your TPU is well dried before printing. 🧪 Step-by-Step Casting Guide for Kids: Preparation: Place the clean and dry TPU mold on a flat, stable surface. Pro Trick for Zero Bubbles: Lightly spray the inside of the mold with a spray bottle filled with water and a single drop of regular dish soap. The soap acts as a wetting agent – it lowers surface tension, allowing the plaster to flow flawlessly into the smallest details without leaving air bubbles on the surface. Alternatively, you can use a release agent made of wax dissolved in alcohol. Mixing the Plaster: Mix standard white hobby plaster with water according to the package instructions. Make sure to mix the consistency a bit thinner (like runny pancake batter) – this is very important to ensure the plaster flows easily and without resistance into all the fine details and crevices of the dinosaur. Pouring: Carefully pour the plaster into the mold. It is recommended to leave about 2–3 mm from the top rim for easier handling. Once poured, gently tap the mold against the table a couple of times (vibration) to release any remaining trapped air bubbles to the surface. Releasing the Mold: Wait about 20 to 30 minutes. Once the plaster is solid and warm to the touch (due to the exothermic reaction), gently peel the TPU mold away by bending it. Thanks to the 1.5 mm thin wall, it will come off effortlessly. Creative Finale: Let the cast dry completely (ideally in the sun or on a radiator until it turns bright white and "rings" when tapped). Then, just give your kids brushes, tempera, or acrylic paints and let them create!

The Starship program represents the culmination of SpaceX's iterative "fail fast, learn faster" philosophy: Early Iterations: Development began with small, low-altitude "hops" using the Starhopper prototype in 2019, followed by high-altitude test flights of various "SN" (Serial Number) vehicles. The Integrated Flight Era: Starting with the first fully integrated launch in April 2023, SpaceX began testing the combination of the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage. description: This remix uses the original launch mechanism and adapts it for mounting on a PVC base. If you have zipper wax or another suitable lubricant, applying a small amount to both the PVC pipe and the printed part can make assembly and operation smoother. I have not tested the design without the heat-gun-created bulge. However, if your fit is tight enough, it may work with only the O-rings. Alternatively, a small dab of super glue on the PVC just below the first O-ring (or before installing the gripper arms) may help keep everything securely in place.

This Montessori-inspired matching game encourages children to develop observation, concentration, logical thinking, visual memory, and fine motor skills through play. The game consists of 16 double-sided sliding tokens , each connected by a small axle: 🍎 One side displays colorful fruits ⭐ The opposite side displays geometric symbols The tokens slide into the four rails of the base, allowing children to create a 4 × 4 grid . For a stronger assembly, place a small drop of glue inside each circular token before inserting the axle. description: This is a 3D printed marble coaster track inspired by an elementary school science project about roller coasters. The original classroom activity was designed to help children observe marble movement, track design, and speed changes, so I turned the idea into a real working tabletop model. It can help children explore questions such as: Why does the marble roll from a higher place to a lower place? How does the slope affect the marble’s speed? How do curves and tunnel sections change the marble’s movement? How can the track be adjusted to make the marble move more smoothly and steadily? The model uses a segmented track structure, making it easier to understand the function of each section and observe how the marble behaves thr oughout the track. description: This Rubber Band Powered Helicopter is a simple, fully 3D-printed flying model with no tail boom, no gears, no electronics, and no extra hardware. Just two contra-rotating rotors and a rubber band between them—that is the whole idea. Wind the rotors, store energy in the band, and let go. The top and bottom rotors spin in opposite directions, canceling torque so the body stays stable without a tail rotor. Lift comes from the combined action of both rotors working together. The design is intentionally minimal. Print the parts, add one rubber band, and you are ready to fly. No screws, bearings, motors, or purchased kit parts are required. ------------ A rubber band runs directly between the upper and lower rotors. There are no gears—the band connects the two rotors and does all the work. When you wind the model, the band twists and stores elastic energy. On release, the band unwinds and drives both rotors at the same time—but in opposite directions. Because the rotors turn against each other, their reaction torques cancel out. That is why this helicopter does not need a tail boom or tail rotor. The contra-rotating setup does the job in a clean, compact way. Everything you need is printed in plastic except the rubber band. The fuselage holds the two rotors in alignment and gives you something to grip while winding. ------------- - A 3D printer and filament - One rubber band - One drop of glue That is it. No other parts to buy or hunt for. --------------------- I printed mine on a Bambu Lab A1 mini using PLA. Keep prints light where you can; less weight means better lift from the same rubber band. Use a drop of glue to secure the hook to the upper rotor from the top.

description: 这是一款机械日地月运行轨道仪，它通过精密的齿轮传动系统，生动模拟了太阳、地球与月球三者之间的运行轨迹和相对位置关系。 这款仪器不仅是一件精美的机械模型，更是一个直观的天文教学工具。它通过手摇曲柄驱动内部齿轮组，带动地球模型绕太阳公转，同时月球模型绕地球公转，完美再现了天体运行的基本规律。其核心设计在于通过不同齿数的齿轮组合，精确还原了地球公转与月球公转的周期比例，使演示过程既科学又富有观赏性。 仪器的中心是一个金色的太阳模型，周围环绕着标有“一月”至“十二月”的刻度盘，用于指示地球在公转轨道上的位置，从而帮助理解四季更替。月球模型则通过一个独立的臂架连接在地球模型上，随着地球一起绕太阳运动，同时自身也在绕地球旋转。 这类仪器的历史可以追溯到18世纪的“七政仪”（orrery），最初用于演示太阳系行星运动。现代版本的三球仪则更专注于日、地、月三者关系，广泛应用于中小学教学、科技馆展览以及天文爱好者收藏。它不仅能演示地球的自转与公转、月球的公转，还能形象地展示日食、月食、月相变化等天文现象，是理解基础天文学概念的绝佳辅助工具。

description: I've printed the SMARS tracked rover to see if I can adapt to use an ESP32-WROVER-CAM Dev.B microcontroller which has a built-in 2Mpx camera so I can turn it into a tracked mobile, WiFi controlled webcam. Although the ESP32-WROVER-CAM has enough GPIOs to use with the L298N dual motor driver, when the webcam is turned on in the sketch along with the WiFi, there are only 4 usable GPIOs remaining. Luckily, I found that it should be possible to use just the 4 GPIOs to control the two motors, but it also requires that the L298N EN-A and EN-B pins be raised to +5V. If you discarded the two jumpers that usually come with the L298N, then use two DuPont wires to connect the two enable pins on the driver to +5V. The print profile available for the BambuLab A1 Mini worked perfectly although I cannot use the IR sensor mount since the chassis is fully occupied by the L298N and the 2S1P 18650 pack with switch and voltmeter, but more importantly, there are no more GPIOs left to use the IR sensor. As you can see from the photo I took of the result is not very good looking but it does move quite nicely. I have two 100rpm DC motors which give it a decent scurry speed. The code I can share upon request if anyone wants to give it a go. Kinetic Galton Board A kinetic Galton board that demonstrates the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution instead of the usual Gaussian you get from a classic bead-and-peg Galton board. It went semi-viral on Instagram (4M+ views), so I'm publishing the files here for anyone who wants to build one. Watch it run: https://www.instagram.com/p/DZauWk2SiXA/ How it works There are two chambers, left and right. The left chamber holds about 400 balls resting on a slider above a fast-spinning cylinder fitted with two fins. The fins agitate the balls and inject energy into the system. The balls collide with each other and with the chamber walls, behaving like gas particles in a box. At the top-right corner of the left chamber there is a small hole, roughly one ball wide. A ball only escapes (effuses) through this hole when it arrives with the right velocity. On the right side there are about 14 bins. The bin dividers are slightly shorter than the height of the escape hole, so a ball that effuses has to fall a small distance before reaching the tops of the bins. The physics is the interesting part: Because the hole is about the size of a single ball, a ball leaving it has essentially no vertical velocity at the moment of escape. So the time it takes to fall the small gap to the bins is the same for every ball . With d = v·t and t constant, the horizontal distance a ball travels (and therefore the bin it lands in) is proportional to its speed at the moment of effusion . Read the bin, and you've effectively measured how fast that ball was moving when it escaped. Do this for all ~400 balls, which have been colliding and exchanging energy like gas molecules, and the bins fill in to trace out the signature Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution . Printing There are two versions depending on what motor you have. Version for CIM (FRC) I built mine around an FRC CIM motor , just because I had some lying around. They're big and frankly overkill for this, but a lot of FRC people have them on hand. If that's you, open the Version for CIM folder and print the STL files there. Version for 775 For everyone else, the most common suitable motor is a 775 . They're cheap and easy to get almost anywhere. Open the Version for 775 folder and print the parts there. Both folders also include the raw STEP files if you want to modify anything. Cover The cover on mine is laser-cut acrylic . If you don't have a laser cutter, there's an STL so you can print it instead out of a transparent material, it just won't be as clear as acrylic. If you want to chase clarity, look up guides on printing crystal-clear PETG, though I didn't have much luck with it myself. Balls You need about 400–600 balls . They are 4 mm diameter , so do not substitute airsoft BBs, those don't work. To save you from duplicating a ball 400 times in your slicer, there's a 20×20 grid of them included. A few notes: Add a brim when printing the grid, otherwise the balls pop off the build plate. The sliced result should look like this: After printing you'll have a sheet with all the balls attached to it. Don't try to pull them off by hand , you'll tear the sheet and it becomes a miserable job getting the sheet off the balls. Instead, use pliers and twist each ball off the sheet. It's tedious, but it works. 400 balls took me about 20 minutes. Assembly and operation You will need 1x 775 motor, 2x M4x8 bolts, 4x M3x8 bolts Assembly is straightforward Place the balls into the device. Insert the slider. Shake the balls into the left chamber. Important: Use the slider to drop the balls onto the agitator while it is already spinning . If the balls surround a stationary agitator and you try to spin it up, it will stall the motor and the whole thing jams. That's it, spin it up and watch the distribution build.

：专业天文教学、初高中地理课堂演示、天文科普研学、天体运动原理实操学习 核心特性说明 ： 本设备为纯手动机械模型，无电机及自动控制，所有运动均需人工操作。 无独立月球自转轴，遵循潮汐锁定原理——月球公转一周的同时自身无相对转动，始终以同一面朝向地球。 设有 地轴岁差旋进轴 （第二轴），用于初始校准或演示地轴长期进动（岁差）。 在常规四季、极昼极夜、昼夜长短等演示中，地轴指向应保持固定不变 ，仅通过地球公转自然呈现全部现象。 精准还原黄赤交角（23.5°）、黄白交角（5°09′），可演示晨昏线、昼夜长短变化、太阳直射点移动、四季更替、极昼极夜、月相、日食与月食等专业天文现象。 目录 产品核心结构与四轴原理说明 专业轨道、天体倾角与模型物理参数（含缩放说明） 整机部件详细说明 首次操作与天文基准手动归位 基础天体运动演示（晨昏线、昼夜长短、直射点移动） 进阶专业天文现象演示（极昼/极夜） 月相、日食、月食完整演示（结合黄白交角） 标准操作注意事项 常见故障与原理答疑 1. 产品核心结构与四轴原理说明 1.1 四大核心轴体功能 轴序 名称 功能说明 第一轴 地球自转轴 控制地球绕自身倾斜轴（23.5°）自西向东旋转，模拟昼夜交替与晨昏线移动，可手动调节转速。 第二轴 地轴岁差旋进轴 用于 初始校准时调整地轴空间指向 ，或演示地轴长期进动（岁差，周期约26000年）。 常规四季、极昼极夜等演示中必须锁定此轴 ，保持地轴指向固定不变。 第三轴 地球公转轴 控制地球整体沿黄道面绕太阳公转，模拟一年轨道运动，配合固定地轴指向呈现四季更替与直射点移动。 第四轴 月球公转轴 控制月球沿白道面绕地球公转，无独立自转。公转时固定面指向地心，还原潮汐锁定。 1.2 月球潮汐锁定原理（设计依据） 真实月球自转周期与绕地公转周期完全同步（27.3天），因此永远以同一面朝向地球。本设备不设月球自转轴，公转时月面固定指向地心，精准复刻真实天体状态。 2. 专业轨道、天体倾角与模型物理参数 2.1 核心夹角参数 黄赤交角（地轴倾角） ：23.5°，固定不变。是四季、极昼极夜、昼夜长短变化的根本原因。 黄白交角 ：黄道面（地球公转轨道面）与白道面（月球公转轨道面）的夹角为 5°09′ 。本设备通过倾斜的月球公转副臂（或轨道支撑结构）机械实现该夹角，与月球是否具备自转轴无关。 月球自转轴倾角（约1.5°）因设备无月球自转，不涉及演示。 2.2 两大轨道平面 黄道面 ：地球公转轨道平面。 白道面 ：月球公转轨道平面，与黄道面成5°09′。 2.3 模型实物尺寸与间距（桌面适配差异化缩放） 部件 直径 / 间距 太阳模型 36 mm 地球模型 80 mm 月球模型 21 mm 地日中心距 200 mm 地月中心距 120 mm 缩放说明 ： 真实日地直径比约109:1，距离比约11700:1。若在桌面模型上同时保真直径与距离比例，模型将庞大到无法用于教学。因此本设备采用科学差异化缩放： 太阳模型取较小直径（36mm）以避免遮挡光源并保证光照均匀性； 地球模型适当放大（80mm）以便清晰展示表面标注（赤道、回归线、极圈等）； 地轴倾角、黄白交角、光照几何、公转与自转相对运动关系均严格保真 ，所有天文现象的演示原理（四季、极昼极夜、月相、日月食）完全不受影响。 ✅ 该缩放方式属于专业天文教学模型的常规设计，并非科学错误。 3. 整机部件详细说明 部件名称 功能说明 太阳光源模型 模拟平行太阳光，恒定发光。光源规格及供电方式可自行适配。 地球模型（带固定地轴） 内置23.5°固定倾角地轴，表面标注赤道、回归线、极圈。支持自转及公转。 月球模型（潮汐锁定） 无自转，公转时固定面指向地心，沿白道面绕地运行。 地轴岁差旋进调节旋钮 用于初始校准地轴指向或演示岁差。 常规演示中应保持锁定 ，不得用于模拟四季更替。 地球公转主臂 带动地球沿黄道面绕日公转，配合刻度底座显示节气位置。 月球公转副臂 带动月球沿白道面绕地公转， 内置5°09′黄白交角结构 。 刻度底座 标注黄道轨道、二分二至点、四季位置，辅助定位。 电源开关 控制太阳光源启停，可按需适配。 4. 首次操作与天文基准手动归位 本设备为纯手动模型，无自动运行功能。所有位置调节均需人工操作。 基准归位目的 ：设定统一的初始状态，确保后续演示符合天文原理。 手动归位步骤 （纯人工对位）： 将地球公转主臂转至底座 春分刻度 位置。 调节地轴岁差旋进轴，使地轴指向与底座上的“北极指向标记”对齐（若无标记，可设定地轴倾斜方向垂直于日地连线，且北极指向远离太阳的一侧——此为春分标准指向）。 锁定地轴岁差旋进轴 ，后续演示中不再转动。 将月球公转臂转至 朔点（日地之间） 基准位置。 目视检查黄道面、白道面倾角无偏移，完成归位。 核心原则 ：除岁差演示或初始校准外，地轴指向一旦设定，在整个公转演示中必须保持固定。四季、极昼极夜等现象完全由地球公转自动产生，无需手动改变地轴朝向。 5. 基础天体运动演示操作 5.1 昼夜交替与晨昏线 开启光源，匀速转动 地球自转轴 （自西向东）。 面向光源为 昼半球 ，背向为 夜半球 ，明暗交界线为 晨昏圈 。 顺着自转方向，由夜入昼为 晨线 ，由昼入夜为 昏线 。 可观察：晨昏线始终与太阳光线垂直，赤道全年昼夜等长。固定地球转角可展示同一时刻全球昼夜分布。 5.2 太阳直射点周年移动 保持地轴指向固定 （已锁定岁差旋进轴），缓慢转动 地球公转主臂 。 公转过程中，由于地轴倾角固定，太阳直射点会在南北回归线之间移动： 夏至（公转至夏至刻度）直射北回归线 冬至直射南回归线 春分/秋分直射赤道 5.3 四季更替演示（正确方法） 前提 ：地轴指向已锁定，不再调节。 按顺序公转至四个节气刻度，观察光照情况： 节气 公转位置 太阳直射点 北半球季节 南半球季节 春分 春分点 赤道 春季 秋季 夏至 夏至点 北回归线 夏季 冬季 秋分 秋分点 赤道 秋季 春季 冬至 冬至点 南回归线 冬季 夏季 注意 ：演示时 不要 转动地轴岁差旋进旋钮，否则会错误地认为四季需要手动调节地轴指向。 5.4 全球昼夜长短差异 在公转不同位置，观察不同纬度的昼夜长度： 夏至 ：北半球昼长夜短，北极圈极昼；南半球相反。 冬至 ：北半球昼短夜长，北极圈极夜；南半球相反。 春分/秋分 ：全球昼夜平分。 5.5 地球五带划分 通过光照范围与直射点移动，演示热带（南北回归线间）、温带（回归线至极圈）、寒带（极圈以内）的划分。 6. 进阶专业天文现象演示（极昼/极夜） 正确演示前提 ：地轴指向固定（已锁定岁差旋进轴），仅通过公转改变地球在轨道上的位置。 6.1 夏至日北极极昼、南极极夜 开启光源，公转主臂转至 夏至刻度 。 保持地轴指向不变（春分时设定的指向），此时地轴北极自然倾向太阳。 观察晨昏线与北极圈相切，北极圈内全为白昼（极昼），南极圈内全为黑夜（极夜）。 转动地球自转轴，极昼/极夜区域不改变。 6.2 冬至日南极极昼、北极极夜 公转主臂转至 冬至刻度 。 地轴指向仍为初始设定，此时地轴南极倾向太阳。 晨昏线与南极圈相切，南极圈内极昼，北极圈内极夜。 6.3 春分、秋分无极昼极夜 公转至春分或秋分刻度，太阳直射赤道，晨昏线过两极，全球昼夜等长，无极昼极夜。 6.4 极昼极夜范围渐变演示 缓慢连续转动公转主臂，观察极昼/极夜范围从极点逐步扩大至极圈，再逐步缩小的动态过程，完整还原全年变化。 7. 月相、日食、月食完整演示（结合黄白交角） 7.1 月相周期演示 开启光源，手动转动 月球公转轴 ，月球沿白道面公转。观察月球被照亮部分的形状变化： 新月（朔）→娥眉月→上弦月→盈凸月→满月（望）→亏凸月→下弦月→残月→新月。 （因潮汐锁定，月球同一面始终朝向地球，但被照亮区域随公转位置变化。） 7.2 日食演示（朔日限定） 将月球转至 日—地之间（朔点） ，并微调月球公转角度以抵消黄白交角偏差，使日、月、地三者近似共线。此时月球影子落在地球上，可演示日全食/日偏食效果。 解释 ：因黄白交角存在，多数朔日不共线，故日食罕见。 7.3 月食演示（望日限定） 将月球转至 日—地延长线（望点） ，微调角度使日、地、月共线，地球阴影覆盖月球，演示月食。同理，并非每望日都发生。 8. 标准操作注意事项 四轴结构精密，转动需轻柔匀速，禁止暴力操作。 常规演示中地轴岁差旋进轴应保持锁定 ，仅当演示岁差或初始校准时方可调节。 演示晨昏线、极昼极夜、日月食时，建议在暗光环境下进行。 可根据需要自主适配光源亮度与供电方式。 设备为精密模型，禁止摔落、撞击、浸泡；儿童操作需成人陪同。 禁止私自拆卸轴体，以免四轴联动精度失效。 9. 常见故障与原理答疑 Q1：为什么月球不会自转？是否为缺陷？ A：不是缺陷。真实月球为潮汐锁定，自转与公转周期相同，永远同一面朝地。本设备科学还原该特性。 Q2：为什么演示四季时不需要转动地轴岁差旋进旋钮？ A：真实地球公转中，地轴在空间中的指向保持恒定（指向北极星附近）。四季更替完全由公转位置改变太阳直射点而产生。若在公转中手动旋转地轴，将得到错误原理。本设备的地轴岁差旋进轴仅用于初始校准或演示岁差。 Q3：为什么太阳模型比地球小？ A：这是为了桌面教学的可行性而进行的工程缩放。真实比例无法在桌面模型中实现，本设备牺牲尺寸比例但保留了所有角度、光照几何和相对运动关系，不影响任何天文现象的教学。 Q4：黄白交角5°09′是如何实现的？月球没有自转轴会影响吗？ A：黄白交角是月球公转轨道面（白道面）与地球公转轨道面（黄道面）的夹角，通过倾斜的月球公转副臂机械实现，与月球是否自转无关。本设备正确保留该夹角，用于演示日月食发生条件。 Q5：为什么无法每次朔望日都演示日月食？ A：设备精准还原了5°09′黄白交角，多数朔望日三者不共线，与现实一致，非故障。 Q6：极昼极夜、晨昏线演示效果不明显怎么办？ A：检查公转位置是否准确对应节气刻度，并确认地轴指向已锁定且倾角无误（未误触岁差旋钮）。重新按第4章归位即可。 Q7：晨昏线为什么不会和经线完全重合？ A：仅春分、秋分两天太阳直射赤道，晨昏线与经线重合；其余时间因地轴倾角，晨昏线与经线存在夹角，本设备可完整呈现该变化。

description: A Rattleback is a physics toy that seems magic/impossible: spin it one way and it spins normally, spin it the other way and it starts to wobble, stops, then reverses direction by itself. It’s a small print that makes for a great physics demo, desk toy or "magic trick" to show friends. I couldn't find a good Rattleback online, I tested them all and I was disappointed on how poorly they reversed (bad shape) and how much sanding and tuning they required to make them work (bad printing orientation). So I decided to do some research to create the best 3D printed Rattleback possible: strong self-reversing effect and ready to use straight off the printer This GOENGINEER article gave me the hope that a better Rattleback shape was possible. So, I designed my own model and did many SOLIDWORKS motion studies and real life tests until I couldn't improve the reversing effect anymore: this way I found the BEST SHAPE which, in my tests, achieves up to ~3 full 360° spins in the reverse direction ! I designed my model to be printed on its side, this orientation makes the curved surface come out smooth straight off the printer with minimal to no sanding required. When laid on the side, it has a big enough first layer and not too steep overhangs. (all other models I found online were designed to be printed flat, which creates layer steps you need to sand... a lot of work that's easy to get wrong) Tips for Maximum Self-Reversing Effect Make sure the curved Rattleback contact surface is perfectly smooth, if not, remove any imperfection with a cutter or by light sanding . The print orientation helps a lot but can't guarantee 100% smoothness for everyone, printing defects can still occur. Those strongly depend on YOUR setup (filament,drying,plate,calibration,printer, etc...). Common defects that will ruin the effect: Blobs and Zits, Ringing, Warping, Layer Separation, etc. Spin it on a hard, smooth surface: glass, hard plastic or wood. Too much or too little friction can reduce the effect, or even stop it from working, so, try many different surfaces. A dusty surface can ruin the effect too. Use PLA or PLA+ . Additives can ruin or weaken the effect due to different friction. Matte, Carbon Fiber, Silk filaments might not work. Self-reverses only when spun counterclockwise, I chose this direction on purpose: tell your friend to inspect and spin the rattleback, 90% of people are right handed and will spin it clockwise instinctively and notice nothing strange. Then you can spin it counterclockwise to make your friend believe it's magic, this trick will work most of the time and leave your friend flabbergasted A Rattleback is a real object, using a real physics effect, it really reverses direction, do a simple research to find out how and why it works. If your 3D printed rattleback doesn't work , it's simply and only cause YOU didn't follow the tips above , it otherwise works as shown in my video and the thousands of videos you can find all over the Internet.

description: 🦌 Lifesize Muntjac Deer Skull This model is based on a real muntjac deer skull collected from the English countryside and reproduced at 1:1 lifesize scale , preserving the proportions, teeth and character of the original specimen. 📏 Size At full scale, the model measures: Skull length: 170 mm / 6.69 in — from the tip of the snout to the back of the skull Total length: 245 mm / 9.65 in — including the antlers/pedicles This is a true lifesize model , based directly on the dimensions of the original skull. About the Muntjac Muntjac are small and rather unusual deer originally native to Asia. Reeves's muntjac ( Muntiacus reevesi ) became established in Britain following introductions and escapes from captivity and are now widespread across much of England. They are classed as an invasive non-native species in Great Britain . They're fascinating little animals. Males have short antlers growing from unusually long pedicles , along with prominent upper canine teeth or “tusks.” They also possess distinctive facial scent glands. Muntjac are sometimes known as “barking deer” thanks to their loud, repetitive alarm calls, which can sound surprisingly dog-like when heard in British woodland. 🖨️ Printing Despite the intricate appearance of the skull, this is a fairly approachable project and should be suitable for a relative newcomer to 3D printing . The trickiest area is between and around the teeth , where support is required and can be a little fiddly to remove. Take your time during support removal, particularly around the thinner teeth and more delicate sections of bone. Apart from this, it's a relatively straightforward and very satisfying skull to print. Segel: Ein einzelner Mast trägt ein rechteckiges, dunkelrotes Segel mit dem goldenen Schriftzug SPQR , umgeben von einem Lorbeerkranz – dem bekannten Symbol des Römischen Reiches. Ruder: Auf jeder Seite befinden sich mehrere lange Ruder, mit denen das Schiff unabhängig vom Wind bewegt werden konnte. Die roten Ruderblätter setzen einen schönen farblichen Akzent. Deck: Das Deck ist offen und schlicht gehalten. Auf überflüssige Aufbauten wurde verzichtet, wodurch das Modell sauber und übersichtlich wirkt. Farben: Natürliche Holztöne werden mit kräftigem Rot und goldenen Verzierungen kombiniert – eine klassische Farbgebung, die sofort an die römische Legion erinnert. Für den 3D-Druck: Dieses Design ist besonders druckfreundlich, weil: nur wenige filigrane Details vorhanden sind, die Formen klar und stabil aufgebaut sind, Mast, Segel und Ruder ausreichend kräftig ausgeführt werden können, das Modell leicht in einem Stück gedruckt werden kann. Das Ergebnis ist ein stilisiertes römisches Kriegsschiff, das den historischen Charakter bewahrt und gleichzeitig optimal für den FDM-3D-Druck geeignet ist.

Meet one of the largest and most impressive predators to live before the dinosaurs. Inostrancevia alexandri was a huge carnivorous gorgonopsid that lived in what is now northern European Russia during the Late Permian, shortly before the greatest mass extinction in Earth’s history. With its long skull, powerful jaws and enormous sabre-like canine teeth, it was one of the dominant predators of its ecosystem. Although it is sometimes described as a “mammal-like reptile”, Inostrancevia was actually a non-mammalian synapsid . This means it belonged to the evolutionary branch that later produced mammals and was more closely related to mammals than it was to dinosaurs, crocodiles or lizards. The printed skull measures approximately 250 mm long . Adult Inostrancevia alexandri skulls are generally reconstructed at around 500–510 mm long , making this model approximately half-scale . A full-sized skull would therefore be roughly twice the length of this print, while the complete animal may have measured around 3 metres from nose to tail . How is it related to other gorgonopsids? Gorgonopsids were a diverse group of sabre-toothed predatory therapsids rather than a single type of animal. They ranged from relatively small hunters to enormous apex predators such as Inostrancevia and Rubidgea . Inostrancevia belonged to the inostranceviine branch of the gorgonopsid family tree and was part of a group containing several primarily Russian genera, including Pravoslavlevia , Sauroctonus and Suchogorgon . Its closest relatives were other species of Inostrancevia , with Pravoslavlevia generally regarded as one of its nearest related genera. The similarly massive South African Rubidgea was still a gorgonopsid cousin, but it belonged to the separate rubidgeine branch . They filled similar apex-predator roles, but were not simply different species of the same animal. This model makes an imposing addition to any collection of Permian animals, prehistoric predators, fossil replicas or unusual skulls. The Basics: This print is a Ranque-Hilsch Vortex Tube (RHVT) cooler or Maxwell Demon's tube, a remarkably simple device that mysteriously separates compressed air into hot and cold streams without any moving parts or electricity. The physics of this phenomena have been a long-running subject of scientific investigation and remain unsettled to this day. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortex_tube Default Print Setup: 0.2mm nozzle preferred for flow dynamics and accurate threads All tolerances are setup for Bambu Labs PETG Basic The Minutia: The design being shared is modular to allow interchanging of internal components for optimal nozzle, vortex and tube diameter geometries. Various vortex generator nozzles and hot pipe divergers with part numbers are included for the user to experiment with. Recommended starting configuration is: Vortex Generator: RF1006-00D-0909 Hot Tube Diverger: RF10-15D Hot Tube Throttle Valve: Close fully and unscrew ~ 3.5x turns Once assembled per the diagram below, simply inject compressed air via the ¼" NPT inlet and appreciate the almost instantaneous separation of hot and cold air from the ends of the device. Feel free to experiment with the included generators, divergers and throttle valve settings to optimise cold vs. hot air fraction for a given inlet air pressure. Notes: Vortex Generators and Hot Tube Divergers are denoted with LF and RF to indicate “low flow” and “regular flow” and are intended to be paired together. RHVT's are capable of generating extremely hot and cold temperatures (-50 ° C to 200 ° C) far beyond the capability of regularly used materials so brittle and melting failures are quite possible depending on how you configure the device and the duration of use. Due to the many factors affecting print strength, it is left to the end user to assess what air pressure can be safely used without compromising the device. I have routinely used pressures up to 60psi on PETG Basic without any failure.

A simple gear set I created for a maker day event at the library. I would have preferred to just use something that was already out there, but as is typical for me, I began to want certain features / tweaks, so I just made my own. These were modeled in TinkerCAD using the gear generator shape. I wanted: something small and simple and lite for kids a grid / board that supports a large number of combinations of gear connections a way to drive the gears without turning them by hand an indicator for direction they were turning Ended up with: 5mm spaced grid board Works with 10T, 12T, 18T, 20T, 21T, 24T, 30T, 31T, 40T gears (most perfectly, some combinations have a tiny spacing error) Small hole direction indicator Handle / driver PDF activity for kids (8+) I initially didn't want to use pegs and fully open pegboard holes because I wanted the gears to be standard with hole in the center and no attached peg. So I initially started with a true board of pegs for gears to slip onto, but then realized I would be very limited with gear placement without some deep hubs on the gears to clear the peg heights. So then I moved onto a design with gears that slotted onto removeable pegs with separate c-clips to keep them on (like @osamutake models). The pegs screwed into slots on the board and then c-clips locked the gears onto them. This worked, but then I realized it wasn't so simple for kids, and the print resolution would have to be very fine to ensure threads were clean and c-clips were strong enough for kids to not break them. Kids screwing pegs in and out of the board and snapping c-clips into place, especially if the prints weren't perfectly clean, was going to be a problem.. So finally I reluctantly accepted a pluggable gears design into a holed pegboard as posted (similar to design by @Ioannis Tsar). The grid spacing evolved from 10mm to 5mm to support more gears. Also evolved from a hexagonal shape to conserve space and keep diagonal distances equilateral, but then the 5mm hypotenuses worked even with small spacing errors, so kept the grid shape for simplicity. The handle didn't work great and could be redesigned. This was my 3rd design, but still not driving the gears as well as hoped. Could definitely benefit from redesign. I had to print about 100 pieces of everything (sans 40T gears), so needed fast prints. Profile defaults to Random seam so seam is less of a hurdle. A grid bound at 0% sparse infill, draft 0.24mm layer print worked fine for me for my event. Gears were printed with 10% infill. A few posts snapped if kids were rough, so consider higher infill for longer lasting model. Sanding posts definitely helps but is time consuming. I would only recommend if you wanted to keep the kit around for a long time. If it's a one-off event, the gears work fine once snapped in and turned a bit.

Bring one of the most unusual dinosaur hands into your fossil collection with this detailed Iguanodon hand replica , based on the specimen displayed at the Natural History Museum in London . The finished hand measures approximately 250 mm from the wrist to the tip of the longest finger . Comparing it with published measurements and illustrations of adult Iguanodon hands, this model is estimated to be around 65–70% scale , or roughly two-thirds life-size . As individual dinosaurs varied in size, this percentage should be considered an approximate estimate. Iguanodon had one of the most specialised hands of any dinosaur. Its famous pointed thumb spike may have been used for defence or handling tough vegetation, while the three central fingers formed a strong weight-bearing structure. The smaller outer finger was more flexible and may have helped the animal grasp or manipulate plants. The hand is presented in a fossil-style arrangement and comes with a separate removable display stand , allowing it to be displayed upright while still being easily removed for closer examination. This is an easy and enjoyable print , with straightforward supports and easy support removal. It makes an impressive display piece for dinosaur fans, fossil collectors, classrooms, museums or anyone interested in prehistoric anatomy. Model Details Approximately 250 mm long from wrist to fingertip Estimated at approximately 65–70% of adult size Based on the Iguanodon hand displayed at the Natural History Museum in London Includes a separate removable display stand Detailed fossil-style surface Easy print Easy support removal Simple cleanup and assembly Suitable for beginners No glue required between the hand and stand Printing Information The hand requires supports, but they have been arranged to be relatively simple to remove. Take a little extra care around the fingers and thumb spike, as these are naturally the narrowest parts of the model. The display stand prints separately and the hand simply rests securely in position, allowing it to be removed whenever required. Standard PLA settings should work well. A smaller layer height can be used to preserve more of the fossil texture, although the model should also print well using normal-quality settings.
