INFO These are magnetic separation racks for 0.2mL PCR sized tubes. Works for SPRI, ConA, or any magnetic beads. My lab is a big fan of the epicypher racks but they cost $500 dollars so we were always fighting over the one, and even then when you have more than 8 or 16 samples it is inconvenient to always switch out tubes while doing high through put experiments. I wanted more racks so I designed these with a similar style and functionality to the epicypher racks with some added improvements. 1.Racks come in 8-tube and 12-tube sizes so you can make full use of the multichannel and scale up easier 2.Magnets are removable, so you can simply slide the magnet out rather than removing the tubes from the rack 3.The magnet can be turned around to work better for either small or large volumes. 4. Less than 1% of the price of Epicypher magnet racks (even with the cost of magnets) BEFORE YOU PRINT While smooth, semi-textured, and textured plates all work, I find that printing on a textured plate results in a tighter fit of the magnet holders inside the rack. I prefer the slightly looser fit I get when printing on my BIQU cool plate. If you use my print profile then you don't need any supports, however, these are kind of tall prints so I recommend making sure you have a clean bed and dried filament to avoid any adhesion errors. If you are having adhesion problems then you can take it a step farther and use a cool plate and/or a brim. ASSEMBLY You will need 10x5x3mm magnets. One 8 tube rack takes 16 magnets and one 12 tube rack takes 24 magnets. After printing, glue the two halves of the magnet holder together with the magnet holes in the same orientation. Then, insert the magnets. While they have a snug press fit, I find that they stay in better if the magnets on either side of the holder have opposite poles facing each other (the orientation where they stick together). A dab of super glue doesn't hurt either.

Die Platte 4 enthält einen Ständer mit Fläche für ein Schild (Siehe in der pdf), die Platte 5 ein Ständer ohne Fläche für ein Schild. - nach meiner Farbkodierung ist: weiß die Antriebswelle, schwarz der Abtrieb von Planetenträger, grau das Gehäuse, rot die Zahnräder, grün die Lager und gelb der Stopfen bzw. die Schrauben - ich habe folgendes geklebt: die Stifte in das Gehäuse, den Stopfen in das Gehäuse, die inneren Lager, direkt am Gehäuse - die Deckel können auf das Gehäuse geklebt werden, dann kann das Getriebe jedoch nicht mehr auseinandergenommen werden. Damit das Getriebe trotzdem zusammenhält ist die Klammer da. Diese kann von unten auf das komplette Gehäuse geschoben werden - die Kleinen Lager gehen lassen sich nur sehr schwer in die Zahnräder pressen. Dafür diese vorsichtig mit etwas diese in die Zahnräder schlagen, bis die Lager deutlich unter der Kante des Zahnrades sind - der Deckel vom Planetenträger hat extra eine Aussparung, sodass man ein Zahnrad sieht. Die „Schrauben“, welche Wirklichkeit nur Stifte sind, gingen bei mir sehr schwer. Wenn ihr das Getriebe wieder gut aufmachen können wollt, diese am besten ein wenig kleiner Skalieren und evtl. an den Deckel vom Planetenträger kleben - das angehängte pdf enthält die Beschriftung (52mmx22mm), ich habe dies auf Papier (DIN A4) ausgedruckt, welches man als Aufkleber verwenden kann. Es lässt sich aber auch mit normalem Papier ausdrucken und aufkleben - das ganze Getriebe mit Gestell braucht ca. 130g Filament - ich habe für die Stützen unter dem Gehäuse ein paar Schichten Support for PLA verwendet. Wenn kein Support for PLA Filament vorhanden ist dies einfach zu PETG ändern. Das funktioniert genauso. (Wenn das Getriebe aus PETG gedruckt wird dann zu PLA wechseln) Daher kommen auch ein paar wenige Filamentwechsel. Wer dies möchte einfach das Profil normale Stützen drucken. Ich habe insgesamt 5 Modelle gedruckt bis das Getriebe die finale Version hattte. Viel Spaß damit! english version: This gearbox is part of a project from the “Design Engineering IV” course in our degree program. I developed the gear together with @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas and two other colleagues. We submitted this in addition to our term paper and are incredibly proud of it. It’s a wonderful demonstration model that has been further optimized beyond the original version we submitted. Here’s the key information about the gearbox: - The planetary gearbox is part of a press’s drive train. Surrounding the gearbox is a significantly larger flywheel, as well as a clutch. - I printed the gearbox entirely out of PLA; I don’t know how it would behave with other materials. - I used a Bambulab P1S and selected very fine settings. I’m not sure if that was necessary. In any case, the result is definitely impressive. - I wouldn’t scale the gearbox, as doing so would proportionally increase the distances between the bearings and the shaft, which are designed to be precisely matched. - To build a complete gearbox, you need to print plates 1–3 and either 4 or 5. Plate 4 includes a support with space for a label (see the PDF); plate 5 includes a support without space for a label. - According to my color coding: white is the drive shaft, black is the output shaft of the planetary carrier, gray is the housing, red is the gears, green is the bearings, and yellow is the plugs or screws - I glued the following parts in place: the pins into the housing, the plug into the housing, and the inner bearings directly to the housing - The covers can be glued to the housing, but then the gearbox can no longer be taken apart. The clip is there to keep the gearbox together anyway. It can be slid onto the entire housing from below - The small bearings are very difficult to press into the gears. To do this, gently tap them into the gears with a small tool until the bearings are clearly below the edge of the gear. - The cover of the planetary carrier has a special cutout so you can see a gear. The “screws”—which are actually just pins—were very difficult for me to insert. If you want to be able to open the gearbox easily again, it’s best to scale these down slightly and possibly glue them to the cover of the planetary carrier - The attached PDF contains the label (52mm x 22mm); I printed this on paper (DIN A4), which can be used as a sticker. However, you can also print them on regular paper and stick them on. - The entire gearbox with the frame requires about 130g of filament. - I used the Super Cool Track Pro plate for the housing and the Textured PEI Plate for the rest. That’s how it’s set up. If you use different plates, be sure to take this into account! - I used a few layers of “Support for PLA” for the supports under the housing. If you don't have “Support for PLA” filament, simply switch to PETG. It works just the same. (If the gearbox is printed in PETG, switch to PLA.) That's why there are a few filament changes. If you don't want those, just change the support settings in the slicer back to normal supports. I printed a total of 5 models before the gearbox reached its final version. Have fun with it!

I wanted to electroplate my models and investigated online for suiting models. Found none that I was happy with. So I decided to design and build my own. The design consists of three main parts: 1) the motor assembly 2) the controlbox 3) the arc bridge assembly The motor assembly is designed so it can easily be fitted on different sized arc bridges, because not all containers have the same width/height requirements. I will share the dimensions of the current container i used, orderable off amazon. If you have another container, I will share the SCAD file as well, so you can easily adapt the width to your needs. Keep in mind that the min dia is always the width of the motormount plate and standoffs to the side of the container. The motor assembly itself houses the stepper (28BYJ-48) and the ULN2003 motor driver board. The controlbox has a couple of easy to acquire and solder components: an ESP32 board (i used a SEED XIAO ESP32-C6, very small board), a LM2596 buck converter, a rotary encoder (KY-040) to control the speed, a battery and an on/off switch. I will share the scheme here as well. The ESP firmware will also be shared (rename the main.c.txt to main.c) IMPORTANT NOTE; make sure to trim your buck convertor to 5v before connecting anything to it, otherwise it may be set too high and you will fry your electronics The arc bridge is pretty straightforward; it clamps on to the side of the container (dont overdo it, just keeps it from moving around) and comes with a nut to secure the motor assembly in place. I also designed a model hook that allows a straight copper wire down into the bath, by easily sticking the wire in from below, where it exits on the side and you can loop it around the rough thread of the hook. this is a 10/10 connection to your model. Moreover; this allows you to prep and test your hookup before you connect it to the hook of the rotary and allows for multiple models to be prepared in parallel. In functional terms; the device is powered either through usb or through a 9v block in the compartment of the control box, it's wired to prefer the USB power when available. The movement is started by pushing in the rotary encoder button, that controls start/stop movement. then turning the knob controls the speed of movement. The movement is designed as an oscillator; it turns 1,25 times and then reverses that movement. This is to make sure your connecting wire (to the negative lead) doesnt get looped (ruining your electrical connection). I added the whole setup in one .3mf on two plates. enjoy and let me know if you have questions or are happy with your build !

This is my Astronomy Without Borders Onesky 130F5 upper tube assembly. I found two major deficiencies with the original upper tube assembly. The sloppy threads in the helical focuser, that does not have adequate rigidity The finicky secondary mirror collimation The sloppy threads in the original helical focuser is well known with kludgy fixes like wrapping the threads in Teflon tape or using grease on the threads… But the bigger problem was the thin plastic cantilevered design. If you tried using any moderately heavy eyepieces the weight was cause it to sag and vibrate intolerably at higher magnifications, making planetary observing incredibly frustrating. And for some reason that I can not imagine, people making these entry level telescopes put the spring between the secondary mirror and the hub thingy. When you loosen the locking screw the whole thing just goes wherever it wants and makes collimation a total pain. Also, having the whole assembly on the one round rod made one more axis it could rotate on and need adjusting. Very annoying. In this upper tube assembly, the whole things is printed thick and solid, allowing for the mounting of a full size Crayford focuser. This upper assembly is very solid and has very little deflection. It uses a four vane spider, and I relocated the spring to the top side of the hub so it's in a push/pull orientation. Now when you loosen the center screw a turn or two, the spring holds the mirror mount against the three screws so you can actually see what effect your adjustments have on your collimation. As an added benefit, the holes for the strut rods are much deeper, which leaves a lot less unsupported rod length further increasing stiffness. And finally, I rotated the focuser around a bit for easier seated observing. IMO, the stock orientation seemed better for standing and hunching over the telescope. Now the focuser is at a 45° angle which I think offers better ergonomics. There are a couple of compromises though. First, it makes the telescope very top heavy. I had to slide the dovetail all the way as far as it can go, and it's still not 100% perfectly balanced but it's good enough. And second, the large Crayford sticks out axially further than the original focuser, requiring the use of 22mm spacers limiting how far the telescope extends to achieve focus. This is the focuser: https://agenaastro.com/gso-crayford-focuser-reflector-telescope-dual-speed-eaf-1-25.html Use the 176mm base curvature option. The design also utilizes this dovetail mounting shoe https://a.co/d/0iBxRjiH It is designed for m6 screws but I wanted to only use M4 on this design so I made this insert that allows the use of two M4 x 16mm countersunk head screws.` The designed it to use 4mm heat set inserts. https://a.co/d/0dv4AGsl Finally, I purchased this red dot finder scope https://a.co/d/04XIdzyd My only criticism is that even on the dimmest setting it's still pretty bright. I printed all the parts in ABS at 0.16mm layers, 6 wall loops, 20-25% gyroid infill with 3 fill lines. PETG or either ABS or PETG CF would also be nice, but I didn't have that and the normal ABS seems plenty stiff enough. This print requires minimum supports. I would not print in PLA, as it will warp if left in a hot car. I flocked the inside of the telescope tube and shroud, and painted the inside of the upper tube and spider in Musou black paint. https://a.co/d/06kpUJR0 https://a.co/d/05EYCLqY When assembling the strut rods into the upper tube assembly, it's a snug press fit and might require some persuasion with a plastic tipped hammer. The ends of the tubes must be flush with the bottom of the counter-bores. A keen eye will notice the end screws are missing on my telescope. I lost one somewhere along the way but I made the counter-bores a little too tight and makes installing the screw difficult. I fixed this on the uploaded model. I contacted Celestron and Skywatcher for replacement screws but neither were any help, so I'm on my own to find a suitable substitute but it seems like an odd thread. The tube extension fits into a groove and is fixed in place with CA glue. The shroud snaps in firmly, glue is optional. I used a soldering iron set to 280-290C to set the threaded inserts. All finished I could not be happier with the performance of the 'scope. It focuses fast and easy, especially with the Bahtinov mask. The 10:1 micro adjust is a dream. Collimation is easy and holds solidly. Vibrations are minimal and settle quickly.

3D Printing and Assembly Instructions for the C60 (Buckminsterfullerene) Model Print the parts and assemble them into a C60 (Buckminsterfullerene) model. The completed model consists of 60 carbon atoms (balls) connected by 90 bonds (rods) , forming a structure that resembles a soccer ball with 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons . The model is printed from two build plates: Rod Plate: Contains 18 rods . Print this plate 5 times (90 rods total). Ball Plate: Contains 15 balls . Print this plate 4 times (60 balls total). For the model picture shown here, PLA Silk Silver was used for the rods, while PLA Black was used for the carbon atoms (balls), creating an attractive contrast that highlights the molecular structure. Once all parts are printed, simply snap the rods into the balls to assemble the C60 molecule. The assembly process is fun, educational, and makes an excellent STEM activity for students and children while demonstrating the unique geometry of one of the most famous carbon molecules.

Pinza Multiuso Gommata (Scala 1:4) | Meccanismo Articolato Porta la vera ingegneria sulla tua scrivania! Questo non è un semplice giocattolo, ma la riproduzione in scala 1:4 di una vera " Pinza Multiuso Gommata " industriale, basata su un efficiente meccanismo a ginocchiera. La Storia del Progetto 🎓 Ho progettato questo cinematismo per un progetto di Laboratorio di Progettazione Meccanica in Università. La versione reale (in scala 1:1) è stata rigorosamente dimensionata e verificata dal punto di vista strutturale per sollevare in totale sicurezza carichi fino a 10 kN (circa 1 tonnellata). Ho deciso di scalarla in formato 1:4 per permettere a tutta la community di testare con mano la cinematica e la fisica dietro questo tipo di macchinari: più l'oggetto da sollevare è pesante, più la forza di serraggio orizzontale delle ganasce aumenta! (Per i più curiosi e gli appassionati di meccanica, ho allegato tra i file anche la mia relazione di calcolo originale completa di verifiche e dimensionamenti in lingua italiana). Dettagli di Stampa Ho caricato il profilo .3mf completo e già ottimizzato per BambuStudio. Il progetto è completamente stampabile in 3D , inclusi tutti i perni di articolazione (non avrete bisogno di viti o ferramenta esterna). Materiali: PLA o PETG per la struttura principale. Stampa Multimateriale SENZA AMS (Il trucco per le ganasce): Nel piatto dedicato alle ganasce ( Jaws ), ho impostato una pausa strategica prima degli ultimi layer. Questo vi permetterà di cambiare manualmente la bobina anche se non avete un AMS. Potete usare del filamento nero per un semplice contrasto estetico, oppure caricare del TPU . Usare il TPU per i primi strati simulerà il vero cuscinetto in gomma industriale, garantendo il giusto attrito per afferrare e sollevare davvero gli oggetti sulla vostra scrivania! Guida al Montaggio 🔧 (Screenshot) Le Chele Principali: Iniziate unendo le due chele centrali tramite il perno di articolazione mediano. I Bracci Superiori: Collegate le bielle alla parte superiore della struttura, posizionando l'anello di sollevamento (cruna) al centro ed i relativi perni. Le Ganasce: Agganciate le due ganasce inferiori (quelle con la presa gommata) ai bracci esterni e collegatele con i rispettivi perni. Nota sui perni: Inserite tutti i perni stampati in 3D nei rispettivi occhielli per chiudere il cinematismo (I perni più lunghi colleganmo gli elementi portanti della pinza, mentre quelli più corti collegano le chedle della pinza con le risepttive ganasce gommate). Buona stampa e buon sollevamento!

description: DESCRIPTION ----------- A three-stage rubber band motor that stores and releases energy through a sequence of rack-and-pinion stages. When the first rubber band contracts, it pulls its rack and turns the gears. Once that stage is fully contracted, a lever trigger releases the second stage, and the same hand-off then fires the third. The complete run lasts about five seconds and is satisfying to watch in motion. This design explores a way to store more energy in rubber bands by chaining stages instead of relying on a single band. The lever-trigger approach works well here, though other methods (for example bevel or worm gears) could also be used. In theory the same idea can be extended to any number of stages, which makes the model a useful base for anyone who wants to understand the mechanism and improve on it. ASSEMBLY NOTES -------------- Assembly needs care so that every trigger and lever engages correctly. A practical approach is: 1. Get the first stage to reliably trigger the second. 2. Glue that hinge in its exact best position once it works. 3. Then set up and tune the third stage the same way. 4. The axle is made of several parts that fit together inside the middle of the pinion gears. Photos of the fully assembled machine are included to show how the finished model should look.

This radius gauge is specific made for Mitutoyo vernier calipers. There are many simular devices on Makerword but ALL of them have a 45 degree angle. That means you must multiply the mesurement by some weird value. My radius gauge has an angle of 60 degrees. This means that if you mesure a round object then you get exact radius on your caliper. You don't have to calculate anything anymore. Just mesure and you have the exact radius on your caliper display. Disclaimer: This still is a printed pard and can bend while mesuring. If you bend the arms too much your mesurement will deviate. Usage: Puss your Mitutoyo calipers end (for depth mesurement) in the hole of the gauge with the display facing the round indent of the gauge all the way in. Close the caliper to zero. Place your round object against the 2 arms of the radius gauge. Hold the round object and push only the part of the caliper with the display towards the round object untill the pin tuches the round object. Now read the radius of the round object from the screen. This should be half of the outer diameter of the round object. It could be off a little bit because of your printers settings and temperature but my mesurements are realy close. Next, you grab the smaller disk and put the strings through the holes Then, you drop the disk inside the tube and push it a little Finally, you pull the strings tight and at the same time tape it to the smaller disk Now it should be done! This high-efficiency mousetrap car is powered purely by the spring mechanical energy of a Windhager mousetrap and utilizes a real gear system to maximize distance. The design runs incredibly smooth and achieved a personal track record of exactly 30 meters! To wind it up, the car must be rotated by three-quarters of a turn at the main gear, featuring a gear ratio of 1 to 64. Required Hardware: 6x 6700 ZZ Ball Bearings (10 x 15 x 4 ) 1x M3 Socket Head Screw 43 mm total length, partially threaded with a 20 mm smooth shank 1x Windhager Mousetrap Step-by-Step Guide: Spring Preparation: Remove the spring from the Windhager mousetrap. Trim the protruding wire ends so that about 2 cm remain, and bend them so they stick out at a 90° angle relative to the spring. Inserting the Spring & Sleeve: Push the printed plastic sleeve inside the spring. Then, insert the spring into the main motor cavity of the chassis with the thicker side of the spring facing inward. Main Gear & Core Screw: Place the large main drive gear onto the spring. Pass the M3 screw through the gear and the spring to lock everything into place. Tighten it enough to eliminate wobbling, but ensure it remains loose enough to spin freely without excessive friction. Gearbox Assembly: Press one ball bearing into each of the middle gears. If the fit is tight, gently tap them in using a hammer. Carefully mount these geared assemblies onto their designated pins on the chassis. Axles & Wheel Bearings: Install the axles along with the remaining bearings onto the frame. Tip: For the wheel axles, you can optionally use 3D-printed bearings. However, for the high-load drivetrain gears (Step 4), real metal ball bearings are strictly required! Attaching the Wheels: Finally, press-fit the wheels onto the axles – the large wheels go in the back, and the small wheels go in the front.

description: 36:1 Dual-Stage Planetary Gearbox for NEMA 17 This is a functional 36:1 dual-stage planetary gearbox designed for a NEMA 17 stepper motor. It was developed as a joint reducer for my base-actuated robotic arm, but it may also be useful for other low-speed rotary mechanisms, positioning systems, and experimental robotics projects. This design is the result of a long process of printing, measuring, disassembling, redesigning, and testing. It was not created using nominal CAD dimensions alone. The final geometry was repeatedly adjusted according to the actual behavior of FDM-printed mechanical parts, including: Bore shrinkage Extrusion and outer-wall spread Temperature-dependent dimensional changes Bearing and shaft press fits Deformation caused by assembly pressure Gear-tooth contact Wear during initial running-in One of the most important features is the lower hub of the central sun gear. It was designed as the primary alignment reference between the motor shaft and both planetary stages. Even accurately modeled gears can develop noise, vibration, uneven wear, and backlash when the sun gear is loose, tilted, or eccentric. For this reason, the shaft interface, bearing support, gear clearances, output structure, and six-point fastening system were developed together as one complete mechanical assembly. The gearbox may feel slightly tight immediately after assembly. During controlled low-speed running-in, microscopic high points on the printed tooth surfaces gradually wear away, allowing the gearbox to reach a smoother and more stable final operating clearance. Running-in should only remove minor surface irregularities. Severe binding, tooth skipping, concentrated heating, or large plastic fragments indicate a printing, dimensional, or assembly problem. Demonstration Video https://youtube.com/shorts/FVjSa3sgb2A Main Specifications Gearbox type: Dual-stage planetary gearbox Total reduction ratio: 36:1 Motor interface: NEMA 17 Output method: Upper ring-gear output Main output bearing: 35 × 47 × 7 mm Recommended material: PETG or another strong, dimensionally stable material Intended use: Robot arms and low-speed rotary mechanisms Backlash: Very low perceptible backlash during manual testing Quantified backlash: Not yet measured using calibrated equipment Required Hardware M3 × 20 mm hex socket screws: 6 M3 heat-set inserts, 5 mm height: 24 M3 × 8 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing: 1 M3 × 12 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 M2.5 × 7 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 NEMA 17 stepper motor: 1 Hex-drive screws are recommended for all connections. Important Printing Instructions Use a Brim on All Parts Except the Sun Gears and Planet Gears A brim is strongly recommended for all printed parts except the sun gears and planet gears . This includes: Housing parts Ring gears Output components Bearing retainers Motor-mounting parts Covers and other structural components The brim helps provide: Reliable bed adhesion A stable and flat bottom surface Accurate alignment between stacked housing parts Proper bearing and heat-set insert seating Reduced corner lifting and warping The flatness of the housing, ring gears, and output components directly affects the alignment of both planetary stages. Even a small amount of warping may cause uneven rotational resistance, bearing misalignment, or periodic binding. A brim is not recommended for the sun gears and planet gears because removing it may damage the lower tooth edges or alter the critical tooth geometry. Remove all brims carefully without damaging the bottom reference surfaces. Use the Manufacturer-Recommended Bed Temperature Always use the normal bed temperature recommended for the selected filament. Do not unnecessarily increase the bed temperature to improve adhesion. Excessive bed temperature may cause elephant-foot deformation, which can: Enlarge the lower edges Distort screw-clearance holes Affect bearing and insert locations Prevent stacked parts from seating flat Change the alignment of the planetary stages The first layer must adhere securely without being excessively compressed or spread outward. Use a Strong Material A mechanically strong and dimensionally stable material is strongly recommended. PETG was used during development, but another properly calibrated high-strength material may also be suitable. The selected material should provide: Strong layer adhesion Resistance to cracking Reliable bearing retention Reliable heat-set insert retention Adequate wear resistance Low long-term deformation under bolt pressure and mechanical load Different materials may produce different dimensions, tooth clearances, friction, and running-in behavior. Test the fit carefully before completing the full assembly. Correcting Tight Tolerances When the printed clearances are slightly too tight, first check: Flow ratio First-layer compression Bed temperature Nozzle temperature XY compensation Hole compensation Actual printer dimensional accuracy If excessive material flow or thermal spreading appears to be the cause, printing at a slightly lower nozzle temperature may improve the fit. Reduce the temperature only in small increments. Do not lower it so far that layer adhesion or mechanical strength is reduced. Never Scale or Modify the Model Do not scale the model or change its geometry to correct a fitting problem. Scaling or reshaping the components changes critical mechanical relationships, including: Gear-tooth thickness Gear pitch geometry Planetary center distances Ring-gear engagement Bearing seats Shaft alignment Motor mounting positions Fastener spacing Output concentricity Even a small dimensional change may prevent the two planetary stages from meshing correctly. Do not modify: Gear profiles Gear center distances Bearing locations Shaft interfaces Alignment surfaces Overall component proportions Printing errors should be corrected through printer calibration, flow adjustment, temperature adjustment, first-layer calibration, and appropriate hole compensation—not by changing the model. Assembly Instructions and Precautions Tighten every six-screw pattern gradually in a diagonal sequence. Do not fully tighten one screw before installing and partially tightening the others. Uneven tightening may distort the housing or shift the planetary stages out of alignment. Use moderate hand pressure. Excessive tightening may: Deform the printed housing Distort the bearing seat Misalign the planetary stages Damage or rotate the heat-set inserts Increase rotational resistance Distort the output ring gear If an M3 clearance hole prints too small, carefully open only that clearance hole using a 3.0 mm drill bit so that the screw passes through freely. Do not drill: Heat-set insert holes Bearing seats Sun-gear or planet-gear bores Motor-shaft interfaces Precision alignment surfaces The 3.0 mm drill should only be used on holes intended to provide free passage for an M3 screw. Press the 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing into the housing evenly through its outer ring. Do not hammer the bearing into place, and do not transmit the insertion force through the inner ring or rolling elements. Before applying an external load: Rotate the gearbox by hand in both directions. Check for hard stops or periodic binding. Operate the motor slowly without load. Run the gearbox in both directions. Inspect the teeth and remove loose wear debris. Confirm that the bearing and housing remain properly seated. Increase the load gradually only after smooth operation is confirmed. Stop operation immediately if you observe: Severe binding Tooth skipping Sharp periodic impacts Concentrated heating Large plastic fragments Cracked gear teeth Bearing movement Shaft slipping Rapidly increasing backlash Development Background This gearbox was developed using a printer that I have repaired, modified, and studied for a long time. A newer machine could have produced prototypes faster, but learning the limitations of an imperfect printer taught me how printed parts actually change between CAD, printing, press fitting, assembly, wear, and real operation. I repeatedly printed and measured parts to understand: How internal holes shrink How external surfaces spread How temperature changes the final dimensions How press fitting deforms printed components Which interfaces must remain completely rigid Which microscopic tooth irregularities may safely wear away How initial running changes the final operating clearance The final design represents the complete process: Printing → Measurement → Dimensional correction → Assembly → Running-in → Final operating clearance This is not simply a generic planetary gear set placed inside a housing. The shaft alignment, bearing support, output structure, six-point fastening, gear clearances, and running-in behavior were developed together through repeated physical testing. The precision of this gearbox did not come from a perfect machine. It came from understanding the machine’s limitations and designing around them.

Atmos Mk 1.2 The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a compact 3D-printable model rocket designed for use with Estes E16-6 and E16-8 motors . It features a dedicated electronics bay that can fit a Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico 2 , GY-BME280 pressure sensor , and a 3.7V LiPo battery , allowing makers to add custom flight computers, altitude logging, and other experimental electronics. Designed with accessibility and customization in mind, the Atmos Mk 1.2 can be printed using a wide range of common 3D printing materials. Whether printed in PLA for easy prototyping, PETG for added durability, or other materials for specialized builds, the design can be adapted to suit different launch goals. The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a platform for makers, students, and rocketry enthusiasts who want to explore 3D printing, electronics, and experimental flight systems in a compact and reusable rocket design. Flight Notes Stability margin: Approximately 1.7 calibers . Estimated altitude: Typically reaches 800–1,000 ft (240–305 m) , depending on launch conditions. Flight history: Successfully tested over 3 flights (with a 4th planned) with E16-8 estes rocket motors, demonstrating reliable performance and durable construction, you could use f motors but i wouldn't go below 15N of force engines to ensure safe liftoff. Recommendations: do not attempt to remove the motor directly after flight wait for the plastic to cool read assembly note carefully to prevent hardware issues higher temp materials ensure more durability but i have printed out of both pla and petg for this project and pla will function and work I assembled a flight computer out of a raspberry pi pico a gy bme barometer and a small quadcopter battery for under ten dollars and this platform was mostly designed to test it i encourage others to do the same but also i plan to drop links to my functioning code later once i have it all ironed out Assembly Notes To assemble the Atmos Mk 1.2, you'll need 3–4 pennies, super glue, a nylon or Kevlar shock cord, a small amount of duct tape, recovery wadding, a small i hook, and your choice of recovery system (streamer or parachute) . The rocket is designed for Estes E16-6 or E16-8 motors . The nose cone includes a dedicated ballast pocket: Payload under 15 g: Glue 4 pennies into the nose cone. Payload over 15 g: Glue 3 pennies into the nose cone. For the best flight performance, try to keep payloads under 30 g . Secure your electronics using M3 screws, electrical tape, or both —tape alone works well for most builds, but using both provides maximum security. If any printed parts fit loosely, adjust the tolerances with a small amount of Scotch tape as needed. Finally, don't forget to add recovery wadding before every launch. Chomp vive en las Placas Quietas de Zoora, donde el suelo cambia de sonido con cada paso. Camina con cuidado, porque sus pisadas son tan fuertes que siempre teme mover algo sin querer. Una tarde vio tres piedras claras colocadas en línea. Intentó rodearlas para no tocarlas, pero resbaló un poco y apoyó las patas justo encima de las tres a la vez. Entonces pasó algo extraño: la piedra vibró bajo él y, por un instante, apareció completa la línea que antes parecía quedar abierta en el gran círculo del camino antiguo . Así Chomp entendió una parte del misterio. La línea no estaba rota ni faltaba un trozo: simplemente solo se completaba cuando alguien presionaba los tres puntos al mismo tiempo. Desde entonces, Chomp ya no intenta esconder sus pasos. Ahora sabe que su fuerza no siempre complica las cosas; a veces también puede ayudar a resolverlas. Moraleja: A veces, eso que creías un problema es justo lo que hacía falta.

description: This is the new version of my popular Instax Mini 12 keychain. It features a functional button that pushes out the film, letting you place a small picture inside—perfect for a heartfelt gift or to keep your loved ones close wherever you go. but in this version everything got better. Step 3 Position the lever and the button/pin as shown in the image (do not try to press the button as the system will not work until the cover is in place) . About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating. description: Take the Guesswork Out of Building a 40K Battlefield 40K 11th edition introduced some really cool predetermined battlefield layouts that show you exactly how to set up the battlefield and what terrain goes where. They didn't do a great job sharing the dimensions of the terrain pieces and figuring out what terrain to use can be surprisingly confusing. There are countless terrain models available, but figuring out which pieces you actually need, what sizes they should be, and how everything fits together on an 11th Edition battlefield can become a project of its own. This collection was created to simplify that entire process. I carefully studied the battlefield layouts shown in the 40K app, determined the different terrain footprints and sizes needed to recreate them, and designed a complete, coordinated set that allows players to print everything required for a functional battlefield in one place. Instead of downloading unrelated models from multiple creators and hoping they work together, this set provides a clear starting point for new players and a convenient, consistent battlefield system for experienced players. Also, I included A1 Mini Print Profiles as well, so the game has never been more accessible. What’s Included The complete collection includes: Battlefield terrain footprints Light terrain features Dense terrain features Standard objective markers Central and expansion objective markers Deployment zone markers Coordinated pieces designed to work together as one battlefield system The terrain footprints clearly define each terrain area, while the light and dense terrain pieces provide the physical structures needed to make the battlefield easy to understand and play on. The objective and deployment zone markers make setup faster and reduce the need to repeatedly measure important locations before every game. AB, CD, EF, and GH Dense Terrain The dense terrain pieces were specifically designed and marked to correspond with the AB, CD, EF, and GH terrain categories shown in the battlefield layouts within the 40K app. This makes it much easier to identify which dense terrain piece belongs in each location when setting up a battlefield. Rather than comparing several similar-looking pieces, estimating dimensions, or trying to determine which terrain feature matches each layout position, simply select the appropriately marked AB, CD, EF, or GH model. This labeling system helps make battlefield setup faster, clearer, and more approachable—especially for players building their first complete terrain collection. Designed for Fast, Reliable Printing Every part of this collection was created with practical 3D printing in mind. The main design goals were: Fast print times Low filament use High printing success rates No support material required Simple, reliable geometry Easy battlefield setup Clear and consistent terrain sizes Minimal preparation after printing All models were designed to print without supports and can be used immediately after removing them from the build plate. There should be no support removal, complicated assembly, or extensive cleanup required. Print the pieces, remove them from the plate, and place them directly on the battlefield. These models are intended to be accessible to newer 3D-printer owners and players who may be building their first complete 40K battlefield. They are functional gaming pieces first. Not overly complicated display models that require days of printing, large amounts of filament, or extensive post-processing. Recommended Printing Approach For the clearest gameplay experience, I recommend printing the footprints, light terrain, and dense terrain in different colors . Using separate colors makes it easier to quickly tell which terrain category a piece belongs to and helps reduce confusion when applying terrain rules during play. This is especially helpful for newer players, teaching games, or anyone trying to make battlefield interactions more intuitive at a glance. For example, using one color for footprints, another for light terrain, and another for dense terrain can make it much easier to determine which terrain rules apply when models move into, through, or around a terrain feature. A Complete Starting Point for New Players This set is especially useful for someone who has recently started playing 40K and is asking: What terrain do I need? How large should each terrain area be? Which pieces are light terrain and which are dense terrain? Which dense terrain piece corresponds with AB, CD, EF, or GH? How do I reproduce the battlefield layouts shown in the app? How many objective markers do I need? Where should deployment zones and objectives be placed? The goal is to remove as much uncertainty as possible so you can spend less time researching terrain and more time printing, painting, and playing. Modular and Easy to Customize The pieces can be printed as a complete matching set or mixed with terrain you already own. Terrain footprints can also be used with ruins, buildings, rock formations, industrial structures, or other decorative terrain placed within the marked areas. This makes the system useful even as your terrain collection grows. Print the included terrain for a quick, lightweight battlefield, or use the footprints and markers as the foundation for a more detailed custom table. Additional Helpful Models Along with this terrain set, you may want something for quick measurements between models. I highly recommend this adjustable compass style range finder by The Moose and Bolter. https://makerworld.com/en/models/2730760-kt-range-finder-the-ultimate-adjustable-compass#profileId-3026517 If you need wound trackers, I have a few listed here on MakerWorld and specifically this one linked below is designed to be lightweight and easy to print just like this terrain set. https://makerworld.com/en/models/3011980-wound-tracker-engagement-range-gauge-11th-ed#profileId-3382976 Important Note This is an unofficial, community-created terrain and battlefield setup system intended for tabletop wargaming. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or produced by Games Workshop. Battlefield requirements, event standards, and tournament interpretations may vary, so always confirm the requirements of your local gaming group or event organizer. The models are designed as a practical way to recreate and organize the battlefield layouts represented in the 40K app while making the process easier for players and 3D-printing hobbyists. Print the set, build your battlefield, and start playing without the guesswork.

Axen vive en los canales tranquilos de Zoora, donde el agua casi nunca se mueve. Le gusta quedarse muy quieto en el fondo y observar cómo cambian las corrientes. Un día, después de una lluvia fuerte, el agua se volvió turbia y muchos pensaron que una entrada del camino antiguo había desaparecido bajo el barro. Axen no salió corriendo ni removió el agua. Se quedó quieto, esperando. Poco a poco, el barro bajó al fondo y entonces pudo ver algo que nadie había notado: una abertura de piedra seguía allí, escondida bajo tres pequeñas marcas azules. Así descubrió que la entrada no se había perdido. Solo estaba oculta. Desde entonces, cuando algo parece haber desaparecido en Zoora, muchos recuerdan a Axen y esperan un poco antes de rendirse. Moraleja: A veces, quedarse quieto es la mejor forma de ver las cosas con claridad.

Bring the raw energy and intensity of ancient battles to your shelf with this highly detailed, dynamic statue of a running Spartan warrior. Due to the extreme dynamic pose, the overhanging cape, and the extended sword, supports are strictly necessary. I highly recommend using Tree / Organic supports for easier removal and to preserve the intricate details of the armor and base. Layer Height: 0.08mm - 0.20mm. This model features extremely fine details. To achieve the highly realistic look of the original sculpt, printing with very thin layers is strongly advised. Infill: 10% - 15% (Gyroid or Grid). Bluegill are a common species of freshwater gamefish native to the the United States east of the Rocky Mountains, but they have also been introduced to most of the other western states too. They're easy to catch and will bite on worms, artificial baits, corn, and even bread. For these reasons, bluegill are usually the first fish that young anglers in the US catch. Their exact coloration can vary between genders and seasons, but bluegill can typically be identified by their dark green bodies, black “ear” at the corner of the gill, reddish, orange chest, and their blue chins and gills. They are usually at the bottom of the food chain and are preyed on by bass, pike, catfish, herons, and other aquatic predators. To defend themselves they have sharp spines poking out from their dorsal fins that teach the young anglers who catch them to be careful when unhooking them. This model has interlocking scale units that allow the model to “swim”. The two halves are printed separately, aligned with the registration pin that fits into the rectangular slot on the bottom of the head segments, and secured together with glue between the head, tail, and perimeter scales. For this model, the pectoral fins are printed separately to maximize strength and then glued into the slots behind the gills. I used bronze silk PLA for most of the body, but a dark olive green PLA might match the real coloration more closely. The full-color model uses 5 colors and requires 2 AMS units, but I've also provided a 4-color version without the dark green on top that can be printed with 1 AMS. Happy printing (and fishing)!

The Typhoon class (Project 941 Akula) is the largest submarine ever built and one of the most iconic symbols of the Cold War. Designed as a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN), the Typhoon combined immense size with exceptional endurance and survivability. Its distinctive twin-pressure-hull design and massive missile compartment made it unlike any other submarine ever constructed. The class gained worldwide recognition through Tom Clancy's novel and the film The Hunt for Red October , becoming one of the most recognizable submarines in naval history. This detailed 1:350 scale model faithfully captures the unique proportions and unmistakable silhouette of the legendary Typhoon class. Assembly is very easy. Brook trout are vibrant and beautiful members of the salmon/char family native to the eastern United States and Canada. They hold significant ecological significance and are designated as the state fish of 5 states (Pennsylvania, Virginia, Michigan, New Hampshire, and New York)! Due to their sensitivity to pollution, they are a great indicator species, meaning that waterways and environments able to house them are very healthy. Before introduction of brown trout and rainbow trout. the brook trout were the only trout species targeted by anglers for the first 100 years of the United State's history. For both of these reasons, Brook trout are seen as a symbol of pristine North American wilderness. These fish hold special meaning to me too. As a kid my grandfather would take me to small streams in northern Pennsylvania to catch them. Each time I caught one I was surprised at just how vibrant they were, even if they were only 3-4 inches long. Those experiences really made me love being in nature and fishing, which has inspired all of my articulated fish models. So I'm dedicating this model to my grandfather, Wayne. Keyring versions are also available on plate 2 of each print profile. The model was designed to fit on the A-mini but can be scaled up as large as you want it! As mentioned before, Brook Trout are very colorful fish which means a lot of filament swaps in 3D printing. The base model is painted in 6 colors and requires 2 AMS units. I used black as the base color, but a dark-olive color would more closely match the real thing. To get around these requirements though, I've also provided a print profile with only the basic black, white, and orange coloration. For that print profile the yellow squiggles and red and blue spots are left out and can be painted on in acrylic afterwards. In my opinion, the painted blue and red dots stood out more when painted on rather than printed on. The only downside to acrylics paint is it's water solubility so the color could be washed away or smear if the model gets wet. However you decide to print/paint this model, I hope you enjoy your new fishy friend! Happy printing (and fishing)!

Cable Buddy - Kitty Hey everyone, I want to share the latest addition to my CripWorks designs: The Cable Buddies. I was looking for a way to stop my charging cables from bending and breaking at the connector, and I decided to make a cute and functional solution. The concept is simple. The Cable Buddy essentially "bites" onto the end of your cable. This not only protects the weak spot of the cord from wearing out, but it also gives you a much better grip when you are unplugging your devices. It is designed to fit standard USB-C cables comfortably. The print requires some support material under the belly and inside the mouth area. This is honestly somewhat fiddly to remove - a small flat screwdriver did the trick for me. Just be careful not to break off the teeth. It took quite a while to design and color them. I redesigned the USB cable to make it more suitable for different USB-C cable types. As a workaround for not repainting them after the redesign, I simply added the new cable as a negative → This should not be removed in the slicer. Print Recommendations: Material: PLA or PETG works perfectly fine. PETG is my favorite as it is a little more sturdy. Layer Height: Variable layer height for more details. Infill: 15% Fuzzy Skin: Enabled Supports: Skinny tree This Kitty is part of a larger Cable Buddy series I am working on, so keep an eye out for more animals coming soon. I hope you enjoy printing this little guy as much as I enjoyed designing it. Happy printing! description: Bring shattered crusader architecture to your grimdark sci-fi battlefield with this detailed Black Templars Ruined Fortress Wall Section terrain piece. This model is designed as a long ruined wall section inspired by the fortress architecture of the Black Templars. The piece combines gothic window elements, battle-damaged masonry, sacred crusader iconography, rubble-strewn ground details and a strong defensive silhouette, creating a dramatic mix of holy ruin, battlefield cover and thematic scenery. With its elongated footprint and damaged upper wall sections, it works perfectly as cover, line-of-sight blocking terrain, objective scenery or a characterful centerpiece for a grimdark sci-fi tabletop. Its long horizontal shape makes it especially useful for structuring battlefields, dividing fire lanes and adding strong visual atmosphere to ruined urban or fortress-style tables. The model fits naturally into crusader strongholds, shattered shrine districts, devastated defensive lines or war-torn imperial cities and helps create a more immersive and believable battlefield. All my models are real test prints, not just digital renders. I always try to find the best balance between print time, level of detail and filament usage, so the terrain looks impressive on the table without becoming unnecessarily difficult or wasteful to print I also put a lot of effort into optimizing the files, removing print issues and making the models as user-friendly as possible. My goal is to offer terrain that prints cleanly, feels solid, and can be used straight from the printer or painted with simple drybrushing techniques. Designed with FDM printing in mind, the piece is suitable for PLA filament printing and looks great in simple grey material without any color changes. About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating. Cable Buddy - Sharky Hey everyone, I want to share the latest addition to my CripWorks designs: The Cable Buddies. I was looking for a way to stop my charging cables from bending and breaking at the connector, and I decided to make a cute and functional solution. The concept is simple. The Cable Buddy essentially "bites" onto the end of your cable. This not only protects the weak spot of the cord from wearing out, but it also gives you a much better grip when you are unplugging your devices. It is designed to fit standard USB-C cables comfortably. The print requires some support material under the belly and inside the mouth area. This is honestly somewhat fiddly to remove - a small flat screwdriver did the trick for me. Just be careful not to break off the teeth. It took quite a while to design and color them. I redesigned the USB cable to make it more suitable for different USB-C cable types. As a workaround for not repainting them after the redesign, I simply added the new cable as a negative → This should not be removed in the slicer. Print Recommendations: Material: PLA or PETG works perfectly fine. PETG is my favorite as it is a little more sturdy. Layer Height: Variable layer height for more details. Infill: 15% Fuzzy Skin: Enabled Supports: Skinny tree This Shark is part of a larger Cable Buddy series I am working on, so keep an eye out for more animals coming soon. I hope you enjoy printing this little guy as much as I enjoyed designing it. Happy printing! description: Kenku Miniature – Cunning Crowfolk Scout and Master Mimic This miniature is part of the Monster Manual 2024 Collection , a series of iconic creatures faithfully reimagined as dynamic, tabletop-ready sculpts. The Kenku is one of the most recognizable avian humanoids in the Monster Manual 2024, combining the appearance of a clever crow with the posture and equipment of an experienced rogue, scout, or thief. Renowned for their uncanny mimicry, stealth, and resourcefulness, Kenku survive through intelligence rather than brute strength. This miniature faithfully follows the uploaded reference, capturing a wary infiltrator caught in the middle of a burglary or reconnaissance mission. The miniature stands on a Medium (25 mm) round tabletop base in a low stalking pose. The Kenku balances with one foot planted firmly on uneven cobblestones while the opposite foot rests atop a weathered wooden crate, giving the impression that it is silently navigating rooftops, alleyways, or forgotten ruins. The crouched posture lowers its center of gravity and immediately communicates stealth, agility, and constant awareness. Every point of contact remains securely connected to the base for excellent print stability. Its anatomy reflects the lean proportions described in Monster Manual 2024. The body is slender and athletic rather than muscular, built for climbing, running, and quiet movement. Narrow shoulders transition into long arms ending in dexterous clawed hands capable of manipulating tools and weapons with remarkable precision. The digitigrade bird-like legs terminate in powerful talons that grip both the ground and the crate naturally, reinforcing the dynamic balance of the pose. The head is unmistakably raven-like, featuring dense layered feathers that create a textured crown across the skull and neck. A long black beak curves gently downward with realistic proportions rather than exaggerated length. Sharp amber eyes peer cautiously toward unseen danger, conveying intelligence and suspicion rather than aggression. The head tilts slightly forward, reinforcing the feeling that the Kenku is constantly evaluating its surroundings before making its next move. The left arm reaches forward with spread talons as though preparing to steady itself or silently grab a nearby object. The opposite arm remains pulled back, gripping a simple steel dagger in a reverse grip suitable for ambushes or close-quarters combat. The blade is intentionally broad and sturdy enough for reliable printing while retaining a realistic profile. Unlike many fantasy birdfolk, the Kenku possesses no functional wings. Instead, its body is covered in layered black feathers that transition naturally into feathered arms and a short fan-shaped tail. The feathers are sculpted in overlapping layers that produce excellent depth when painted while remaining thick enough for clean printing. The tail extends naturally behind the miniature, providing visual balance without creating unsupported elements. Its clothing reflects the practical lifestyle of an experienced infiltrator. A hooded travel cloak drapes across the shoulders before falling behind the body in thick layered folds. Beneath the cloak, multiple leather straps cross the torso to secure pouches, satchels, and equipment. A weathered belt carries additional supplies including small utility bags, bottles, and tools appropriate for scouting or lockpicking. Layered cloth panels protect the hips while maintaining complete freedom of movement. The wrapped forearms and lower legs reinforce the impression of an adventurer accustomed to dangerous environments. The scenic base follows the uploaded reference closely. Uneven cobblestones form the primary terrain while a sturdy wooden crate elevates one foot, creating vertical variation without distracting from the figure itself. Beside the crate lie a small sack, a discarded cup, and scattered debris, suggesting a back alley, marketplace, or smuggler's hideout. These scenic details remain fully integrated into the base and are designed for straightforward printing. The recommended paint scheme matches the reference miniature. Feathers should be painted deep charcoal black with subtle blue-grey highlights applied through careful drybrushing to reveal individual feather layers. The beak and talons use satin black highlighted with cool greys. Leather equipment ranges from warm browns to dark chestnut with lighter edge highlights, while the cloak combines muted olive, brown, and weathered grey fabrics. Metallic buckles and the dagger receive aged steel finishes with selective silver highlights. The amber eyes provide a bright focal point that immediately draws attention to the miniature's expressive face. Every shadow hides opportunity. Every voice can become its own. The silent watcher has already memorized your final words. ✨ Key Features Faithful Kenku based on the Monster Manual 2024 . Closely matches the uploaded reference miniature. Dynamic stealth pose with one foot resting on a wooden crate. Distinctive raven-like head with layered feather detail. Reverse-grip dagger ready for ambushes. Practical adventuring gear including belts, pouches, bottles, and satchels. Fully feathered body without functional wings, true to the classic Kenku appearance. Scenic cobblestone base with integrated crate and urban clutter. Strong silhouette designed for tabletop visibility. No floating parts, magical effects, smoke, or unsupported scenery. Optimized for resin printing and suitable for carefully tuned FDM printers. 🎨 Great for Painting Prime the miniature black before building the feathers using successive layers of charcoal, dark blue-grey, and subtle light grey drybrushing across the raised feather texture. Paint the beak and talons in satin black with cool grey edge highlights to create natural contrast. The cloak works well in muted olive-brown or weathered grey, shaded with dark brown washes before lighter edge highlights. Leather belts and pouches should be painted using varying shades of brown to break up the equipment visually, while metallic buckles and the dagger benefit from dark steel tones highlighted with silver. Finish the eyes with vivid amber or golden yellow to emphasize the Kenku's alert and calculating expression. The base combines layered stone greys for the cobblestones, weathered brown wood for the crate, dusty earth pigments between the stones, and small touches of muted green on the scattered bottles to create subtle visual interest without overwhelming the figure. 📏 Scale & Compatibility Creature Size: Medium Recommended Base: 25 mm round tabletop base Compatible with standard 28 mm, 32 mm, and heroic-scale fantasy tabletop games, urban adventures, thieves' guild encounters, wilderness scouting parties, rogue-themed campaigns, and Monster Manual 2024 miniature collections.

model_name: Court of the Vampire Queen Illya'Dra
description: The Court of the Vampire Queen Illya'Dra, Former Matron of House 'Dra All models in this series are set in a .2mm Nozzle Profile. These are long prints . To ensure success: Clean the build plate before you start the print. A clean build plate is essential before starting a long print. Nothing worse than a support coming off the plate ¾ of the way through. The supports are designed to be thin and easy to remove. With that stated, some of the points of connection are on or around small details. They will come away cleanly, just go slow and use the proper tool. Flusher Cutter, Razor, etc. The models are designed and positioned for success, so be patient when removing the supports particularly around the Axe , the Sword , and the Cane . If you have not tried my print profile, just use it. It is a high detail, slowed, increased wall and thinned out support profile designed to work well with these models. I post many .4mm profiles models on makerworld as people tend to like the speed over the detail but for home use I print every model in this .2mm profile. For an example see the .2mm Profile Beholder in my models. It takes longer, but it is worth it. The Beholder shown here is cleaned up and thats it. No primer and no paint. For the Vampire with the sword, there is a point on the base with a very tiny hole that the tip of the sword will slip into. If you do not line it up with the hole in the base, the sword point will actually be a fraction of a mm longer than his legs and make it challenging to glue him to the base. For the most part the bases are interchangable, but slightly different per model. If you see one you like more than the rest, resize it to the correct size and print it again. The bases are quick and use very little filament. So use what you like. The Queen is a much larger size model. I did this because I like it. That doesn't mean you need to love it. Resize any or all of these to fit your needs. They are scaled to work with a 32mm TTRPG of your choice, with the Queen being much large and daunting. The others hover right near there, give or take a few mm. if you run into any issues printing these, let me know! I have printed each of them two times. Once for my personal use and once as a followup test print. That doesn't mean all machines and filament are the same. I printed these using Sunlu HS PLA+ 2.0, which is currently a bit of a meta filament in the FDM miniature community as it prints with clean, high detail and cleans up easily. I have also taken the steps to calibrate that filament on my machine. If you find issues during your print, leave a comment and I wil see what I can do to address the comments and help. Aside from some stringing my filament is very dialed in. The stringing i have intentionally left in the pictures so that you can see what it looks like before being cleaned up and primed or painted or whatever else people do to these things to make them seem impossibly clean. These are thinner models with higher level, smaller details. IMO that leads to higher stringing when using a .2 on HS filament even when dried, dialed in retraction and calibrated. So my pictures of the printed models can and will look better after clean up and paint. I have a terrain build that I created spefically to with this Vampire Encounter, my first larger terrain piece. Here is what it looks like but I still on the fence about releasing it. It takes about 1kg of filament to print the entire thing, it has verticality to it as it is supposed to be a fallen temple that has begun to sink into an ever expanding swamp lands. Many might not like the verticality of it as it gently slopes. I have a couryard and a few other areas that would fill an entire table. But they are unique pieces that probably don't see much play, take a ton of filament even on 4% infill, and take up a great deal of space when not in use. I don't know that I want to go down this road. I will let people see it though to help me decide if it's worth releasing or not. I have several projects like this I created over the last couple years that are original and specific to the story I was running at the time. I just don't know how well they fit into anyone elses worlds. Anyway, happy printing all! ***UPDATE NOTE*** I will be adding some .4mm nozzle profiles for the model that I can. If they are just going to fail on people at .4 I won't put the profile up. There are some thin points that will prove challenging in .4

description: Bring the terrifying scale of Greek mythology to your desk! This model depicts a fierce Laestrygonian , one of the legendary giant cannibals who nearly ended Odysseus’s journey home. Designed smartly to allow striking multi-color results without requiring an AMS (Automatic Material System) , this print separates the main body, the hands, and the weapon into independent plates. Just print, assemble, and enjoy a stunning display piece! 📜 The Legend of the Laestrygonians "They were not like men, but like giants... They speared the men like fish and carried them away for their ghastly feast." > — Homer, The Odyssey (Book X) After escaping the island of Aeolus, Odysseus and his fleet of twelve ships sought refuge in the quiet, cliff-rimmed harbor of Telepylos. Believing they had found safe harbor, eleven captains moored their ships inside the basin. Only the clever Odysseus, ever cautious, kept his ship anchored outside on the rocky coast. His caution saved his life. The harbor was a trap. This was the land of the Laestrygonians —monstrous giants of immense strength. Emerging from the cliffs, they pelted the trapped fleet with boulders so massive they shattered the wooden ships like toys. In the chaos that followed, the giants speared the drowning sailors to carry them off for a gruesome feast. Of all the fleet, only Odysseus's ship slipped its cables and escaped into the open sea. This miniature captures the raw, imposing power of those ancient mythical titans—silent, armored, and ready to strike. 🛠️ Print Settings & Configuration This model is optimized for fast, beautiful prints. Cable Buddy - Panda Hey everyone, I want to share the latest addition to my CripWorks designs: The Cable Buddies. I was looking for a way to stop my charging cables from bending and breaking at the connector, and I decided to make a cute and functional solution. The concept is simple. The Cable Buddy essentially "bites" onto the end of your cable. This not only protects the weak spot of the cord from wearing out, but it also gives you a much better grip when you are unplugging your devices. It is designed to fit standard USB-C cables comfortably. As you can see from the pictures, the print requires some support material under the belly and inside the mouth area. This is honestly somewhat fiddly to remove - a small flat screwdriver did the trick for me. Just be careful not to break off the teeth. It took quite a while to design and color them. I redesigned the USB cable to make it more suitable for different USB-C cable types. As a workaround for not repainting them after the redesign, I simply added the new cable as a negative → This should not be removed in the slicer. Print Recommendations: Material: PLA or PETG works perfectly fine. PETG is my favorite as it is a little more sturdy. Layer Height: Variable layer height for more details. Infill: 15% Fuzzy Skin: Enabled Supports: Skinny tree This Panda is part of a larger Cable Buddy series I am working on, so keep an eye out for more animals coming soon.
