description: Looking for Ramps? Look no further. This OpenSCAD script lets you generate fully parametric ramps and wedges with configurable dimensions, slope, rounded corners, and surface finish. Whether you need a doorstop, riser, shim, leveling block, fixture, or custom ramp, this generator gives you complete control. Choose between flat, stepped, or ribbed top surfaces, and optionally hollow the model with lightweight lattice patterns to reduce material usage. Click on Customize to open the generator 🚀 Quick Start 1. Set Your Ramp Dimensions Choose the overall width, length, and height of the ramp. You can also enable angle-based sizing to automatically calculate the final height from the desired slope angle. 2. Customize the Surface Choose the surface that best fits your application: Flat : smooth incline. Stepped : stair-step incline. Ribbed : textured incline. Rounded corners can also be added for a cleaner appearance and improved handling. 3. Add a Hollow Interior Remove material by enabling a hollow interior. Optionally add internal cutout patterns and customize the wall thickness, cell size, spacing, staggering, and rotation to achieve the right balance between strength and weight. 4. Render and Export Generate the ramp at the desired resolution and export it for slicing and printing. Ecco un progetto semplicissimo per rinfrescarvi nelle estati roventi davanti al pc. Un creativo e funzionale modello di Ice Cooler, a praticamente costo zero. L'idea è piuttosto semplice: sfruttare il ghiaccio per rinfrescare l'aria. Mettete una bottiglia di plastica da 500ml nel vostro freezer (attenzione a lasciare la bottiglia piena solo al 75/80% massimo, altrimenti esploderà!) e lasciatela congelare. Inseritela nell'alloggiamento del mio Ice Cooler e avviate la ventola. Entro pochi secondi, aria freschissima uscirà e vi donerà un gradevolissimo refrigerio. E può funzionare per diverse ore prima che il ghiaccio sia completamente sciolto e perda la sua efficacia!!!! Tutto quello di cui avrete bisogno è: - 1 ventola da PC 120x120mm a 12v - Un alloggiamento Batterie da 9v - 4 viti almeno da 50mm Io ho utilizzato questo hardware perchè il più comodo per me: ciò non toglie che potete valutare un'alimentazione da USB, o da PowerBank, con Regolatori di velocità etc etc. Sta solo a voi: il mio modello esige solo una ventola da 120mm; il cavo della ventola fuoriesce dal posteriore del Case e da lì potete fare quello che preferite. Una volta stampato tutto, testate i contatti della ventola unita al pacco della batteria da 9v, in modo da poter verificare la corretta direzione di rotazione della ventola (deve buttare aria FUORI dal Case, non dentro). Sì, la ventola è un 12v e la batteria un 9v, ma funzionerà benissimo, ad una velocità leggermente inferiore. Una volta verificato questo e segnato i corretti fili, inserite il filo della ventola nel buco in alto a sinistra e fatelo uscire dal posteriore, unendolo poi al pacco batteria. Avvitate la ventola nel case e inserite l'alloggiamento della bottiglia nel Case, prestando attenzione che la parte aperta sia in direzione della ventola. Ora, potete inserire la bottiglia ed accendere! Potete anche utilizzare il tappo per contenere al meglio la temperatura della bottiglia, migliorando la resa grazie anche ad un piccolo effetto “Venturi” causato dai piccoli fori in alto da cui viene aspirata l'aria che, scendendo attraverso la spirale, si raffredda più velocemente. Entro pochi secondi, sentirete una magnifica aria fresca uscire dal vostro nuovo Ice Cooler! Non dimenticate, quando cambiate la bottiglia, di verificare se la vaschetta di raccolta dell'acqua causata dalla condensa è da svuotare (alla base del Case dove va in appoggio la bottiglia). Buona estate a tutti!!!

description: Kumihimo Marudai Bracelet/Rope braiding stand This is a beginner friendly Kumihimo Marudai stand to make bracelets or rope using the ancient Japanese artform of Kumihimo , which is done by weaving strings of silk, rope or yarn together using a disc to form a rope/bracelet with artistic patterns in the process. The Marudai (Japanese, lit. “ Round Stand ”) allows you to move multiple strings at once using even back and forth movements of string to interlace the strings to form the weave of the bracelet or cord. This results in a faster weave compared to a hand-held portable Round Kumihimo Disc for round bracelets , but is less portable due to its larger form factor. Marudai stand with weighted bobbins and counterweight Usage A Kumihimo weave being formed through the center hole and pulled down by a counterweight attached to it The Marudai is used together with a center weight to pull on the formed weave through the hole in the center, and smaller weighted bobbins , called tama, on each individual string around the outsides. Commonly, the ratio of the weight is that the center weight will be between ½ to ⅔ of the combined weight of the outside weights. This balance ensures that the woven pattern will be consistent between each movement and result in a uniform shape and pattern of the bracelet/ropes. There is no hard rule of which side of the spectrum you decide on, it can depend on the particular use case of the weave. Using a heavier center weight will increase the pulling force and can result in a looser weave, whereas less center weight will provide lower resistance and give a tighter weave. You may purchase weighted bobbins and counterweights online or use 3D printed ones such as my Weighted Bobbin for Kumihimo braiding - Tama . Many different patterns of braids can be formed using a Marudai, such as alternating lines, dotted patterns, spirals and more. Assembly The assembly is quick and easy and can be done without tools. Hardware required Printed base , I recommend printing the weighted base, which gives the stand a stronger support Printed top disc , pick from a series of different discs depending on your level of experience and convenience desired Numbered Top disc with 32 notches and markers for 8-string and 16-string braids Great for beginners or those transitioning from a Kumihimo hand disc due to the familiar style Numbered Top disc with 32 round guides and markers for 8-string and 16-string braids A nice balance between full notches and a fully round disc, giving the best of both worlds holding the strings loosely in position, but being able to move them with a push rather than having to lift them out of the notches to re-arrange for complex patterns Top disc with 32 round guides and markers for 8-string and 16-string braids Same disc, but without number labels Numbered Top round disc without indentations. Markers for 8-string and 16-string braids This is the traditional form of a marudai disc and allows for quick re-arranging of strands following a series of moves. This requires practice as the strings will only be held in place by gravity as they are not guided to a particular location Top round disc without indentations. Markers for 8-string and 16-string braids Same disc, but without number labels Connecting rods (4x) You can either: Get 1/2 inch (12.7mm) round dowel rods (such as round wooden dowels ) from your local hardware store and cut them to size (I recommend a length of ~9inches, or 20-25cm for each rod) Or print the provided rods (24cm in length - you may resize the length as desired and based on your printers print bed) Optional rod connectors to extend the heigh of the stand, by connecting multiple rods together to form a taller stand A1 mini print size variant Someone requested a variant to fit on the A1 mini print bed, so I've published a A1 mini (180mm) size print profile - the top discs are resized to fit the bed and the connecting rods shortened as well. The weighted base is the same between the A1 mini and regular size and can be used interchangably with the same spacing between rods. The A1 mini profile contains 3 top disc variants: Notches with numbers and guide marks Round guide petal with guide marks Round disc with guide marks Assembly steps Place the bottom disc on the table or stable surface - this may either be the weighted bottom disc Weighted bottom disc or you can also decide to use one of the other pattern top disc as a bottom disc Round top disc being used as a bottom disc Push the four (4) connecting rods into the slots If you want to give it a stronger hold, you may use some glue and attach them permanently to the base Now attach the top disc to the top side of the connecting rods If you want to be able to change between different top plates, then I recommend not using glue for the top side. Optionally: if you want to make the stand taller , use the printable rod connectors to connect multiple rods to form a taller stand You may want to place additional weights onto the bottom to ensure the stand remains stable Rods extended using the optional rod connector Print Settings Supports / Brim: No Layer height: 0.20 mm Infill: 15% cubic for parts, 100% rectilinear for weighted base Walls: 2 Wall generation: Arachne for smooth curves Top/bottom pattern: Monotonic Orientation: Flat on the bed Material: PETG or PLA Kumihimo collection I've made a series of Kumihimo braiding related models to help me make neat Kumihimo braids, check them out: Weighted Bobbins for Kumihimo braiding To complement your Marudai, if you don't already have weights, you can print a set of Weighted Bobbin for Kumihimo braiding which make it easier to make neat braids by maintaining an even tension on the braid. Square Kumihimo disc for Flat bracelets If you're interested in making flat bracelets, you can check out my Square Kumihimo disc for flat bracelets which allows you to make some beautiful flat patterned bracelets. 32-slot Round Kumihimo disc for round bracelets If you are just starting out and want to make simpler bracelets, check out my 32-slot Round Kumihimo Disc for round bracelets which allows you to easily make Kumihimo bracelets with up to 16 strings (and if pushing it up to 20). 64-slot Large Kumihimo disc for complex pattern bracelets If you are looking for a way to make more complex patterns with more than 16 strings in a single weave, check out my 64-Slot Large Kumihimo disc for complex bracelets which allows you to make Kumihimo bracelets up to 40 strings, which is the practical limit for round Kumihimo braids.

description: 3D Printable Kerfmaker (Bridge City Inspired) Precision Joinery Without Measuring A kerfmaker is one of those simple woodworking tools that quickly becomes indispensable. It allows you to accurately size dados, grooves, rabbets, and other cuts to perfectly match the actual thickness of your material—without measuring, calipers, or complicated math. This is my own interpretation of the classic kerfmaker. I did not invent the kerfmaker , and credit for the original concept belongs to the woodworking community. My goal was to create a version that closely matches the functionality and style of the excellent Bridge City Toolworks Kerfmaker , while being easy to print, simple to assemble, and built with inexpensive, commonly available hardware. After searching MakerWorld, I noticed that many of the available printable kerfmakers were incomplete or required significant modification to become functional. This design is my attempt to provide a complete, easy-to-build solution that any woodworker with a 3D printer can make. Features Compact footprint 100 mm overall length 15.5 mm wide 38 mm tall Adjustable for a wide range of material thickness Captured hardware prevents nuts from spinning during adjustment Tight sliding keyway for accurate, repeatable settings Uses only four inexpensive pieces of hardware Perfect for table saws, router tables, dado setups, and joinery work Hardware Required You'll need: 1 × M4 × 16 mm flat head (countersunk) machine screw 1 × M4 × 20 mm flat head (countersunk) machine screw 2 × M4 hex nuts I used this metric hardware assortment: Metric Machine Screw Assortment Kit (Amazon) https://a.co/d/0eF5b6EH Any standard M4 hardware of the same sizes should also work. Assembly Assembly is straightforward and only takes a few minutes. The M4 nuts are captured inside the printed knobs during a pause in the print , creating comfortable hand-tightened knobs without requiring glue. The sliding fit between the parts is intentionally snug. The screw joining the two smaller pieces rides inside the keyway of the main body. The first 15–16 mm of travel may require some firm pressure as the screw head enters the slot. This is intentional and helps keep the assembly together during use. Once the screw passes this initial section, movement becomes much smoother while still maintaining a precise fit. If your printer runs slightly oversized, a light pass with fine sandpaper or a small file can make initial assembly easier. Why I Designed This I enjoy designing woodworking tools that solve practical problems in the shop. After looking around MakerWorld, I couldn't find a printable kerfmaker that checked all the boxes I was looking for, so I decided to design my own. My goals were to create a kerfmaker that was: Easy to print Easy to assemble Compact Durable Accurate Built using inexpensive, readily available hardware It's become a permanent addition to my own woodworking shop, and I hope it becomes one in yours as well. Disclaimer This is an original CAD model created by me. The kerfmaker concept has existed in woodworking for many years, and this design is inspired by the style and functionality of the Bridge City Toolworks Kerfmaker. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or produced by Bridge City Toolworks. If You Enjoyed This Model If you decide to print one, I'd love to see your build! description: A modular filament storage system inspired by one of the best designs on MakerWorld. Before anything else, I want to give full credit to Antiphrasis. Their modular filament rack has deservedly become one of the most popular storage systems on MakerWorld, with thousands of downloads, and it was their design that inspired me to explore a different engineering approach. Could I redesign the modular connection system so that each joint only required a single upright while still creating a strong, rigid structure? Rather than trying to improve every aspect of it, I focused on solving one specific engineering problem: Creating a connection system that locks adjacent modules together while using a single shared upright instead of two. The result is a storage system that is solid and stable while reducing the number of uprights required and maintaining a clean, modular appearance. I genuinely recommend taking a look at Antiphrasis' original design as well, then deciding which approach best suits your needs. 📦 Modular by design Each module baes stores three filament spools. Using two base sections and two uprights creates storage for six rolls, with additional modules simply extending the system. 🇪🇸 Férula Termoformable 3D de Ostec3D: Guía Oficial Descripción del Producto La Férula Termoformable de Ostec3D es una solución ortopédica avanzada, diseñada para sustituir las escayolas tradicionales. Fabricada mediante impresión 3D, esta férula se imprime de forma completamente plana y adquiere flexibilidad al sumergirse en agua caliente. Esto permite un moldeado anatómico directo sobre el paciente, garantizando un ajuste perfecto, peso ultraligero y excelente ventilación para la piel. Parámetros de Impresión 3D Para garantizar la flexibilidad correcta durante el calentamiento y la rigidez estructural una vez fría, la férula debe imprimirse estrictamente con la siguiente configuración: Altura de capa / Perfil: 0.24 mm Standard BBL Densidad de relleno: 8% (Relleno poco denso) Patrón de relleno: Rectilíneo Nota de fabricación: El uso del relleno rectilíneo al 8% es crucial. Si el relleno es más denso, el plástico no se ablandará de manera uniforme; si es diferente al rectilíneo, la férula podría perder su integridad estructural al doblarse. Guía de Uso y Moldeado 1.Calentar el agua: Temperatura del agua: 80°C - 95°C. Calienta agua en un recipiente lo suficientemente amplio para que quepa la férula plana. El agua debe estar a una temperatura de entre 80°C y 95°C. Es muy importante tener en cuenta que esta es la temperatura del agua, y no pasa con esa misma intensidad al material plástico. El propósito de usar el agua a esta temperatura es, simplemente, permitir que el plástico llegue a su punto de ablandamiento de forma mucho más rápida y sencilla. 2.Proteger al paciente: Antes de colocar la férula, cubre la extremidad del paciente con una malla tubular de algodón (vendaje tubular) para proteger la piel del contacto directo y del calor residual. 3.Sumergir la férula: Introduce la férula impresa en el agua caliente durante 1 a 3 minutos. Observarás que el material rígido comienza a volverse flexible y maleable como la goma. 4.Moldear sobre la anatomía: Retira la férula del agua (usa pinzas o guantes si es necesario), sacude el exceso de agua y comprueba rápidamente la temperatura tocándola ligeramente. Colócala sobre la extremidad del paciente y moldéala suavemente para que copie la anatomía exacta. 5.Enfriar y fijar: Mantén la férula en la posición deseada mientras se enfría a temperatura ambiente. Este proceso es muy rápido y tomará solo de 1 a 2 minutos. Una vez fría, recuperará su rigidez total. Fíjala con correas de velcro o vendaje según sea necesario. 💡 Modificaciones y Re-termoformado: Si la férula no queda perfecta en el primer intento o si el paciente requiere un ajuste posterior por cambios en la inflamación, el material puede volver a calentarse. Simplemente sumerge la férula (o la zona específica que deseas ajustar) nuevamente en el agua caliente, y podrá ser termoformada nuevamente para cualquier modificación. 🇬🇧 Ostec3D Thermoformable 3D Splint: Official Guide Product Description The Ostec3D Thermoformable Splint is an advanced orthopedic solution designed to replace traditional plaster casts. Manufactured via 3D printing, this splint is printed completely flat and becomes flexible when submerged in hot water. This allows for direct anatomical molding onto the patient, ensuring a perfect custom fit, ultra-lightweight feel, and excellent skin ventilation. 3D Printing Parameters To guarantee the correct flexibility during heating and structural rigidity once cooled, the splint must be printed strictly using the following settings: Layer Height / Profile: 0.24 mm Standard BBL Infill Density: 8% (Sparse infill) Infill Pattern: Rectilinear Manufacturing Note: Using an 8% rectilinear infill is crucial. If the infill is too dense, the plastic will not soften evenly; if a different pattern is used, the splint may lose its structural integrity when bent. Usage and Molding Guide 1.Heat the water: Water temperature: 80°C - 95°C (176°F - 203°F). Heat water in a container wide enough to fit the flat splint. The water must be heated to a temperature between 80°C and 95°C (176°F - 203°F). It is important to note that this is the temperature of the water, and it does not fully transfer to the plastic material. The purpose of using water at this temperature is simply to help the plastic reach its softening point much more easily and quickly. 2.Protect the patient: Before applying the splint, cover the patient's limb with a cotton tubular stockinette to protect their skin from direct contact and residual heat. 3.Submerge the splint: Place the printed splint into the hot water for 1 to 3 minutes. You will notice the rigid material begin to turn flexible and rubber-like. 4.Mold to anatomy: Remove the splint from the water (use tongs or gloves if necessary), shake off the excess water, and quickly test the temperature by touching it lightly. Place it over the patient's limb and gently mold it so it contours to their exact anatomy. 5.Cool and secure: Hold the splint in the desired position while it cools to room temperature. This process is very fast and will take only 1 to 2 minutes. Once completely cool, it will regain its full rigidity. Secure it in place using velcro straps or bandages as needed. 💡 Modifications and Re-thermoforming: If the splint doesn't fit perfectly on the first try, or if the patient needs an adjustment later due to swelling changes, the material can be reheated. Simply submerge the splint (or the specific area you wish to adjust) back into the hot water, and it can be thermoformed again for any required modifications.

I was tired of "one-size-fits-all" sink caddies that sat loosely in the middle of my divided sink, slid around, and got in my way. I also hated that I couldn't put them at the top or bottom of my sink due to its curves. So, I designed a sink caddy that looks “built in”; it hugs the dimensions of my sink, fits flush with the upper or lower curves, and eliminates wobble. Sweet. I wanted to make some for friends, but their sinks were all shaped differently… Lame. My only viable option was to turn the model into a parametric caddy that could be customized after taking a few measurements of their sink. When that was done, I decided to go ham and make the basket sizes individually customizable, and then added a single basket option as well. 🧮 Customization for everything but the kitchen sink Use the customize button to tweak your dimensions and even print a fit test before committing to the full caddy. Basket sizes and combinations: Adjust the total length of the caddy from front to back. Independently configure how deep each basket sits inside your sink and how far out it extends into the basin. (Height + Width) Toggle either side on/off to generate a single sturdy basket. Generate unlimited combinations sized for various items or needs, while keeping a clean, built-in look. Sink dimensions (measurement guide at the end): Inner Sink Curve Radius: Hugs the exact rounded (or straight) corners of your basin where the divider meets the sink walls. Divider Width and Top Curve Radius: Generates a perfectly snug bridge over your sink divider. The top curve can be 0 (flat), but it looks nicer if there are no gaps. Advanced/Optional Settings: Counter Overhang - My sink has a nasty overhang so I created this setting to automatically notch the back of the baskets so they slide underneath. If you also have an overhang, I'm sorry. But at least it gives us added stability. Sink Taper/Grade - Angles the baskets to match the slope of your sink walls to sit flush. Most people won't have to touch this. Fit test for the filament frugal: Toggle the “Generate Fit Test Cutout” option to remove the baskets and print only the divider bridge to ensure everything sits flush. “Fit test height” allows you to print a taller or shorter segment to test your sink’s taper, or test only the bridge itself. Note: fit tests get printed upside down to minimize support filament. 🖨️ Printing Instructions & Best Practices using Bambu Studio/Handy If you follow the measurement guide below you will be fine printing directly from the Bambu Handy customizer to get a sturdy flush-fit caddy. The only exception being a multi-height basket (see support section). Included Profile to boost customizer print quality in Bambu Studio: Because the parametric model maker only allows limited slicer optimization, I made the “Customizer Profile” to apply all my highly-optimized global slicer settings (walls, seams, speed, overhangs, strength, etc.). The only other thing I might suggest is adding extra cooling to your filament profile. I set my Bambu Matte PLA to 100% Part/Aux fans after the 2nd layer. Here is how to use it: Generate your caddy via the customizer, download STL (optional) Enable “fit test” in customizer, click generate, download .3mf, print to ensure fit Download/Open the “Customizer Profile” in Bambu Studio Import your customizer STL file, replace model on the plate You are ready to roll!! Bridge/Basket Support: Same height baskets will print with slim trees to support the divider bridge via the .3mf. It works great, but of course if you have a dual nozzle you can flip the support interface to PETG. If you are printing a "Multi-Height" variation where one basket floats in mid-air, a 0 Z-gap PETG support interface is strongly recommended to provide a solid floor for the basket corners to print on. Bambu Studio will probably want you to use normal support, but tree [strong] is just fine. 🛠️ Advanced 3D Printing Engineering This model is a bunch of pieces that all sync together with code based on your inputs. The geometry is heavily optimized for customization but a few caveats: I spent an incredible amount of time testing various sink dimensions and basket sizes, tweaking the code to ensure a clean print and that all reasonable dimensions will work without breaking the model. That said, I can't guarantee every single combination of basket size, sink curve, height, etc will work, and there may be small issues and edge cases. If you find one, comment with your dimensions and I’ll take a look. If you aren't sure about your measurements, please use the print test customization option to print a small section to ensure a good fit! 📏 How to Measure Your Sink for a Flush-Fit Caddy These don't have to be exact, but you'll have a sturdier and better looking caddy the closer you get. If you aren't sure about any measurements, print the customizer’s fit test option before printing a full caddy. Measuring will take about 5 minutes once you have what you need. Let’s go! 1. Inner Sink Curve Radius This is the curve of your sink's corners. Because it's hard to measure with a ruler, I suggest printing this awesome tool: If you have a large curve: RadGauge Dual Mega If you have a small curve: RadGauge Dual Quick hack: Find any circular object (I initially used a coaster) that fits nicely in your sink’s upper divider corner, measure the width, divide by two, done. Alternatively, tie some string to a pencil and make some circles on paper. 2. Divider Width & Top Curve Radius Measure the thickness of the bridge between your two sink basins. Make sure to measure the thickness below the top curve (where the walls straighten out) so the caddy doesn't get stuck. If the top edges of your divider are curved, you can use the outer-curve side of the RadGauge Dual to measure it. Quick hack: You can get away with measuring tape on the width (when in doubt round up) and leaving the top curve at low number. 3. Sink Taper / Grade Grab any straight flat object like a ruler or remote and press it flat against the top half of your sink divider. If it looks perfectly vertical, go with 0. If it looks only very slightly off, leave the preset .5mm or bump to 1mm. You can also measure how much the sink wall moves inwards per 100mm with two rulers. When in doubt, use the customizer fit test height option to print a tall test. If anyone wants taper tests let me know, I'll upload a plate. 4. Counter Overhang (if needed) If you have an under-mount sink where the countertop sticks out over the basin, measure how far the counter protrudes past the sink wall. Input this number in mm to generate a custom notch so your baskets slide underneath. 🔥And that's it! 🔥 Thanks for checking out my project. I’m new to 3d printing so if anyone has any advice or suggestions on how to improve the model or profile settings, I’m all ears. If you decide to print a basket, I would love to see it. Cheers, WK Changelog Update 7/24/26: Based on feedback, added adjustable chamfers to all interior and exterior edges that are not hugging the sink (enabled by default). Should be easier to clean and much harder to get scraped by a sharp edge. Update 7/24/26: Fixed chamfer extrusion when generating single basket caddy.

Rim Thickness Controls how far the rim extends outward. 📏 Spout Controls Setting What It Does Spout Length Controls the total centerline length of the complete spout, including all straight and curved sections. Spout Style Selects a straight-diameter or tapered spout. Spout End Diameter Controls the outlet diameter at the very end when a tapered spout is selected. Spout Path Selects a straight spout, one bend, or two bends. The spout length is measured along the entire path, not just vertically from the funnel. Increasing a bend angle or radius uses more of the selected spout length. ↪️ First Bend Controls Setting What It Does First Bend Start Distance Controls how far the spout travels straight down before the first bend begins. First Bend Angle Controls how far the first bend turns away from vertical. First Bend Radius Controls how tight or wide the first curve is. First Bend Direction Selects whether the spout bends left or right. A larger bend radius creates a smoother, wider curve. A smaller radius creates a tighter elbow. ↩️ Second Bend Controls Setting What It Does Distance Between Bends Controls the straight section between the end of the first bend and the beginning of the second. Second Bend Angle Mode Selects whether the second bend automatically matches the first bend or uses a custom angle. Second Bend Angle Controls the second bend angle when Custom mode is selected. Second Bend Radius Controls how tight or wide the second curve is. Second Bend Direction Selects whether the second bend continues in the same direction or bends back the opposite way. Match First Mode When the second bend is set to Match First and the direction is set to Opposite , the second bend automatically cancels the angle of the first bend. For example: First bend: 55° right Second bend: 55° left Final outlet direction: straight down This creates an offset spout while keeping the outlet vertical. Custom Mode Select Custom to control the second bend independently. This allows the final outlet to point inward, outward, sideways, or at any angle between the available limits. 🛡️ Automatic Geometry Protection The generator automatically checks the selected measurements and adjusts impossible combinations that would otherwise create broken geometry. This includes: Bend angles that consume more than the available spout length Bend start distances that are too long Excessive spacing between the bends Bend radii that are too tight for the selected spout size Negative final straight sections Invalid outlet or wall-thickness combinations Any automatic adjustments are shown in the OpenSCAD console so you can see which setting was limited. 💡 Possible Uses Automotive fluid funnels Oil and coolant funnels Bottle filling Powder transfer Seed and pellet funnels Resin and paint transfer Workshop machines Aquarium equipment Kitchen containers Hard-to-reach fill ports Offset container openings Custom replacement funnels Because every dimension is adjustable, the same generator can create a small precision funnel or a large workshop funnel. 📐 Design Notes The curved spout is generated as one continuous swept tube. Both the inside and outside follow the same centerline path through the straight sections and bends. This creates: Smooth internal transitions Consistent wall thickness No sharp joints between sections One continuous watertight model Proper tapered geometry through the curves

description: Fly Swatter Fan – Holographic Fly Deterrent Help keep flies away from your food without chemicals or loud buzzing! This Fly Swatter Fan uses spinning TPU blades that display the holographic texture transferred from a textured PEI build plate. As the blades rotate, they create constantly changing flashes of reflected light that discourage flies from landing near your food. How It Works Flies have compound eyes that are highly sensitive to movement and rapidly changing light. As the holographic blades spin, they create constantly shifting reflections that can make the area appear unstable or difficult for flies to land in. Because of this, flies will often choose to fly somewhere else instead. Unlike sticky traps or chemical repellents, this design relies only on motion and reflected light to help discourage flies from landing near your food. Features 🪰 Designed to help discourage flies from landing on food. ✨ Uses a holographic/textured PEI build plate to create reflective effects. 🧪 Chemical-free operation. 🔇 Very quiet while running. 🔋 Powered by 3 AAA batteries using the Maker's Beginner Kit motor and battery hardware. 🛡️ Flexible TPU blades are designed to stop spinning if they encounter resistance, such as being touched, helping reduce the chance of injury. Printing Recommendations Print the blades in TPU for flexibility. Print the reflective side directly on a holographic/textured PEI build plate for the best effect. Use a light-colored filament to maximize the holographic reflections. Balance the blades for smooth, quiet operation. Disclaimer This device is intended as a fly deterrent, not a guaranteed insect repellent. Effectiveness may vary depending on lighting conditions, fly species, and the surrounding environment. This is my first design including motors so issues may arise and I love to hear feedback. If you enjoy this design, please leave a like, upload a Make, and share your print settings. I'd love to see your finished Fly Swatter Fan! Credits Thanks to Bam Bam Design for the “ Planetary Gearbox for 030 Motor ” it was a very helpful template to start with the motor housing. Download link (won't work for this model since its modified): https://makerworld.com/en/models/1948420-planetary-gearbox-for-030-motor#profileId-2093403 I also used the triple A version of Viltzu's “ Battery Holder for Maker's Beginner Kit ” Download link is https://makerworld.com/en/models/1146858-battery-holder-for-maker-s-beginner-kit#profileId-1150232 Assembly Instructions Print Plate 1 in PETG preferably but PLA will work(might deform in heat) then print plate 2 in TPU. Print the triple A version of Viltzu's “ Battery Holder for Maker's Beginner Kit ” Download link is https://makerworld.com/en/models/1146858-battery-holder-for-maker-s-beginner-kit#profileId-1150232 Battery Box Begin by assembling the battery box using Viltzu's assembly instructions . Motor Assembly Place Part 1 (pictured at the bottom from left to right) over the motor. Slide the gear Part 2 onto the motor shaft. Install Part 3 on top of the gear. Insert the completed motor assembly into the bottom of Part 4 . Apply a small drop of glue to Part 1 to secure the motor assembly inside Part 4 . Slide Part 5 into place and snap the assembly together. Blade Assembly Slide the two TPU blades into the slots on the top hub, making sure the holographic textured side is facing upward . Main Tower Assembly Connect the motor to the battery box using the supplied wires. Insert the + (cross-shaped) axle into the motor shaft. Apply a small amount of glue around the outside of Part 5 inside the motor housing. Slide the completed motor assembly into the bottom of the cone until it is fully seated, making sure the cross-shaped axle protrudes through the top. Install the battery box by fitting its four corners into the matching slots in the cone. Ensure the ON/OFF switch is facing downward . Press the blade assembly onto the cross-shaped axle until it is fully seated. Install 3 AAA batteries , switch the fan on, and enjoy a quieter, chemical-free way to help discourage flies from landing near your food.

Want a cute storage solution for your knick-knacks? Wish you had a quick and easy setup for displaying them at a market or craft fair? Look no further! I combined these concepts into one 3-tiered solution. This is the mini version, meaning each box is ~45mm wide and ~35mm deep (except for the bottom box, which is closer to 40mm deep). (Full-size version is near-complete, but it doesn't stay together as securely as Id like!) I designed them to sit nicely on top of each other when closed, and used the back-brace as a way to secure it all together as well as support it when displayed. When fully open for display, I noticed the middle box sagged backwards a little, so I made a little spacer that wedges into the middle divider and against the topmost box to keep it straight! The back-brace also shifts down to support the full height of the display when open, and back up when it's packed up again. I can hold and shake this thing sideways, frontways, upsidedown, and toss it into a large box with other loose things, and it stays closed quite well! I recommend PETG for the bolts that hold the screws on, but PLA should work too. (Just be sure to sloooow down the first layer of PETG if you use it, I had a fun time working out how to get the thing to stick down with such a small object). Requires: Two (2) 2.5mm x 10 mm screws (to hold the back brace on) and Sixteen (16) 2.5mm x 8mm screws (to attached the levers to the boxes). I used machine screws as that's what I had, but any screw in those sizes should work! The holes for the screws may need a bit of loosening if your filament has sagged down, I found this was easier than dealing with supports for them. Assembly is as simple as attaching the levers and the back-brace to the boxes as shown in the photos. The top lid slides on and off, and has a small lip to secure it in place when closed. I usually just keep the spacer wedge for the middle box inside one of the middle compartments for when I open it up. This is my first proper 3D model! I'm very open to improvements, so please try it out for yourself and let me know what you think!

The pin diameter, barrel size, clearance, retainer thickness, and end spacing can all be adjusted. Small breakaway tabs support the pin during printing. description: Press the Customize button to customize! Funnels glug because a sealed bottle neck traps air with nowhere to go, so the liquid backs up and chugs instead of pouring in a steady stream. This funnel fixes that with vent ribs that hold the neck slightly open the entire time it's inserted, letting air escape while liquid pours in fast and uninterrupted. As far as I could find, no parametric fast-flow funnel existed anywhere before this one, so I built one from scratch: a fully parametric design built around a single smooth curve running through four diameters, from the spout tip up to the top opening, so you can shape anything from a classic single cone to a bulged, hourglass, or S-curved profile just by dragging four diameter sliders and three height sliders. Add a rim flange for a sturdier print and a hanging handle. Prints wide mouth down, spout pointing up, with no supports needed. I've tested the flow rate and the one in the default profile can fast flow a 2L bottle at about 200mL/s, so it can fill a 2L bottle in about 10s. Key Features Fast, glug-free flow: raised, round-profile vent ribs follow the shell's exact curve all the way from the spout tip to the rim, holding a bottle's neck slightly open so air can escape while liquid pours in at full speed instead of backing up and chugging; this is the entire reason the funnel exists Four-diameter taper profile: set diameter_1 (the spout tip) through diameter_4 (the top opening), and the three heights between them (height_1, height_2, height_3), for full control over the funnel's shape One continuous curve: the three tapered segments blend into each other with zero-slope tangency at every diameter, so there's no visible kink or seam anywhere along the profile True exterior diameters: every diameter you set is the actual printed OD at that height, including the vent ribs' bulge, so what you dial in is what comes off the bed Rim flange: optional flat flange around the top opening, wider than the taper, for extra bed contact and rigidity Hanging handle: optional flat handle with a hanging hole, with adjustable length, width, hole size, and placement angle around the rim Cross-section preview: switch view to cross_section and sweep cross_section_angle to inspect the wall thickness and curve before you commit to a print Print Settings Setting Recommended Orientation Print exactly as generated: wide mouth down on the bed, spout pointing up Supports Not required; the diameter only ever decreases going up, so every overhang is self-supporting Perimeters 2-3 Infill 10-15% Material PLA is fine for water and dry goods; use PETG, ASA, or ABS if you'll be pouring hot liquids, oil, fuel, or other automotive fluids through it Download the optimized print profile from this page, delete the sample models off the plate, and import your STL into it. How to Use Funnel Dimensions: set diameter_1 through diameter_4 and height_1 through height_3 to shape the taper, plus wall_thickness. Rim (optional): leave add_rim on for extra bed contact and rigidity, and adjust rim_added_diameter to taste, or turn it off. Vent ribs (optional): leave add_vent_ribs on for glug-free pouring, and adjust vent_rib_count and vent_rib_width, or turn it off. Handle (optional): leave add_handle on and adjust handle_length, handle_width, handle_hole_diameter, and handle_angle, or turn it off. Export the STL, delete the sample models off the plate, and import your STL into the print profile. Customization Use the MakerWorld Customizer. All parameters are grouped and annotated. View - view: funnel for the printable model, cross_section to preview a cutaway - cross_section_angle: angle of the cutting plane, degrees (cross_section view only) Funnel Dimensions - diameter_1: exterior diameter at the spout tip (bottom-most point), including any vent rib bulge (mm) - height_1: height of the tapered section from diameter_1 up to diameter_2 (mm) - diameter_2: exterior diameter at the first midpoint, including any vent rib bulge (mm) - height_2: height of the tapered section from diameter_2 up to diameter_3 (mm) - diameter_3: exterior diameter at the second midpoint, including any vent rib bulge (mm) - height_3: height of the tapered section from diameter_3 up to diameter_4 (mm) - diameter_4: exterior diameter at the top opening, including any vent rib bulge (mm) - wall_thickness: thickness of the funnel wall (mm) Rim - add_rim: add a flat rim flange around the top opening - rim_added_diameter: how much wider the rim flange's diameter is than the top opening (mm) Vent Ribs - add_vent_ribs: add vent ribs along the wall for fast, glug-free pouring (leave this on unless you have a specific reason to print a plain smooth cone) - vent_rib_count: number of vent ribs, evenly spaced around the circumference - vent_rib_width: width (diameter) of each vent rib's round cross-section (mm) Handle - add_handle: add a flat handle with a hanging hole, attached at the rim - handle_length: how far the handle extends outward from the rim (mm) - handle_width: width of the handle, and diameter of its rounded ends (mm) - handle_hole_diameter: diameter of the hanging hole (mm) - handle_angle: angle around the funnel where the handle is placed Why Fast Flow Every funnel I could find, printable or store-bought, seals against a bottle neck so tightly that air can't get past the liquid, which is exactly what causes the glug-glug-glug and slows the pour to a crawl. This design's vent ribs run the full length of the funnel wall, from spout tip to rim, so they hold the neck open just enough for air to escape the whole time liquid is flowing. That's the actual purpose of this project; the parametric taper, rim, and handle are all built around that one goal. Since I couldn't find a parametric fast-flow funnel anywhere else, this one is meant to fill that gap, so pull the sliders to whatever size and shape you need and it'll still pour fast. Shaping Notes Since all three tapered segments blend together with matching tangents at every diameter, you can make diameter_2 or diameter_3 larger than their neighbors on either side for a bulged, hourglass, or barrel shape instead of a plain cone, with no added kink or fillet needed to keep the curve smooth. Setting diameter_2 and diameter_3 equal to diameter_4 (a common case) collapses the middle section into a straight-sided neck between two tapers.

Customizable size The model is fully customizable using the below parameters: When you export the model from the “customize” tab, it will appear as a fully assembled box. In the slicer, you can right click and “split to objects" as shown: once split it will all be in 1 pile on the plate you must drag each piece to position it, and make sure the lid and hinge flat side is on the plate. Adjustable Parameters The model includes parameters for: Number of vial spaces (Width) Number of vial spaces (Length) Vial diameter Vial spacing Box length (automatic) Box width (automatic) Latch width Hinge spacing Hinge insert clearance Hinge opening Wall thickness Base height Lid height Please ensure you are adjusting the base height and lid height for you vial needs. These do not update as it is difficult to tie those together so must be manually updates Important Notes ⚠ Single Hinge / Single Latch Design This version uses a single hinge and single latch . It performs exceptionally well for small and medium-sized boxes. As the box becomes larger, you may notice a small amount of lid movement or "wiggle" due to the increased span. This is normal for a single-hinge design and does not generally affect functionality. For very large configurations, a future multi-hinge/multi-latch version may provide additional rigidity. ⚠ Box Height Does NOT Automatically Resize The box automatically adjusts its length and width , but it does not automatically adjust the height for different vial sizes. If you change to a taller or shorter vial, you must manually adjust: Base Height Lid Height A good starting point is to make the combined base and lid height approximately 2 mm taller than your vial to provide adequate clearance for printing tolerances and easy removal. Example: 40 mm tall vial → Total inside height ≈ 42 mm To calculate inside height you must add wall thickness for both the lid and base, otherwise the inside height will be off by wall thickness X 2 ⚠ Latch Width The latch width is user adjustable. Larger boxes may benefit from a wider latch for additional strength, while smaller boxes can use a narrower latch. ⚠ Changing Vial Diameter Changing the vial diameter automatically resizes the footprint of the box, but remember to verify and adjust the box height separately if your new vial has a different overall height. Printing Recommendations PETG is highly recommended. This design has been extensively tested in PETG across a wide range of sizes and configurations with excellent results. PLA should also print and function well , although it has not been tested as extensively. No supports required. Print the parts in the supplied orientation. No hardware, screws, magnets, or additional components are required for assembly. description: Hey guys, the new mushroom hole punch you’ve been waiting for is finally here! This is the first in a new series of fully 3D printed mushroom-style punches designed for discbound notebooks and pocket-sized planners. It lets you punch your own paper, photos, dividers and other inserts, so you’re no longer limited to buying pre-punched sheets. The entire punch prints in place in around 1.5 hours , including the smooth hinged mechanism. Small side guides help position paper up to approximately 108 mm wide , making it ideal for smaller notebooks and pocket-sized discbound systems. A lot of testing went into this design. I went through nearly ten different versions of the mushroom cutting profile alone, trying to get the cleanest and most reliable cut possible. I eventually narrowed it down to two profiles: W-Shaped Profile This gave me the best overall results across most of my testing. Curved Profile This performed better with certain paper types and thicknesses. Directions for Use Place the paper right up against the hinge, then move the guide into position so it just touches the edge of the paper. Put both hands on the press and apply equal pressure on both sides. Push down firmly in one clean motion until you hear and feel a solid click. If one side goes down before the other, the cuts may vary. For the cleanest result, press straight down evenly with both hands in one smooth “thoom.” …………………………… Both versions are included, so you can test them and decide which works best for the paper you use. One of my main goals was to make it capable of punching 160 GSM paper , as this is a popular thickness for making sturdy notebook pages. It can also work with thinner or thicker paper, although results may vary depending on the material and cutting profile. Occasionally, some paper may leave a tiny whisk of material that can be removed with almost no effort. Considering this is a fully printed, free alternative to an expensive metal discbound punch, I think that is a pretty fair trade-off! As always, this model went through plenty of testing, tweaking and re-tweaking before release. I’m really proud of how smoothly the hinge works, and I hope it helps you create your own custom notebooks and planners. hope yous enjoy the pile of test prints haha :) ####I’ve also included a simple front and back cover , along with a ready-to-download print profile, to help you get started with your first pocket-sized discbound notebook.#### share your makes, results and which cutting profile worked best for you! This is only release one! Next up should be the eight-hole version , as I know that is the one a lot of commenters have been waiting for. After that, I’ll also be remaking the seven-hole version , and then we’ll see how far we can take the series from there. Thank you all for helping keep me motivated throughout this journey. This originally started as a fun little project for a family member, but your support has turned it into something much bigger than I expected. This is now my full-time job, so any boosts, shares, downloads, or support through my Buy Me a Coffee page would be massively appreciated. Thank you all so much for the encouragement and inspiration. Have a great day, everyone!

As a dedicated car audio guy , I build a ton of custom grills for subwoofers, door speakers and cooling vents. Using MakerWorld's MakerLab / Parametric Model Maker, you can adjust everything on the fly: 3 Distinct Mesh Patterns: Choose between Honeycomb (classic hex), Grid (clean square mesh), or Circles (staggered bubble pattern). Fully Adjustable Outer Rim: Dial in the exact outer diameter, rim width, and total thickness. Smart Mounting Holes: Set your screw hole count (from 0 to 24), hole diameter, and edge spacing. The code automatically spaces them symmetrically! Custom Edge Chamfers: Add a smooth 3D chamfer to the top, bottom, or both sides of the outer rim to give your build a highly polished, professional finish. 🎛️ How to Customize Your Grills Click the Customize button here on MakerWorld. Main Dimensions: Put in your target outer diameter and desired plate thickness. Pattern Settings: Swap between honeycomb, grid, or circles, and adjust the cell size and wall thickness to control how "open" or "dense" the mesh is. Chamfer Settings: Set your chamfer size (e.g., 1mm or 1.5mm) and choose where you want it (e.g., select top to give your mounting screws a slightly countersunk look). Mounting Holes: Set the exact number of mounting screws your speaker or vent frame requires. MODYLO Quiver Same idea as the MODYLO Column rod, but for tubes. Open the Customizer, set the length and the inner diameter you want, hit Generate. It works out how many segments you need, lays them out on the plate, and you screw them together afterwards. I built it to store posters. Then I built a fat one to hold the tablecloth that lives rolled on a Column. If you read one thing, read this Segments print standing on the bed, and tall standing prints topple if adhesion is not right. This is the single thing that goes wrong. The Quiver is much steadier than a Column rod, because a 40 to 90 mm tube has a far wider footprint than a 30 mm stick. I did not need a brim. But if you have had tall prints fail before, here is the order to reach for: Clean plate. Soap, then isopropyl. A Cool Plate SuperTack helps a lot. Lower Max segment height. More segments, shorter ones, far less leverage. This is the most effective dial you have. Add an external brim to the segments (not the caps). Use Quiver Braced. Two versions in this listing Quiver - no internal bracing. Fewer parts, less filament, faster. Use this if you have your process under control. Quiver Braced - generates a sacrificial support tube inside each segment. It has a wide base for bed grip and is held to the inner wall by a few small tabs, so the segment can't pivot on its base and the tabs break away cleanly afterwards. Minimum length 180 mm. Both use the same geometry and the same thread. The braced version just leaves the support features enabled. Pick whichever suits your printer, they assemble together. The bracing costs about 185 g and 3h40 on a 1.4 m tube. If your printer handles tall prints and your plate adhesion is good, skip it. If you have had segments fall, it is worth every gram. MakerWorld's Customizer cannot switch a Fusion feature on and off, which is why this is two entries rather than one checkbox. What you can set Parameter Range What it does Total length 30 to 3000 mm (Quiver) 180 to 3000 mm (Quiver Braced) The usable space inside the finished tube. Inner diameter 40 to 90 mm The narrowest opening inside the tube. Whatever you want to store has to fit through this. Extra wall thickness 0 mm and up Added on top of the 2.8 mm default wall. Max segment height Quiver only The longest a single segment is allowed to be. Lower it for more segments, shorter ones, and less chance of anything toppling mid-print. Length is usable internal length. It does not include the threads or the caps. If your poster is 841 mm, ask for 841 mm. Ask for 850 if you want a little slack. Add roughly 17 mm to the outside length when you are working out shelf space. Inner diameter is the narrowest point, which is the wall inside the top thread, not the middle of the tube. So the number you set is the number that matters: if it says 60, a 60 mm roll goes in. Extra wall thickness does two jobs: a stiffer tube, and a heavier, more stable segment while it prints. At 40 mm diameter and full height, a millimetre or two is cheap insurance. Max segment height is the toppling dial. If your printer struggles with tall prints, bring it down. You get more joints and a slightly longer total print, and much less risk. It is only on the unbraced version, since the braced one solves the same problem a different way. What size do I need? Length, by content: Content Short side Ask for A3 297 mm 300 mm A2 420 mm 425 mm A1 594 mm 600 mm A0 841 mm 850 mm US 24 × 36 in 610 mm 615 mm Inner diameter, by use: Use Suggested ID One or two posters, light stock 40 mm Several posters, or heavy / matte stock that creases 60 mm Rolled around a 30 mm Column rod (tablecloth, fabric, banner) 60 mm Rolled around a Column with a thick fabric, or a big stack 90 mm Tight rolls leave memory creases in heavy paper. If in doubt go one size up, the extra filament is mostly in the length, not the diameter. Printing Segments print standing on the bed, threaded socket down . The caps print flat. The Customizer lays this out for you, but the plate layout is not preserved if you re-slice from a saved profile, so check it. Quick self-check: if your slice is full of supports, the orientation is wrong. Layer height: 0.2 mm Walls: 2 Infill: lightning. This one matters. A gyroid or grid infill sends the toolhead darting back and forth on every layer, and on a tall thin segment that is exactly the force that tips it over. Lightning leaves the head running smooth continuous loops around the wall. Less filament, less time, and much less shaking. Supports: none. All overhangs clear along the vertical axis. Brim: I did not need one. The tube footprint is much wider than a Column rod, so it sits far more solidly. If you see any lifting, or you have had tall prints fail before, add an external brim to the segments and leave it off the caps. Filament: standard PLA Real slice, 1.4 m tube, 60 mm inner diameter, 7 segments of 200 mm on one plate: Version Filament Time Quiver 595 g 12h39 Quiver Braced 780 g 16h19 If you have had segments topple, print fewer per plate. The risk is not really about any single segment, it is about how long they all stand there and how much the toolhead has to travel between them. Seven segments standing for twelve hours is seven chances, and one faller can take out its neighbours. Printing them one at a time costs surprisingly little: about 1h50 each plus a few minutes of prep, so roughly 40 minutes more machine time across the whole tube. You pay for it in plate changes, not in printing. Worth it if the alternative is losing a plate at hour ten. Worth being straight about this: a cardboard poster tube costs a few euros and this does not beat it on price. What it gives you is the exact length you asked for, a screw cap that actually closes, segments you can reconfigure later, and an object that will outlive twenty cardboard tubes. On the wall: the 2.8 mm figure is the wall envelope, not 2.8 mm of solid plastic. Inside it, two printed skins with lightning infill between them. That is deliberate: faster, lighter, and far more stable on a tall segment. Plenty stiff for storage. Do not stand on it. Assembly Screw the segments together. The thread is a 3-start thread with a detent, so it seats firmly and does not back out on its own. Every segment is identical, so: Assemble them in any order A cap screws onto any segment, at either end A 900 mm tube can be taken apart and rebuilt as two shorter ones with a second pair of caps Print one spare segment now and extend the tube later instead of reprinting it Dry-fit keeps it adjustable. A drop of glue on the threads makes it permanent and noticeably stiffer. Your call. Seam tip: set seam position to Back before slicing. Not Aligned. Aligned drifts the seam around from segment to segment and you can never line them up. Back puts it in the same place on every segment. Then, because the thread is 3-start, each joint seats in three positions 120° apart. Dry-fit and try all three at each joint, keep the one that lines up. You end up with a seam running close to straight down the whole tube instead of spiralling. Pairs with MODYLO Column MODYLO Column is the same idea as a solid rod. Roll fabric onto a Column, slide the whole thing into a Quiver, cap both ends. That is the setup I use for the tablecloth, and it is what a 60 mm inner diameter is sized for. Tell me what you put in it I make things because I need them, then share them in case someone else does. description: 🦷 Dental Tooth & Gum Demonstration Model with Weighted Display Stand This is a realistic dental demonstration model (cartoonish picture with the real dentist for proprotions) designed for dentists to clearly explain treatments and procedures to their patients. It represents a cross-section of a tooth and surrounding gum , allowing patients to better understand tooth anatomy and what their treatment involves. The project was developed in collaboration with a practicing dentist , ensuring it meets the needs of daily clinical use while remaining practical, durable, and visually engaging. The tooth and gum are separate pieces , allowing the tooth to be removed from the gum and shown more closely to patients during consultations. The display stand was designed in Fusion 360 , while the tooth and gum were sculpted in Nomad Sculpt to achieve a realistic organic appearance. The stand includes a hidden cavity that can be filled with weights, such as old screws, nuts, or other metal pieces, giving it excellent stability and preventing it from tipping over during demonstrations. For the model shown in the photos, I used clear UV resin to recreate the enamel, producing a remarkably realistic translucent effect. I also used thin electrical wires to represent the nerves and blood vessels inside the tooth. Once positioned, they were secured with super glue and encapsulated with UV resin for a clean, natural finish. Rather than using an AMS, I chose to hand-paint the entire model using an airbrush and fine brushes. This gave me much greater control over the colours and subtle shading, resulting in a unique, highly realistic finish. Of course, if you have an AMS, you can also download the individual parts and create your own multicolour version. I would recommend printing all the parts in white filament and treating the painting as part of the project. It's incredibly rewarding and allows you to achieve a truly professional-looking result. This model has taken many months of design, sculpting, testing, and refinement , and I'm incredibly happy with how it turned out. My dentist friend was genuinely surprised by how professional and useful it looked, which made all the effort worthwhile. If you decide to print it, I'd be truly grateful if you could share a photo of your make . Seeing other people enjoying and using my designs is the best reward I could ask for. Thank you very much, and I hope you enjoy building and painting it! The display stand looks stunning on Wood PLA, also includes a small name plate at the front, allowing you to personalize the model with a dentist's name, clinic name, or logo from the bambulab text option . This adds a professional touch and makes it ideal for use in dental practices, consultation rooms, or educational displays. Features: Realistic cross-section of a tooth and gum Designed in collaboration with a dentist Removable tooth for closer patient demonstrations Weighted display stand for excellent stability Tooth and gum sculpted in Nomad Sculpt Stand designed in Fusion 360 Ideal for dental education and patient communication Perfect project for painting and customization Compatible with both hand painting and AMS printing Optimized for FDM and resin printing Happy printing, and I'd love to see your finished model!

Parametric Side-Release Buckle — V3 Robust snap-fit, 8 attachments interchangeable between male and female, Customizer in 5 languages — pure OpenSCAD only, no external libraries V3 is the evolution of the parametric side-release buckle written entirely in pure OpenSCAD, with no external libraries, designed for the MakerWorld Customizer. It builds on V2's aesthetic restyling — rounded body, central anti-wobble guide tongue, fillets at the root of the arms, chamfered mouth — and adds a robustness pass on the latch holes, a true new D-ring attachment, independent bulge controls on X and Y, optional insertion guides, and a reorganized, multilingual Customizer menu. Every dimension stays parametric and protected by automatic safety clamps. What's New in V3 Robustness pass: the minimum wall margin around each drilled attachment has been increased from 1.2 mm to 1.6 mm, for cord/paracord/D-ring tabs that print reliably. Fixed a latent flaw: the window (female cavity) now extends far enough to let the arms fully relax once they have snapped into place. New true D-ring attachment ("d_ring"), for closed/welded D-ring hardware: it is a straight round hole, drilled horizontally through the tab from side wall to side wall (like a hinge-pin hole), not vertically through the top/bottom faces. It is invisible from above and shows only as a hole in the side walls of the tab. The diameter matches the dring_wire parameter, i.e. the diameter of the ring's wire/stock (not its overall size): the ring opens, hooks into the hole and closes again, without having to thread the whole buckle through it. The "loop" attachment has been renamed (sewn eyelet / carabiner opening) to clearly distinguish it from the new d_ring. New independent bulge controls for a more organic, less "boxy" look: bulge_x (barrel bulge on the long side, applied to both male and female) and bulge_y (bulge on the short/head-to-tail edge). The safety rule is kept: the female edge facing the mouth never bulges, because it must stay flush against the base of the male during assembly. New optional insertion guides (guide_rails): two visible funnel-shaped notches, cut into the top/bottom caps at the mouth, on either side of the central guide tongue, to make blind insertion easier (assembly without looking). Disabled by default, with no effect if there is no central guide tongue. Customizer menu reorganized into a more logical order for the average user: Part -> Dimensions -> Attachment -> Snap-fit tuning -> Aesthetics -> Thicknesses -> Advanced. Removed the now-redundant "language" selector: every parameter label already shows all 5 languages (Italian/English/French/German/Chinese) at once. The "guide" mode (parameter legend in the 3D preview) now prints all 5 languages side by side. Every Customizer section (Part, Dimensions, Attachment, Snap-fit, Aesthetics, Thicknesses, Advanced) is now preceded by an emoji icon, so you can scan the panel at a glance. Main Features Side-release snap-fit mechanism: two spring arms with latch teeth click into the female cavity; you press on the exposed side windows to release. Optional central guide tongue (guide_width parameter): eliminates lateral play, guides insertion and acts as an anti-over-flexion end-stop for the arms. Every dimension is parametric and derived with built-in safety clamps: the script automatically limits values that would produce walls that are too thin, latch teeth that are too long, self-intersecting bulges, etc., displaying on-screen NOTES when it intervenes — it is very hard to generate invalid or unprintable geometry. Fully native OpenSCAD: no external libraries, works directly in the MakerWorld/OpenSCAD Customizer. Male and female attachments are chosen completely independently from 8 types, each with its own dedicated sizing parameters. Covers a wide range of strap widths (10–60 mm) and thicknesses (5–14 mm), with wall and cap thickness adjustable separately. 8 Attachment Types sewn_slot : Sewn slot/eyelet for attaching directly to the strap by stitching. belt : Wider pass-through opening, for threading a belt or a band. triglide : Adjustable tri-glide (two slots + central bar) for length-adjustable runs of strap. paracord : 2 or 4 round holes for lacing paracord or thin cord. loop : Large sewn eyelet / carabiner opening. cord : Single round hole for a cord or rope. flat : Solid tab, with no cut-out, for permanent glued or riveted mounting. d_ring : New in V3: a horizontal hole drilled sideways through the tab, sized to the diameter of the ring's wire (dring_wire), for closed/welded D-ring hardware. Print Notes Designed to print flat on the print bed, without supports. FDM print tolerance is adjustable via the clearance parameter (default 0.35 mm). With the d_ring attachment, the hole is drilled sideways through the tab (from side wall to side wall): the tab dimensions must be large enough to keep the hole within solid walls relative to the chosen dring_wire diameter; the script's safety clamps intervene automatically and flag on-screen with a NOTE if an entered value is not compatible. Works across a wide range of FDM printers and materials. In general, if a set parameter would lead to walls that are too thin, latches that are too long or self-intersecting bulges, the script corrects it automatically and flags it on-screen with a NOTE. Ideal For V3 is meant for people who actually need to use the buckle: pick the strap width and thickness, pick the attachment for the male side and for the female side even in combinations that differ from each other, adjust clearance and bulges to taste, print flat without supports, and assemble. description: You drop it in the hole, give the knob a turn, and it locks. No wiggle, no lifting out when you plane or sand. A wedge inside the pin spreads three collet fingers against the wall of the dog hole, so the harder your workpiece pushes back, the more the pin bites in. When you are done, back the knob off half a turn and it drops right out. This is the locking version of my In-Line Bench Dog Clamp . The original held with friction alone, which works for planing but can creep out under vibration from an orbital sander. This one grips mechanically and stays put. Two variants, pick the one that matches your holes: EU / MFT for 20mm holes US for 3/4 inch holes Both use the same cheap M6 hardware. Key Features Locks into the hole, does not lift out under sanding or side load One pin covers a range of hole sizes, so slightly worn or oversized holes still grip Uses standard M6 hardware, a dollar at any hardware store and available worldwide Releases with half a turn, no tools Collet body prints support free, only the pusher arms need light support Which variant EU / MFT : fits holes 19.7 to 20.1mm US : fits holes 18.8 to 19.2mm If your holes were drilled with a 20mm bit, use EU. If drilled with a 3/4 inch bit, use US. When in doubt, measure an actual hole with a caliper, the number matters more than the bit that made it. Hardware you need One M6 x 60mm screw One M6 nut A standard hex nut is fine. Both parts press into their sockets, no glue needed. Assembly Press the M6 screw head into the hex socket on the underside of the cone Push the cone up into the pin, ribs lining up with the slots The screw shaft comes up through the top of the pin Set the T pusher onto the pin crown Press the M6 nut into the knob Thread the knob onto the screw and tighten Using it Drop the pin into the dog hole. Turn the knob to lock, the cone pulls up and spreads the fingers against the hole wall. The pusher end presses your workpiece. To release, back the knob off about half a turn. If it was cranked down hard and the cone stays wedged, unscrew a bit more and press down on the knob, it pops free. Hints PLA works, tested under an orbital sander with no lift The pin prints vertical as oriented on the plate and needs supports The pusher prints flat, add brim ears at the narrow tip so it does not lift Cone and knob print flat, they only need support inside the nut socket Do not leave it clamped down for long stretches, PLA can take a set under constant load. For a permanent setup or a warm shop, PETG holds up better. If you print it, please leave a rating - it helps a lot.

model_name: Customizable Gridfinity Socket Holder with Text
description: I am still working on a adding Gridfinity to my toolboxes, and came across some specialized socket sets, one ratchets down like a drill, and the other was a Husky Passthrough Ratchet set. Problem was there wasn't really any Gridfinity holders for them. Especially with adding text like I needed for the socket set. So I decided to do a custom design via OpenSCAD that lets me define all the socket diameters (not the socket size) and in addition I can define text to match. The set can be as large or small as you like, the only real limitation is that I limited to two row (once I figure the math out, I may expand that). The nice thing about it, the script autosizes to standard grids, based on the diameters and text. So if the diameters and Grids edge into a wider or longer grid pattern, it sizes it for you. You can also play with some of the parameters to tighten that up, if needed. Need to do oversized sockets, here is the script. Need to do a set no one else has, here is your chance. So here are the parameters you can modify, also please read the notes, as they help to understand the script: Socket Diameters: a comma separated list of diameters of each socket in the set, not the size but the actual diameter in mm. (add 1 for variances in printers. Socket Depth: how far down do you want the socket to sit, when placed in the holder. Going too deep will cause the Height units to be limited. Socket to Socket Separation: when placing the sockets in the patter how far edge to edge. Making this smaller my reduce the X grid size. Number of Rows: the list can be split it two (if even), so that the second part of the list wraps under the first. See notes. Tray Height: how many Gridfinity 1U (7mm) units. The tray will always have a lip (so include that). Also because of socket depth, you may not be able to select below a certain size. Margin X: minimum margin between left and right walls, this may increase if the spacing requires it. Margin Y: minimum margin between top and bottom walls, this is also used if there are two rows to separate them. Socket Text: a comma separated list of text that will go under the socket holes. If the field is left blank no text is added, if there is text the number of items in the list must match the number of socket diameters list. Font Size: a set of predefined font sizes to choose from (the font is not selectable at this time). Arial Bold was chosen as it worked the best, with smaller fonts. Raised Text: do you want the text raised or embedded in the holder. Text Color: what color should the text be, you may need to do some painting on other spaces like the lip. Here are some examples of dia/text combinations. Example 1: The orange holder was done with no text, and the diameters looked like this. [32.5, 31.5, 27.7, 26.6, 25.2], the text field was empty. Single row was selected. Example 2: The yellow box with the wire strippers [23.5, 23.5, 23.5, 23.5, 23.5, 23.5], Text [8 awg, 10awg, 12awg, 14awg, sp, Cut], notice they are all the same diameter and the text is under this]. Since the set was even, I selected 2 rows so it wrapped it around (check the text). This also could have been done as a single row. Example 3: The Husky socket set, the diameters were [28, 25.2, 25, 24, 23, 20, 20, 20, 25, 24, 24, 23, 20, 20, 20, 20], and the text was [3/4, 11/16, 3", 5/8, 3/16, 1/2, 7/16, 3/8, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10]. Notice how it goes high to low and second set also goes high to low. Have SAE on top, Metric on the bottom. Two rows were selected, it could have been done on one, but that would be very long. The only thing about the model is that the library adds colors to the lip and sides (I have not figured out how to remove them yet). So you will either need to keep them, color them, or select your own. Let me know if you run into any issues, I tested the combinations, but may have missed something. If you get a chance checkout some of my other organization items ( https://makerworld.com/en/collections/17112635-gridfinity ) or ( https://makerworld.com/en/collections/16603099-multiboard-hsw-opengrid ).

I love this model because it is easier to push, stronger, and more comfortable to hold than many commercial models I've bought in stores. I've gone through 23 iterations of the fan blade, and I made an Onshape Featurescript for it. It hits 6.525 revolutions per squeeze of the fan blade, so that's about 870-900 rpm. It creates a noticeable breeze even from a more relaxed distance so you don't have to hold it right in front of your face. List of Materials 85g of filament A 6.5x22mm extension spring (the place I bought it from is now unavailable, so any extension spring that's around 20mm long and < 9mm OD will work, but it may be harder to push in or slower to come out) 3 M3x8 self-tapping flat head screws Oil lubricant (Super Lube Multi-Purpose Synthetic Oil) Printing Make sure your filament is dry because if the axles for the gears have too much stringing, then they will turn less smoothly, and the fan blade won't work as efficiently. Also, the fan blade is using a layer height of 0.14mm, so don't mix it with the other objects, which use a layer height of 0.20mm. Assembly Confirm the spring's loops are in the correct position; make sure one of the loops of the spring is perpendicular to the coil and the other side is separated into a single cord, not a closed loop. I had to separate it myself and do some finicking to make the coil sit flat with the loop flat on the bottom. Put the spring in the tiny hole in the pusher part. Oil the big hole (the rotation axle) on the pusher part and then put it in the frame. Put in the gears in the order of the numbers in the picture, oiling the center hole and the teeth as you go. Put on the top cover, then the fan blade. Make sure the blade is pushed down until it is almost touching the frame. Screw it in (self-tapping), and then flip the whole thing over and screw in the bottom-most hole that's farthest from the blade. Screw in the hole on the middle-left, and only screw it in a tiny bit or the handle will be very hard to push in; the screw's top can even be flush with the bottom of the frame. If the model is hard to push in, the most likely reason is that this screw is screwed in too much. Happy printing!
