model_name: BambuPlot Free Pen Plotter G-code Generator
description: Turn your Bambu Lab 3D printer into a pen plotter completely free, no subscriptions, no accounts, no uploads. Everything runs locally in your browser. The included test file uses the boat drawing shown in the preview image a detailed line-art illustration that works great as a first plot to verify your setup. When using the tool please consider using the included print profile test model. This helps me out and helps supporting this project with since i could not upload the Bambuplot file directly on Makerworld. ⚠ Read this first this is a tinkerer's project This tool is made for people who enjoy experimenting, troubleshooting, and figuring things out. It is not a plug-and-play product. It will probably not work perfectly on the first try , and that is completely normal. Getting a pen plotter working on a 3D printer requires patience: dialing in the Z height, finding the right pen, getting the paper flat, tuning the feed rates, and sometimes just accepting that the first few attempts are learning runs. I do not cover any damages to your printer, pen holder, bed, or any other part of your setup. Using this tool is entirely at your own risk. Sending custom G-code to a 3D printer always carries a risk of unexpected movement, crashes, or damage if settings are wrong. Always supervise the printer, always do a dry run first with the Z height raised so the pen cannot touch anything, and never leave it running unattended especially not on a first test. If you are not comfortable with that, this project is probably not for you yet but if you enjoy the process of making something work from scratch, welcome aboard. What is BambuPlot? BambuPlot is a single HTML file you download and open in your browser. It lets you design drawings and convert them into G-code that your Bambu Lab printer can execute with a pen instead of a nozzle. No internet connection is required after download — it runs 100% on your computer. Supported printers all current Bambu Lab models: Printer Bed size Notes A1 mini 180 × 180 mm A1 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested P1P 256 × 256 mm P1S 256 × 256 mm P2S 256 × 256 mm X1 carbon 256 × 256 mm X2D 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested A2L 330 × 320 mm H2D 325 × 320 mm H2S 340 × 320 mm A custom bed size option is also available for any other setup. What you can draw: Text three modes: single-stroke plotter font (looks like real handwriting), your own custom handwriting (draw each letter yourself, up to 5 versions per letter for variety so repeating letters never look identical), or filled outline using any of 13 fonts Shapes square, circle, triangle, star, line, with optional hatch fill Freehand draw directly on the bed preview with your mouse or stylus Images drop any photo or logo, adjust the threshold and line density, and convert it to plotted lines 3MF import drop a Bambu Lab .3mf file and BambuPlot extracts the 3D geometry and renders the top-down footprint as plottable paths, in either vector outline or hatch-fill mode What you need A Bambu Lab printer or anything else that takes gcode A pen holder that mounts on your toolhead (search MakerWorld or Printables for your specific model many different designs exist.) (I used this one: https://makerworld.com/models/2886015?appSharePlatform=copy ) A ballpoint pen that fits your holder Paper to draw on, attached to the bed (see bed preparation below) A way to get pure gcode on your printer (USB stick/microsd) Bed preparation protecting your print surface This is important. The pen tip will press directly down onto whatever is on your bed. Printing on bare paper placed directly on a softer printing bed can cause damage, especially with a stiff pen or too much Z pressure. My recommendation: place an old flat PEI sheet (Like mine from my old ender 3 v2), a thin sheet of plastic such as a folder cover or binder sheet, or any similarly flat, smooth piece of thin plastic underneath the paper. This gives the paper a firm, even surface to rest on and takes any wear from the pen instead of your actual print bed. An old or scratched PEI sheet you no longer use for printing is perfect for this. Attaching the paper: I use small magnets placed along the edges to hold the paper flat and in position they are quick to place, leave no residue, and hold very reliably. Other options that work fine include masking tape or binder clips on the edges. Whatever you use, make sure the paper is completely flat with no bubbles or lifted corners, as any unevenness will cause the pen pressure to vary across the drawing. How to download and open BambuPlot Go to : https://joep648.github.io/BambuPlot/bambuplot-v1.0.1.html to use it online. or Download the bambuplot.html file from: https://github.com/Joep648/BambuPlot/tree/main Open it with any modern browser (Firefox recommended for best performance Chrome and Edge work fine too, but Firefox handles large designs more smoothly) That is it no installation, no internet needed after that Step-by-step: from design to plot Step 1 Select your printer In the top bar, choose your printer model from the dropdown. The bed preview updates to the correct size. This ensures your G-code coordinates match your actual print surface. Step 2 Add content to the bed Use the tabs on the left panel: Text tab type your text, choose a style (single-stroke is best for plotting), adjust letter spacing and line spacing, then click Add text to bed Shapes tab pick a shape and click Add shape to bed . Enable Filled to get hatch-fill lines inside the shape Image tab click the drop zone or drag an image in. Adjust the threshold slider until the preview looks like clean black lines on white, then click Convert & add to bed . High-contrast line art like the included boat image gives the best results 3MF tab drag a .3mf file onto the drop zone. Choose Vector outline for a clean single-stroke contour of the model, or Top-down silhouette for a hatch-filled footprint Freehand in the Shapes tab, click Draw directly on bed and sketch with your mouse Step 3 Position and size your content Once an item appears on the bed preview: Drag the body of the item to move it Drag a corner handle to scale it the line density automatically recalculates to stay consistent at the new size Drag the white circle above the item to rotate it Use the Layers tab to show/hide, duplicate, or delete items Step 4 Configure pen settings Go to the Pen tab and set: Setting What it does Suggested starting value Z draw How far down the pen tip presses 0.5 mm Z lift How high the pen lifts between strokes 8 mm Draw feed Speed while drawing 1500 mm/min Travel feed Speed while moving between strokes 6000 mm/min Z move feed Speed of Z moves 600 mm/min Pen settle time Dwell after each Z move to prevent stray marks 120 ms These values are starting points every pen holder and pen combination is different. Adjust Z draw until the pen just barely touches the paper with light pressure. Step 5 Generate and download the G-code Click Generate G-code in the right panel. The code appears in the preview (large designs only show the first few thousand lines the full file is always in the download). Click the ⭳ button to download the .gcode file. Step 6 Send to the printer and plot My personal workflow: Home the printer manually via the touchscreen or Bambu Studio After homing, clip the pen holder onto the toolhead with the pen inserted Place your protective plastic sheet on the bed, lay the paper on top, and secure it with magnets, tape, or clips Start the file with in bambuplot Home all axes (G28) at start option turned off Always do a dry run first: temporarily raise the Z draw value by 5–10 mm so the pen stays off the paper, and watch the full motion to confirm the design lands in the right place before doing a real plot Alternative workflow using the dwell option: The Dwell after homing checkbox in the Pen tab inserts a G4 S30 command (a timed pause) after the G28 home command, giving you time to clip the pen on before plotting starts. This feature is experimental and untested I have not personally used it this way. Bambu printers do not support the standard M0 unconditional pause command, so a timed dwell is used as a workaround. If you try it, set the duration long enough to comfortably attach the pen holder (60 seconds or more). Tips for best results Use the right paper smooth, slightly heavier paper works best. Thin paper can wrinkle from pen pressure Ballpoint pens are the most reliable. Felt-tips can bleed on paper and dry out if the pen sits in one spot for too long Start with a short test plot a small shape first to calibrate your Z height before committing to a full design Line density matters lower density (higher number on the slider) = fewer lines = faster plot and less ink bleed. Higher density looks more solid but takes much longer to plot The settle time setting (default 120 ms) adds a brief pause after every pen up/down move. This is the main fix for random stray lines on the paper if you see faint marks between strokes, increase it to 150–250 ms Mirror X or Y if your plot comes out flipped Saving your settings In the Pen tab, click Save profile + handwriting to file to save all your pen settings, printer choice, and your custom drawn handwriting alphabet to a single .json file. Load it again any time even on a different device with the load button. Questions, problems, and ideas for future versions If something does not work, you have a question about the setup, or you just want to share your results feel free to leave a comment on this MakerWorld page or send me a message directly through MakerWorld. I am happy to help where I can, though keep in mind this is a hobby project and responses may not always be instant. If you have ideas for features you would like to see in a future version, I would love to hear them. BambuPlot is actively being worked on and new features get added regularly. Things on the radar include better SVG import, more letter styles, and improved multi-layer support. If there is something specific you need for your use case, suggest it in the comments the best ideas from the community are what shape where this goes next. BambuPlot is a fan-made tool and is not affiliated with Bambu Lab. Pen holder designs are not included search MakerWorld or Printables for a mount that fits your specific printer model. Always run a dry pass before plotting on good paper. Use at your own risk.

description: One print. Ten common failure checks. Every test labels what to inspect and what to adjust next. Most calibration prints tell you that something is wrong. Print Doctor helps you understand what the failure means and what to try next. This is a single connected diagnostic print containing ten purpose-built tests. Each card includes: The print symptom A labelled failure point showing where to inspect Three likely slicer or printer adjustments Geometry designed to make that problem easier to see Print it with your normal material profile, leave supports off, and let the model reveal where the profile needs attention. The small connecting tabs keep everything together during printing and can be snapped afterward if you want ten individual reference cards. The cute cat-shaped Print Doctor header, mushroom cooling test, and elephant-foot paw make it friendly enough to keep beside the printer instead of hiding it in a drawer. Included tests Under-extrusion — thin-wall frame and narrow ribs reveal gaps, weak strands, and missing sections. Over-extrusion — labelled 0.20, 0.40, and 0.60 mm gaps show when excess flow begins fusing nearby features. Poor pressure advance — repeated sharp corners expose corner bulges and line thinning. Stringing — four separated spires create travel moves at different heights. Weak bridging — unsupported 8, 16, and 24 mm spans reveal sagging bridge undersides. Cooling issues — three mushroom caps use increasingly demanding overhangs. Z-seam quality — a smooth thin-walled cup makes seam zits, gaps, and inconsistent starts visible. Elephant foot — the paw specimen sits directly on the build plate so first-layer flare remains visible. Layer adhesion — three labelled bend paddles help reveal splitting between layers. Inconsistent wall thickness — circular, square, and hexagonal walls provide multiple surfaces to measure and compare. How to use it Slice the model with the profile you actually want to diagnose. Keep supports disabled; the unsupported features are intentional. Print the complete kit flat in its supplied orientation. Follow each raised WATCH label and inspect the indicated feature. Use the three adjustments printed on that card as your troubleshooting shortlist. Change one setting at a time and reprint when necessary. The printed suggestions are starting points, not absolute rules. Material condition, hardware, motion settings, and slicer behavior can produce similar-looking symptoms. Recommended print settings Material: PLA is recommended for the first diagnostic print Nozzle: 0.4 mm Layer height: 0.20 mm Walls: 2 Infill: 15–20% Supports: Off Brim: Off when possible, because a brim can hide elephant-foot behavior Orientation: Print flat exactly as supplied Profile: Use your normal profile rather than a specially tuned calibration profile Model dimensions Footprint: 203.8 × 180.2 mm Maximum height: 22.2 mm Assembly: One connected, manifold print with optional breakaway cards The full kit fits a typical 220 × 220 mm build plate. Confirm the slicer's skirt, purge line, and machine-specific exclusion zones before printing.

description: ## Device Description Circle Bambu Monitor is a compact desktop display for monitoring Bambu Lab 3D printer status in real time. It is built around an ESP32-C3 SuperMini development board and a 1.28 inch round 240x240 TFT display with a GC9A01 driver . The electronics are housed in a snap-fit 3D printed enclosure designed for a clean front view and easy rear access. The device connects to Wi-Fi and reads printer data from Home Assistant entities. It does not connect directly to the printer. Instead, it uses Home Assistant as the data source, which makes it flexible and easy to adapt to different Bambu Lab printer setups. --- ## Main Components - TENSTAR ESP32-C3 SuperMini development board - 1.28 inch round 240x240 TFT LCD display with GC9A01 driver - 7-wire display connection - 3D printed main body - 3D printed rear cover - USB-C power supply - Home Assistant with Bambu Lab integration/entities --- ## What It Does Circle Bambu Monitor shows the current status of a Bambu Lab printer on a small round display. It can display: - Print progress - Printer state - Current print phase - Nozzle temperature - Bed temperature - Filament information - Current layer and total layers - Print weight - Estimated finish time - Idle clock screen The device also includes a built-in web configuration interface. On first startup it creates its own Wi-Fi setup network. After connecting to it, the user can configure Wi-Fi, Home Assistant URL, access token, timezone, and the Home Assistant entities used for printer data. Firmware updates can be installed through the browser using the web installer, so users do not need to use the Arduino IDE. --- ## Data Source The device uses Home Assistant as its data source. It reads configured Home Assistant entities for: - Print phase - Print status - Print progress - Active filament slot - Estimated finish time - Nozzle temperature - Bed temperature - Current layer - Total layers - Filament weight Initial values are loaded using the Home Assistant REST API. Live updates are then received through the Home Assistant WebSocket API. --- ## Firmware and Web Installer Latest firmware: `v0.11.16` Firmware can be installed using the browser-based web installer: https://michalkmr7.github.io/circle-bambu-monitor/web-installer/ A supported browser such as Chrome or Edge is recommended. No Arduino IDE is required for normal installation. --- ## Installation and Setup Guide ### 1. Wire the Display Connect the display to the ESP32-C3 using the wiring diagram from the project documentation. The display uses SPI communication. Make sure all wires are connected correctly before powering the device. Project documentation and wiring diagram: https://github.com/MichalKMR7/circle-bambu-monitor --- ### 2. Flash the Firmware Open the web installer in a supported browser: https://michalkmr7.github.io/circle-bambu-monitor/web-installer/ Then: 1. Connect the ESP32-C3 to your computer using USB-C. 2. Click `Connect`. 3. Select the ESP32-C3 serial device. 4. Click `Install`. 5. Wait until flashing is complete. 6. Disconnect and reconnect the device if needed. --- ### 3. First Startup After flashing, power on the device. If the device is not configured yet, it will start in setup mode and create its own Wi-Fi network. The display will show: - Wi-Fi network name - Setup password - Setup IP address Connect your phone or computer to the setup Wi-Fi network shown on the display. Then open the displayed IP address in your browser. --- ### 4. Configure Wi-Fi and Home Assistant In the web configuration page, enter: - Your Wi-Fi network - Wi-Fi password - Home Assistant URL, for example `http://192.168.1.100:8123` - Long-lived Home Assistant token After saving, the device will restart and connect to your Wi-Fi network. --- ### 5. Find the Device on Your Network After restart, the device will no longer use the setup Wi-Fi network. Find the new IP address in your router, DHCP client list, or network device list. Open the device IP address in your browser to continue configuration. --- ### 6. Configure Home Assistant Entities After the device connects to Home Assistant, the configuration page allows you to select the required entities. Configure entities for: - Print phase - Print status - Print progress - Active filament slot - Estimated finish time - Nozzle temperature - Bed temperature - Current layer - Total layers - Filament weight You can use the searchable entity fields to find matching Home Assistant entities. For example, typing `nozzle` will show matching nozzle temperature entities. Entity names depend on your Home Assistant setup and integration. --- ### 7. Configure Timezone Select your timezone in the configuration page. The timezone is used for: - Idle clock screen - Estimated finish time display Choose the timezone that matches your location. --- ### 8. Save and Restart After all required fields are configured, click `Save and Restart`. The device will restart and begin showing printer data. --- ## Display Screens ### Setup Screen Shown when the device has not been configured yet. It displays the setup Wi-Fi name, setup password, and setup IP address. ### Loading Screen Shown while the device connects to Wi-Fi, synchronizes time, and loads the initial Home Assistant states. ### Printing Screen Shown during an active print. It displays print progress, printer status, temperatures, filament information, layer progress, print weight, and estimated finish time. ### Pause / Warning Screen Important printer states are highlighted visually. Pause states can be shown with an orange blinking ring. Warning or object detection states can be highlighted with a red blinking ring. ### Finish Screen Shown briefly after a print completes before returning to the idle screen. ### Idle Clock Screen Shown when no print is active. It displays the current time and date. The second ring is green when the printer is online and grey when the printer is offline or unavailable. --- ## Updating Firmware To update the firmware later: 1. Open the web installer. 2. Connect the ESP32-C3 over USB. 3. Flash the latest firmware. 4. The saved configuration should remain stored on the device. model_name: Noodle Nexus 2: Modular AMS Stacker Drawer
description: Introduction Another one? Yes. Clear up some desk space by stacking your AMS's! This version uses 45mm steel slides to slide out the lower AMS, making a super compact stacker. This is compatible with the original AMS and the AMS 2 Pro. The top AMS is positioned forward to ensure that the lid can open fully. Even so, with 350mm slide travel, the AMS lid will open enough to stay open without falling closed. The dimensions are: Height including an AMS 2 Pro on top: 475 mm Width: 443 mm Depth excluding handle and optional counterweight basket: 355 mm Handle adds 32mm of depth Counterweight basket adds 45mm of depth If this isn't exactly for you, check out this collection for alternatives. Modules Feet extensions to put this on top of your H-series printer 3rd/4th AMS Extension (link coming very soon!) Upcoming: AMS HT adapter Upcoming: Various Storage attachments, perhaps a tool drawer? Difficulty This project is designed for beginners . It is easy because: All parts print with minimal supports and all overhangs are easy to print. There is minimal post-processing required. There is only one type (and length!) of fastener needed with no heat-set inserts, no glue and no other specialty fasteners. You don't need "advanced" materials such as ABS. The challenging aspects are: Large parts, even PLA and PETG parts, can warp and your build plates need to be clean. You may even consider using some glue if you have had issues with your particular material and plate. You need to be able to print TPU, and to do this cleanly, you will need a filament dryer. Filament I recommend: PETG for the frame PETG or PLA for the drawer (if you plan on putting this on top of a printer though, do not use PLA) TPU 90A or similar for the feet If you use ABS or ASA, you must consider shrinkage compensation as the parts are large and the overall dimension can be affected by 2-3mm. Please feel free to post your print profile. Add lots of pictures and a detailed description please! It will help other people decide which one to use. Hardware for Assembly Only one type and length of screw is needed: BT3x14 BHCS Self Tapping Screw (AA223). This is a 3mm diameter, 14mm long screw designed for plastic with coarse deep threads that cut into and grip well onto holes in plastic. They are not expensive extremely easy to use as you don't need to embed heat set inserts or seat little M3 nuts. They also make the printed parts simpler and use far less material than using printed fasteners or bowtie joints. Alternatives: If you have 12mm screws or the socket head style of BT3 screws, they will be perfectly fine too. If Bambu doesn't ship to your country, the key words to search are “3mm self-tapping screw hex socket”. Try to get some without a pointy tip as they have a slightly longer usable thread length and a head height of 2mm or less. I found some products on AliExpress ( Listing 1 , Listing 2 , Listing 3 ) which look promising, but I have not tried them. Do NOT use countersunk screws as most holes in the design are parallel to the print bed plane and the screws can split your layers if you're not careful with tightening. You will need: 43 for the frame assembly 10 for the drawer assembly 16 to attach the steel slides to the frame and drawer assemblies 8 to attach the AMS's Optional: 4 to attach the counterweight basket 81 screws total (if I counted correctly…). If you ever wanted an excuse to buy an electric pencil screwdriver, here it is! In the bill of materials, I have put 5 packets of 20 screws but I suggest ordering extra if you are interested in making the future modules. You will also need 350mm or 14-inch nominal length, 45mm nominal width (can be a little wider as there is nothing below the slides), 12.7mm thick full extension slides. Here in Germany, I got Stahlia branded slides direct from their website , also available on Amazon.de . You do not need to get exactly the same one. I took specs from several different brands and accommodated for them all in the design and you just need 3-4 holes that line up. Worst case, you might need to make some new holes but I think that's unlikely as slide manufacturers just copy each other. IMPORTANT : If you are using soft-close slides, check that they are truly full extension and extend 400mm. Many 3-section slides that are labelled “full extension” are not really full extension, particularly some of the soft-close ones. Slide designers, when taking their regular slide and making a soft-close version, need to decide whether to reduce the load rating of their slide or reduce the extension to try to fit the extra mechanisms into the design. Some brands have lowered weight ratings (say, 35kg down from 45kg), some reduce their travel. Parts for Installation You will need a longer PTFE tube than typically supplied with printers (or a coupler to connect two shorter ones) as the AMS travels forward and back. The length needed depends on your particular setup. If the tube is brand new and tightly-wound for shipping, they will need to be relaxed to form gentle curves. Don't get the "star shaped" tubes, that's a gimmick. If you use a coupler, note that there is an entry side (tapered inlet) and an exit side (not tapered). You may also need longer 6-pin AMS connectors depending on your printer and AMS arrangement. Print Settings General Tips Flow rate calibration is highly recommended for every spool you use! Many clearances in the design are 0.1mm. For proper fit, the parts should not be under or over-extruded. Dry your filament (even PLA) to minimise risks with dimensional accuracy. Aux fan OFF if you've had issues with part warping. Don't worry, all of the overhangs are super easy. Specific Settings These are all set in the print profile. However, if you download it on PC and change the printer, some of these may get overwritten so I will list them here. These are the settings I use and are quite conservative and a little slow for a clean print with sharp corners, it's a balance between Bambu's “High Quality” and “Standard" profiles. Feel free to deviate as you see fit. Speeds Outer wall: 70 mm/s Inner wall: 150 mm/s Top Surface: 120 mm/s Everything else: default for your favourite profile Accelerations Normal printing: 4000 mm/s² Outer wall: 2000 mm/s² Inner wall: 0 (same as Normal) Top surface: 2000 mm/s² Sparse infill: 8000 mm/s² Everything else: default for your favourite profile Strength Parts are designed for a 0.4mm nozzle printing 0.2mm layer heights. Wall loops Top/bottom shell layers Infill Frame Parts 3 7/5 10-15%, your choice of pattern Slider Parts 3 7/5 10-15%, your choice of pattern TPU feet 6 5/3 Your choice All other parts 2 5/3 10-15%, your choice of pattern Bonus tip If you want the perfect 🧑🍳👌🏼fit between parts, make sure your beds are trammed! They're not always trammed out-of-factory; 3 of the printers I got in 2026 were not trammed. Manual Bed Leveling / Manual Bed Tramming | Bambu Lab Wiki P2S & X2D Heatbed Manual Bed Leveling | Bambu Lab Wiki Assembly and Installation As all screws are the same, this is quite straight forward. Just one thing to note: screws can get hot while tightening; tighten them most of the way and give them a minute before final tightening. Frame Assembly Assemble each half first. Use the screws to attach the 5 pieces of one side together. Insert the TPU feet - they are press-fit and should stay-in firmly without glue. Remove the inner part of the slide and attach to the frame using at least 3 screws. When tightening, push the slides up to the flat parts on the frame - this ensures that the left and right slides are parallel and level. Repeat for the other side and put the two halves together with more screws. Attach the top AMS with 4 screws. This will stiffen up the frame assembly considerably. For some versions of the original AMS, there are some small pieces of plastic that need to be trimmed. This is not necessary for the AMS 2 Pro and some original AMS variants. Drawer Assembly Assemble the drawer assembly with more screws. Attach the inner slides using at least 3 screws on each side. When tightening, try to get the two inner slides parallel. You can look at the unused holes to determine the positioning. If the holes are too big, you can use some washers (mine is OK without, this is just for illustration). Now slide this into the frame. Attach the lower AMS Put some filament inside the top AMS to provide some counterweight. Pull out the drawer and place the second AMS. Use 4 more screws to secure it in-place. And finally, post a picture here! Counterweight Options As you can guess, the whole assembly can tip forward when the drawer is opened fully. I have 3 options to reduce this risk. You can use one or more of the methods at the same time. Option 1 - Counterweight Basket Attach the counterweight basket using 4 screws (same screws as above!). The file for this is in a separate print profile, on this page. Fill an empty filament box with heavy stuff - try to get at least 2kg in there (a bag of sand, depleted uranium, a brick, whatever you have around the house). Put the box into the basket. You can make the box smaller too. Option 2 - Feet extensions These extensions extend the front by 95mm - if you have the table space these work great. Option 3 - Add another AMS Coming soon™! And only when my nephew comes over and says the same thing once again I thought to myself, I need to make a little dumpster to catch all the poop my printer makes. I pictured the Home Alone 2 movie where the house Kevin rigs up has a chute outside the window going into a dumpster. So that's where the idea for project came from. There are tons of “poop” bins and baskets for the other printers but I wanted to make one for my new Bambu Lab A2L printer. She's a beast. Very detailed and prints well. I love it. It does shake the house though being a large sized bed slinger. I have been printing on silent mode to calm it down in most cases. This took me a week to create. A little longer than usual but I needed to get the tolerances perfecta. My main goal was to make it easy and reliable to print. That was the challenge. I tried several ways to get the chute to print as one piece but it never worked out. So clip or bracket that connects to the printer is separate and has to be glued to the chute. I did make a connection socket so the two fit together perfectly so all is needed is a drop of cyanoacrylate glue (Super Glue) or something similar on each edge of the connection opening and hold it in place for the appropriate time (depending on your glue). I have printed 19 sets of the chute and bracket and glued them together successfully with no problem. Supports were absolutely necessary to accomplish my goal. I have had several people that don't have a printer me to print them one just because they wanted the cute little bin. I have even been changing the sizes per their requests. The dumpster itself is scalable and you can make a smaller or larger one depending on your needs. I am sure it will have many uses. This is the A2L model version. model_name: True Spring Filament Clip ⧸ Tangle Free Storage
description: A filament clip that solves the three most common problems of traditional filament clips. Plastic Fatigue Most filament clips rely on a printed flex geometry to generate clamping force. Repeated use and elevated drying temperatures gradually reduce the clamping force as the plastic permanently deforms. True Spring Solution The clamping force is generated by a real steel compression spring. The printed parts only guide the movement. No Plastic Fatigue. Constant tension. Filament Stress Many filament clips bend the filament sharply by securing it through spool holes or around the spool rim. Brittle materials may break after long term storage. True Spring Solution The filament is secured close to the spool core with a large bending radius, minimizing unnecessary stress while keeping the filament securely retained. Tangle Risk Some clips secure the filament directly to the wound filament. This can increase the risk of accidental tangles when the spool is handled carelessly. True Spring Solution The filament is retained independently of the wound filament. Nothing is attached to the filament winding itself. Hardware The clip uses two inexpensive compression springs. You can either use a compatible spring from the BOM or simply try the spring from an old ballpoint pen. Many common pen springs fit perfectly. No screws. No glue. No tools. Everything simply snaps together. Printer Tolerance Test Every printer and every filament behaves slightly differently. Since this model relies on precisely fitting moving parts, I strongly recommend printing the Printer Tolerance Test first. The test consists of one plunger and six labeled test sockets with clearances of 0.05 mm , 0.10 mm , 0.15 mm , 0.20 mm , 0.25 mm and 0.30 mm . The correct fit should move smoothly with minimal friction while having as little play as possible. Don't feel like running the calibration? Simply print Print Plate 1 (0.15 mm clearance) . It provides a good fit for most printers and materials. Temperature Testing Successfully tested after 24 hours of continuous filament drying: PETG - 45 °C ASA - 65 °C ASA - 80 °C PC - 85 °C For comparison, I tested a popular Flexi Filament Clip under identical print settings, using the same material and identical drying conditions. After 24 hours at the respective drying temperatures, the flex geometry had permanently deformed and the remaining clamping force was no longer sufficient for reliable reuse. If you have ever dried filament while using this type of clip, you probably know exactly what I mean. Recommended Materials PETG works perfectly for everyday use. For frequent filament drying or elevated temperatures I recommend ASA or PC . Assembly Printed parts and two compression springs. Insert the filament clamps. Insert the springs. Insert the Double Plunger and press firmly. Finished, enjoy.

description: Always there when you need it. Never in the way when you don't. Like other filament clip giants before me, I decided to throw my hat into the ring. Meet The Wingman . Every spool deserves one. The Wingman securely parks your filament when it's not in use, then quietly stays out of the way while you print. No snags. No rubbing. No surprises. Just a simple clip that's there when you need it and invisible when you don't. Why Yet Another Filament Clip? Because I kept trying the "good" ones and finding little things that annoyed me. Some snagged filament. Some didn't stay attached very well. Some required threading way more filament than seemed necessary. Some were so aggressively optimized to save filament that they forgot they actually needed to print successfully. None of these were deal breakers, but together they convinced me to make my own. So I did. Why The Wingman? Curves in all the right places Some clips have sharp edges, straight walls, or little ridges that can catch filament as it moves around the spool. The Wingman was designed with smooth, rounded surfaces wherever filament might encounter it, because nobody wants a multi-hour print to fail because of a 1-cent piece of plastic. Secure enough to forget about Some clips rely on a single spool hole. Others barely fit. The Wingman uses two mounting points and confidently snaps into place with a satisfying click, staying exactly where you put it. Quick filament parking Some clips are designed to capture a long length of filament before they're satisfied. Why? The Wingman only needs a very short section of filament for a secure hold, making loading and unloading quick and painless. Optimized for actual printing Some designs appear to be competing in a least amount of filament contest. Unfortunately, saving 0.05 grams doesn't help much if the part fails halfway through printing. The Wingman was designed to print reliably first. Once that was achieved, material was trimmed away until only what was needed remained. Features Works with the AMS Lite (with or without top mount), AMS HT, AMS, and AMS 2 Pro Secure dual-pin design snaps firmly into place No pliers, tools, or colorful language required Designed to remain attached during printing and drying Specifically optimized for Bambu spools Gently angled filament path for a secure hold and easy insertion Integrated guide line helps with filament insertion while adding a subtle finishing touch Only 0.47g per clip Important Notes Print with a filament intended for functional parts. PLA Matte and other brittle materials may not survive repeated use. To remove a clip, simply push the pegs back through the spool holes using any small object. Depending on filament shrinkage, the filament opening may initially fit tightly. If needed, run a short piece of filament through the opening a few times before use. This is most noticeable with abrasive filaments such as PLA Glow. If using a filament dryer, print The Wingman using a material capable of handling the temperatures you intend to use. Instructions Print as many Wingmen as your spools deserve, keeping the supplied orientation unchanged for best results. Align the pegs with the spool holes and push until they snap securely into place. Feel strangely satisfied. Let the guide line do the aiming, then push the filament into place. model_name: P2S X2D - BIQU CryoGrip Pro Glacier ArUco Marker
description: Successful detection. Every time. No compromises. This model is part of my ongoing BIQU Build Plate Accessories collection. Each model is conceived, printed, and endurance-tested on my own machines, refined through dozens of iterations to match the printer’s true mechanical behavior. Precision isn't assumed here, it’s verified layer by layer. Explore the full collection: BIQU Build Plate Accessories Follow me if you like my work, that kind of appreciation really dries my filament. Likes and boosts feed the Maker World algorithm and keep the new models coming v2 (Dev) Notes During my testing with the newer BIQU FrostBite build plates without the honeycomb handle, I made some interesting observations about the X2D's ArUco detection. The marker was reliably detected between 5 mm and 14 mm in size. Positioning along the Y axis had virtually no influence, as long as the marker remained between the printer door and the printable area. Along the X axis, the center of the marker could be placed anywhere between approximately 35 mm and 135 mm from the left edge of the build plate. These findings differ from my early experiments when the X2D was first released. Back then, the marker seemed to require very precise positioning. Based on my current testing, the detection system appears to be significantly more tolerant than it used to be. Testing on the Glacier plates with the honeycomb handle revealed something different. The honeycomb pattern can interfere with reliable detection, especially when using smaller markers. Based on these findings, I redesigned the marker for v2 (dev). It now uses a 35 % larger ArUco marker and is positioned to provide a cleaner visual background for the camera while remaining well inside the measured detection range. If you're experiencing detection issues, I'd really appreciate it if you could try v2 (dev) and let me know whether it improves reliability on your printer. Back To The Model Tested Compatibility, Fitting And Detection Checked Blue BIQU Panda CryoGrip Pro Glacier Build Plate for Bambu X2D/X1/P1/P2/A1 (256mm*256mm) Purple, Green, Pink, Yellow and Blue BIQU Panda CryoGrip Pro Build Plate for Bambu Lab X1C/P1S/A1 (256mm*256mm) Mechanically Incompatible (No Honeycomp Handle) Matte Orange and Blue BIQU Panda CryoGrip Pro FrostBite Build Plate for Bambu X2D/X1/P1/P2/A1 (256mm*256mm) The BIQU CryoGrip Pro Glacier is an outstanding build plate for ASA, but there is one annoying drawback: the printer cannot reliably detect it, and the supplied adhesive ArUco stickers are, frankly, a joke. This model puts an end to that. Two print profiles. “Smooth PEI Plate / High Temp Plate” as suggested by BIQU. “Cool Plate Super Tack” as requested by the community. Developed specifically for the BIQU CryoGrip Pro Glacier on the Bambu Lab P2S and X2D, it provides a precisely aligned ArUco marker that delivers reliable build plate recognition every time. The integrated clips engage directly with the plate's honeycomb pattern, ensuring perfect alignment and a secure mechanical fit. For additional retention, a small strip of 3M 9080 LED tape can be applied underneath the mount. The design has been tested in both PETG and ASA. For science, I even printed the ArUco marker itself in PLA and used it on an ASA print with a chamber temperature of 65 °C. Surprisingly, it held up for several weeks. PETG is an excellent long term choice, while ASA is the ultimate install it once and forget about it solution. No more failed recognition. No more crooked stickers. Just perfect alignment and reliable detection, every single time.

model_name: Poo Chute & Dumpster For All A Series
description: *** Update *** Upon request, I have made it so you are now able to print this Poop Chute and Dumpster for the A1 and A1 Mini printers. I added a new Clip to the existing Chute. You now just need to select the correct plate that matches your printer and you on your way. I also added a wider version of the dumpster so it pushes out the dumpster walls so they do not hit the extruder head assembly. You can choose which ever you like best. If you pick the appropriate chute and clip the extruder should be clear. There is the original chute which is longer but I got a few comments stating that the chute will hit the dumpster, which it would if you placed the dumpster walls under the chute, I would suggest not to do this. It would be like placing your cup of coffee under the extruder assembly or print bar, you wouldn't do that right? So funny story. I love printing things. Therefore I have a lot of plastic waste from poop to supports etc…. A while ago my husband says “your going to need a dumpster for all that plastic”. Then my neighbor noticed the several bags of plastic “poop” I have and said the exact thing. And only when my nephew comes over and says the same thing once again I thought to myself, I need to make a little dumpster to catch all the poop my printer makes. I pictured the Home Alone 2 movie where the house Kevin rigs up has a chute outside the window going into a dumpster. So that's where the idea for project came from. There are tons of “poop” bins and baskets for the other printers but I wanted to make one for my new Bambu Lab A2L printer. She's a beast. Very detailed and prints well. I love it. It does shake the house though being a large sized bed slinger. I have been printing on silent mode to calm it down in most cases. This took me a week to create. A little longer than usual but I needed to get the tolerances perfect. My main goal was to make it reliable and easy to print. That was the challenge. I tried several ways to get the chute to print as one piece but it never worked out. So clip or bracket that connects to the printer is separate and has to be glued to the chute. I did make a connection socket so the two fit together perfectly so all is needed is a drop of cyanoacrylate glue (Super Glue) or something similar on each edge of the connection opening and hold it in place for the appropriate time (depending on your glue). I have printed 19 sets of the chute and bracket and glued them together successfully with no problem. Supports were absolutely necessary to accomplish my goal. I tried to keep the settings simple but tweaked the settings like the top and bottom Z distance, speed etc… to get dumpster and chute to come out clean. Just be sure to keep my settings. You can add to them if you please but it wont be necessary as you can tell by my photos. I have had several people that don't have a printer me to print them one just because they wanted the cute little bin. I have even been changing the sizes per their requests. The dumpster itself is scalable and you can make a smaller or larger one depending on your needs. I am sure it will have many uses. Thank you ahead of time and please enjoy. Have a nice day.

description: DISCLAIMERS This is a fairly invasive modification. It requires drilling eight 3 mm holes into the acrylic top cover and replacing two of the factory screws on the side of the machine with longer ones. If you are not comfortable making these modifications, I recommend not attempting this. I do not take responsibility for any damage that occurs during the installation or use of this model. If I encounter any issues myself or someone reports any, I will try to release an updated version with a fix or, if that is not possible, I will remove the model to prevent further problems. Please watch the video to see the installation process and the finished result. Somebody will most likely come up with a more elegant or more secure solution in the future. I simply wanted to give this idea a try. I do not recommend printing these parts in PLA or PETG. In the video I used PLA only because I was prototyping. I later replaced every part with PA612-CF. A rigid, temperature-resistant filament is highly recommended. You will need several M3 screws in different lengths. The design is fairly forgiving in some areas, so multiple lengths can work. Below I have listed the sizes I used, along with alternative recommendations based on my testing. I also recommend keeping the parts in their supplied/uploaded print orientation for printing. They were arranged specifically to maximize strength by avoiding weak layer line orientations. All of the strength settings have been tested my be. I do not recommend reducing the amount of walls, top/bottom layers or infill percentage. Increasing is fine. Different infill pattern should also be fine. The model consists of: A - 2 hinge assemblies (2 parts each) B - 2 backplates C - 2 side reinforcements D - 1 middle reinforcement Only minimal supports are required. The holes are intentionally designed with very tight tolerances. In most cases you will need to use the screws themselves to thread the holes slightly during assembly. This is intentional to eliminate unnecessary play. If your printer struggles with dimensional accuracy, you can carefully open the holes up using a 3 mm drill bit. Step 1 Assemble the hinges. Refer to the photos for the correct orientation. The two hinge halves fit together tightly. Each hinge requires: 1 × M3x40 mm screw 1 × M3 nut The screw direction does not matter as long as it passes completely through the hinge and is secured with the nut. Step 2 Remove the factory screws from the toolhead communication assembly. Insert the assembled hinges by pushing the locating pins into the holes where the factory screws were removed. Make sure the pins are fully seated. You may need to twist or wiggle the hinge slightly while pushing it into place. If the pins are excessively tight, lightly sand or shave them until they fit. Secure each hinge with a screw, but do not fully tighten them yet. On my printer, an M3x40 mm screw was almost a perfect fit if you want it to sit flush from the inside (see the video, XXXX timestamp). I personally used M3x45 mm screws and secured them with a nut on the inside. Step 3 Place the top cover back on the printer and make sure it sits straight, flush, and pushed as far toward the hinges as possible. Flip the hinges upward so they sit flush against the cover. Install the mirrored side reinforcements onto the hinges. Each reinforcement only fits on one side. With the reinforcements installed, you can rotate the hinges slightly left or right to fine-tune their position. If the hinges move too freely, lightly tighten the screws from Step 2. The goal is for the side reinforcements to sit perfectly flush against the walls and corners of the top cover. Repeat on the opposite side. Once you are satisfied with the alignment, use the eight mounting holes in the hinges to mark the drilling locations on the acrylic cover. Take your time during this step. This is the point of no return. Up until now, every modification has been completely reversible. After marking, use the square backplate (B, Pictured below) to confirm markings are aligned properly. Huge thanks to @UncleJessy for testing and this tip! Step 4 Remove the top cover and place it on your work surface. Using a 3 mm drill bit, drill all eight marked holes. Make sure your drill is sharp and drill very slowly to avoid cracking the cover. After drilling, remove all burrs and debris. Step 5 Install the screws into the backplates. Top holes: M3x20 mm Bottom holes: M3x10 mm for flush fit. Longer screws will work but reduce the opening angle. The 12 mm screws will protrude slightly and slightly reduce the maximum opening angle of the lid. If you want the cover to open a little farther, use M3x10 mm screws instead. Longer screws can also be used if you prefer a smaller opening angle. There is some room for personal preference here. Insert the screws through the acrylic from the inside until the backplate sits completely flush against the inside wall of the cover. Repeat for the opposite side. Step 6 Remove the hinge assemblies from the printer (see Step 2). Slide the hinges onto the screws protruding from the backplates. Because of the tight tolerances, you may need to rotate each screw gradually with a screwdriver instead of simply pushing the hinge into place. Step 7 Secure the lower four screws (two per hinge) with nuts. Install both side reinforcements, then place the middle reinforcement across the top. Secure the remaining four screws with nuts and tighten everything firmly. Step 8 Flip the hinges outward and reinstall the entire assembly onto the printer. Guide the two locating pins back into the holes from Step 2. Having a second person helping makes this step much easier. Once both pins are fully seated, close the cover and reinstall the side screws from Step 2. Tighten everything completely. Installation is now complete. A few things to keep in mind When closing the cover, you may occasionally need to wiggle it slightly so the two locating pins slide back into the frame correctly. If everything was aligned properly during Step 3, the cover should sit just as flush as it did before the modification. Do not slam the cover open or closed. Do not place objects on the open cover in the opened state. I have no idea how durable the acrylic will be over time. It is not particularly thick, and additional weight or force could cause it to crack. I also do not recommend leaving the cover open on the hinges for extended periods. Open it only when needed. Think carefully before deciding whether this modification is right for you. Finally, I cannot guarantee that every current or future Creator 5 will be manufactured identically. Small design changes may occur without notice, so fitment could vary between machines. description: AMS HT X2D / P2S mount - Standalone and AMS Flipper - V2 This is my brand new and completely (re)built and revamped mount for the AMS HT for X2D/P2S printer frames that can now be used either standalone with the printer by attaching it directly to the printer frame on the back, or with an AMS Flipper from @ Jakob_K_Design attached to the back and integrating with the AMS Flipper handle. The model has been built from the ground up, taking prior experience and designing a fully modular, easy to print frame of the mount that is almost support free for printing, and assembled together using standard hardware forming a strong base for the AMS HT that sits even horizontally with the top of the printer to be side by side with an AMS Pro 2 on top of the printer. The mount can also be extended with the new Filament Track Switch to allow dynamic inputs for the extruders. Core features of the mount The AMS HT mount conveniently sits on the side, flush with the top of the printer, allowing installation of an AMS Pro 2 or other Risers on top of the printer without interference. You can choose between installing the mount directly to the printer frame, or if you are using an AMS Flipper, to the Flipper handle, using the provided compatible bracket. AMS HT mount allowing full view of the side window with minimal obstruction Some highlights of the model: Strong triangular brackets, balancing strength and material use to mount the AMS HT to the side of the X2D/P2S printer frame Full view of the side window below the AMS HT with minimal obstruction Side bracket provides extra strength and vibration dampening from the printer for the front side of the mount Easy to print flat on the bed with no supports needed for the frame and only minimal supports required for the interfacing slots for precision Easy assembly by slotting the four (4) parts of the mount together using standard hardware of M3 screws and square nuts for a strong hold Can either be used: Directly with the printer using the Standalone main bracket or using the AMS Flipper compatible main bracket which slots around the AMS Flipper handle The mount allows access to the l inear rail belt tensioning ports for maintenance The model print profile has been fine tuned for strength, optimizing extrusion settings to maximize strength and limit support interface swaps and harnessing the power of the X2D dual nozzle system. The print profile is optimized to be printed using the X2D using PETG for the frame, with PLA as support interface support layer for crisp results and easy support removal. Note: As the printer frame is shared between the X2D and the P2S, if printing using the P2S, you will have a few nozzle swaps for the interface layers, but they are minimized to just a few, so it shouldn't affect print time dramatically. NOTE: Please be careful with resetting settings, they have been carefully set to have repeatable successful prints and hold to the print bed. Optional Add-on : Designed to be compatible with my X2D Filament Track Switch mount by having a cutout reserved for the mount and utilizing triangles for chord organization. Optional Add-on: Cable organizer using the triangle brackets. Upon request by another user, I designed another add-on to make the cable organization of the 6-pin cable even neater using a figure-8 cable organizer loop that snap-fits into one of the triangle brackets and can be mounted either vertically or horizontally depending on your preference. Hardware required for assembly and installation You will need a few types of M3 Socket Head Screws and thin M3 square nuts: 7x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA042 x2 3x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm for the mount assembly 4x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm for the installation to the X2D/P2S printer frame 2x Socket Head Screw M3x20mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA040 x1 5x Socket Head Screw M3x10mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA159 x1 10x thin M3 square nuts (DIN 562, ≤2mm height) Optional: If you plan to install the Cable organizer you will also need 4x size 8x3mm round magnets (Bambu Lab store part CA008 x1) for the mount in the frame (and another 4x for the organizer itself ) Assembly The assembly is fairly simple and requires just a few standard hardware M3 screws and square nuts, providing a strong hold. You can follow the below step by step instructions, or follow the annotated images for location of screws, nuts and (optional) magnets. As the mount sits right next to the printer frame, for durability the model should be printed using PETG - so dry your filament prior to use! - you want to avoid stringing, warping or lifting off the bed. Print the four (4) parts - To help avoid any warping, you may want to reduce the Aux Fan speed to avoid spot cooling, which can contribute to lifting of large prints, or consider installing an Aux Fan deflector . Print the Main Bracket Pick either the Standalone Main Bracket if you want to install the mount directly to the printer frame or pick the AMS Flipper compatible Main Bracket if you are using the Flipper to mount the bracket to the Flipper Handle Print the Side Bracket for strong support of the mount and provide dampening to limit vibrations from the printer Print the Top Front Mount Bracket that holds the AMS HT and interfaces with the back and side brackets Print the Top Back Mount Bracket that holds the AMS HT and interfaces with the front and main brackets Print optional add-ons as desired: (Optional): Print the Filament Track Switch add-on to mount the Filament Track Switch to the frame over the AMS Flipper Handle and into the AMS HT side mount frame (Optional): Print the Cable Organizer add-on for extra neat organization of the 6-pin cable connecting to the AMS HT Annotated location of mounting hardware: Step by Step instructions: Connect the Top Front and Back brackets through their connecting interface Install two (2) thin M3 square nuts into the inside slots on both left and right side of the top arms Screw two (2 ) socket head screws M3x10mm length from the outside through each of the two arms to connect to the nuts to lock the front and back brackets together Slot the assembled Top Bracket into the Main Bracket through the four trapezoid interface arms note this is a precise interface with 0.15mm tolerances, so check that your printer printed the interfacing arms without any blobs or give them a light sand on the edges as needed Make sure the interface arms are aligned straight and push down using the back of your palm until the top and main brackets are flush - if things are tight and get stuck, a light sideways wiggle can help to loosen things Slot the Side Bracket into the Main Bracket through the two trapezoid interface arms using the same technique Install thin square nuts M3 in all remaining slots, sliding them to their embedded depths: One (1) - Inside of the Top Back bracket One (1) - Upper side of the Top Front bracket Two (2) - Inside of the Side bracket Two (2) - Sunk into the two slots on the back of the Main bracket - use a thin long screwdriver or pliers to push them into place Screw one (1) M3x10mm socket head screw from the bottom of the side bracket through the front bracket , watching until the screw surfaces through the square nut and locks the two parts together Screw two (2) M3x20mm socket head screws from the top of the Main Bracket through the interface arms, meeting the sunk square nuts Screw three (3) M3x30mm socket head screws from the back of the Main Bracket into the remaining holes connecting the Main and Top bracket with one (1) and the Main and Side bracket with two (2) screws (Optional) Install four (4) size 8x3mm round magnets into the holes on the back of the Main Bracket if you plan on installing the optional Cable Organizer. Installation Directly to the printer Remove the four (4) screws from the left backside of the X2D/P2S printer frame Remove the external spool holder mount if it is currently installed at the top and move it tothe bottom of the printer Attach two (2) M3x30mm socket head screws to the top of the mount and two to the bottom of the mounting holes aligning them with the four holes from which you removed the screws Using AMS Flipper Lift the left side (from the back) AMS Flipper Handle up and clip the mount into the handle - this should sit evenly almost flush on both sides -the mount will minimally protrude prior to tightening of the screws to create a counter clamping force to the AMS Flipper Handle to ensure a strong tight fit, but it will still allow the Flipper Handle to sit flush against the printer frame once aligned correctly as pictured below. Lower the Handle onto the printer and align the top and bottom evenly. A small gap before tightening the screws is ok but it should only be 1-2mm and be even between the top and bottom of the handle. If mount was correctly clicked into the handle and the handle sits even as shown above, screw the four (4) M3x30mm socket head screws onto the printer frame. I recommend starting with one of the bottom screws, but without fully tightening it, and then moving to the top and then finishing the rest of the screws and tightening things into place. Check that the flush fit hasn't shifted in case you tightened one screw before alignment was locked into place. The AMS HT mount and the top and bottom of the AMS Flipper handle should sit basically flush with the printer if the AMS HT side mount was clicked into place together correctly once everything is tightened as shown below: If things don't sit flush correctly, repeat Step 1-3, check the fit and try again until the mount is properly set in the center of the handle, resulting in a flush fit. If this is your initial installation of the AMS Flipper, follow the rest of the AMS Flipper installation instructions to finish installation of your AMS Flipper. Install optional add-ons Optional: Install the Filament Track Switch mount . Utilize the triangle cutout in the frame or use the cable organizer to store and tuck away the cords of the AMS HT: If you installed the External Spool holder on the bottom of the printer frame, you could route the power chord of the AMS HT through the triangle frame and down and using a cable tie (ideally a good quality Velcro one) attach the chord to the external spool holder for a clean installation. Optional: Install the Cable Organizer for AMS HT side-mount to organize the 6-pin cable using a neat figure-8 loop Done, enjoy easy access to your AMS HT on your X2D/P2S printer. Print Settings Supports: yes, with top interface layer enabled for smooth finish on supported portions Only the interface arms and the cutout for the linear rail adjustment screws require supports Brim: no Layer Height: 0.20mm Infill: 25 % cubic for strength Walls: 2 Print orientation: Flat on the bed Material: Parts: Dry PETG for strength and temperature resistance due to the close proximity to the printer. Loaded into Primary (left) nozzle Support Interface: PLA or specific support material to make removal easy (PLA won't bond strongly with PETG, so removal is easy, but the bond is strong enough for print support and using just interface layer reduces nozzle swaps). Loaded into Aux (right) nozzle if printed on X2D

description: This is a remixed model originally created by the very talented morph91 . Original model link: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2749412-bc-250-gaming-pc-case-mk-ultra-uno . I'm naming this model the MK Ultra Uno Plus : ) Case Highlights: Can be printed in only 3 plates with less than 600g of filament Tool-less design (no screws required) Fits the FSP500-30AS, Apevia ITX flex, and Metalfish flex PSUs Customizable front plates Ability to fit 40 & 50 mm fans on rear Internal clips to attach both halves of case together securely & internal psu lock to securely hold psu in place without external latch Heatsink mod (stick on heatsinks) to help improve thermals Important Considerations: There are two different versions of the fan shroud. One is the exact same as the original, the other is a modified version that allows active airflow to flow to stick on heatsinks that I personally made for my build. You can reference the assembly instructions for photos. Please make sure you only print the plate relevant for your build! Both the apevia and metalfish variants of the back case contain one less internal clip/latch due to space constraints. So these variants may be slightly less rigid when the two case halves are put together The internal psu lock was created specfically for the FSP500-30AS variant. It might fit the apevia variant, but will most likely not fit the metalfish variant. If someone prints either version, I'm more than happy to create a working psu lock for these versions. I just need accurate measurements and someone to test any prototypes. If you're interested then leave a comment/DM me : ) If anyone ends up printing the apevia or metalfish variants, please let me know if anything needs to be adjusted (besides the internal psu lock)! I used morph91 's measurements for the metalfish variant and also lolheyaj 's measurements for the apevia variant, since I do not personally own either of those psus. Also, as a temporary solution for the internal psu lock issue - you could probably use glue to keep the psu secure in the case as a temporary measure. If you have a different flex psu, and can take some accurate measurements for me - I am more than willing to create new versions to suit your psu (as long as dimensions fit the case)! : ) Expected Thermals: Thermals may vary slightly, given differences in thermal paste and depending whether you use the stick on heatsinks like I did. Also depending on 24CU vs 40CU, fan curves, overclock, undervolts, etc. For reference here's my configuration: GPU: 40CU 2000MHz @940mV (+16CU and +500 MHz from stock) CPU: 3800MHz @1060mV (+300MHz from stock) And here are some max temps from a couple games @1080p: My Part List: BC250 PSU (fsp500-30as, apevia itx flex, or metalfish flex) https://a.co/d/0gOMs9rW black petg https://a.co/d/04eTZ6sm for the two brown pla's from this bundle for my fake wood texture front panels makerworld.com/en/models/2527214-bc-250-scooper fin scooper to straighten fins https://a.co/d/0hZ28ifs for 12mm latching button (you may need a wire stripper, wire crimper, and dupont connectors if you copy me 1:1) https://a.co/d/0jdT5jNV arctic p12 pro pst https://a.co/d/0iLAR7Ty arctic mx-4 thermal paste (optional) https://a.co/d/063cMg66 noctua NF-A4x20 (optional) https://a.co/d/00RnzoEo stick on heatsinks, I bought 2 of these kits and used 3 out of the 4 heatsinks (optional) This looks to be a cheaper alternative: https://a.co/d/038s6cPO - it would be the same size as what I used, but as one large piece instead. Based on reviews, it looks like a thermal pad of some sort is already preapplied. If you end up buying this one, let me know how it fits! (optional) https://a.co/d/066uYDJ8 rubber anti vibration screws used to mount noctua 40mm fan Print Instructions: Print the main case components in PETG, and dry filament for 8 hours before printing (reduces stringing). Make sure to print only one of the fan shroud plates. For more information read the important considerations at the top. If you want to make your front panel have the fake wood texture like mine, then use this as a modifier: https://makerworld.com/en/models/1492898-wood-grain-modifier-add-wood-grain-to-any-models?from=search#profileId-1560821 . You can print the front panels in PLA. I recommend using a 0.2mm nozzle if you're doing the wood texture like I did. If you are downloading the model to modify or use with a different slicer (and not bambu studio), then make sure to paint a straight line seam on the bottom part of back half of the case. This helps reduce VFAs: Assembly Instructions: Take off the IO shield and the small bracket next to cmos battery Use the fin scooper to straighten the fins underneath where the fan shroud is gonna go. model_name: Light and Fast Dual AMS Mount for H/X/P Series
description: I wanted a mount that didn't take too long to print or require too much material so I designed a mount that utilizes the weight of the AMS itself to help the mount clamp against the machine and keep the structure light. Unfortunately, the machines are not exactly the overall dimensions that Bambu cites. To accommodate this, the structure is broken into pieces that can be connected at various lengths to accommodate various printer sizes. This also makes them compatible with various models of Bambu machines. I also managed to fit all the parts in a single X/P series bed. H2C/H2S/H2D P2S X1C /X1E P1S/P1P AMS 2 AMS (3 Cavity) AMS (5 Cavity) Verified X X X X X Compatible X X Incompatible Note for High Temp Users: High temp printing with chamber heating will heat the printer glass beyond the glass transition temperature of PLA. This will cause warping of the structure. Please print the mount from a high temp plastic if you plan on printing chamber heated materials. If you only print PLA, this should not be an issue. Here is how the structure works: AMS weight hanging over the edge of the machine pushes down, forcing supports to pivot around the edge of the machine. Supports are retained by central tension member, which drives force into the side of the machine. Forces driving into side of machine increase friction between support and machine, improving grip. Small nubs on the central support posts retain both AMS units against each other, and prevent them from moving when the printer shakes. Size the frames so they are snug to the machine. If the notches only allow a slightly loose or slightly tight fit, choose the tight one. Once the weight of the AMS is loaded on top, any bowing in the structure will flatten out. The assembly utilizes toothed connections which are finely tuned to slide together and retain themselves with the layer lines of the print. If parts are too tight, they can likely be tapped together with a hammer without issue, just dont expect to get them back apart. If too loose, you can scale just the tensioning rods (the thin rectangular parts) to 101% to get a tighter fit. This gif shows the assembly process:

description: The YAPR™ (pronounced "YAP-er") — Yet Another Purge Receptacle Featuring BinLock™ push-button locking technology Not being completely satisfied with the first purge bin I ever printed, I set out to design (overengineer?) my own after getting the A2L. I wanted a purge bin that looked like it belonged on the printer , stayed exactly where I put it, and came off with a simple button press—without magnets, awkward removal angles, or extra hardware. I was tired of: Awkwardly angling or shifting the purge bin to remove it every time I emptied it (and sometimes spilling purge in the process) Constantly nudging the bin back against the printer because it would slowly vibrate away after a print or two Small pieces of purged filament finding their way between the bin and the printer Liners that frequently broke or cracked and needed to be reprinted The YAPR is a push-button A2L purge (or poop!) bin that locks securely in place, prints mostly in place, and requires no magnets or extra hardware . Designed to be the last purge bin you'll ever need to print. Features Easily attaches and detaches using exclusive BinLock™ push-button technology—no bin gymnastics required Securely locks in place and won't slowly vibrate away from the printer Matching side contour helps prevent stray filament from falling between the bin and the printer Contoured to match the printer's lines for a clean, OEM-inspired appearance Prints mostly in place with only a small amount of support beneath the button Available in three sizes: Slim (100mm wide — best for tight spaces), Standard (125mm wide — the daily driver), and Wide (150mm wide — ideal for heavy AMS printing and lower maintenance) Optional liner fully protects the bottom of the bin (unlike many liners with fully cut-out patterns) while also helping reduce purge rattling Won't block your printer's ventilation ports Angled bottom makes it easy to grab those last stubborn pieces of purge Assembly Notes This is specifically designed for the A2L only. For the easiest assembly, assemble within two hours of printing. The BinLock™ mechanism is intentionally designed with a tight initial fit and has a short break-in period. It will become noticeably smoother with use. If the button doesn't move smoothly after pressing it several times, grasp it with pliers and work it in and out a few times. The additional travel and force help speed up the break-in process. Instructions Choose your preferred size, print the bin , peg , and peg cover , then remove the small amount of support beneath the button. If using the optional liner, print the matching size in PETG (or PLA if you primarily print PETG). Press the BinLock™ button (located on the bottom right of the bin) several times to begin the break-in process (The first press requires a fair amount of force, so using two thumbs while bracing the bin against a countertop or table is recommended.) Hold the BinLock™ button down and rub a crayon over the small internal slide (see the second to last model photo for the exact location). While this may seem like an unusual step, it is important for smooth operation of the BinLock™ mechanism. The next few assembly steps are a little tricky—but thankfully, you only need to do them once. Turn the peg cover upside down with its tallest side facing you. Insert the peg upside down so the shortest side of the peg's triangular base faces to the right. The angle of the peg should *not* match the angle of the peg cover. Please see the last model photo for up close pictures. Without disturbing the peg, and with the longest side of the peg cover facing you , insert the peg and cover together into the bin until the cover snaps into place. Turning the bin upside down during this step usually makes assembly easier, and engaging the snap-fit may require a firm push. With the bin upright, press the BinLock™ button several more times. You should notice the peg moving slightly with each press as the mechanism continues to break in. If the button mechanism isn't working correctly, the peg may not be fully seated. Grip the peg firmly with pliers, pull it straight out with steady force (the peg and cover will come out together), then repeat the installation process. Connect to printer Hold the BinLock™ button. Slide the bin fully against the rear frame and side of the printer. Release the button to lock the bin in place. Disconnect from printer Hold the BinLock™ button. Pull the bin straight toward you. Print one. Lock it in. Forget about it.

description: AMS HT Side Mount für Bambu Lab H2 Serie Diese Halterung ermöglicht es, das AMS HT seitlich am oberen Rahmen eines Druckers der H2-Serie zu befestigen. Dadurch kann TPU direkt über die Bypass-Öffnung des AMS HT zum Druckkopf geführt werden. Der große Vorteil dieser Positionierung ist der extrem kurze und nahezu geradlinige Filamentweg. Durch die modulare Bauweise, kann der Halter durch austauschen des Hakens auch für andere Druckermodelle genutzt werden. Nur eines der drei Bauteile benötigt eine winzige Stützstruktur. Einfache Montage Für die Montage muss lediglich der Glasdeckel des Druckers entfernt werden. Anschließend wird die Halterung einfach über den oberen Rand des Druckers gesteckt. description: Successful detection. Every time. No compromises. This version is designed exclusively for the Bambu Lab P2S and X2D. Each model is conceived, printed, and endurance-tested on my own machines, refined through dozens of iterations to match the printer’s true mechanical behavior. PTFE Clips Helps prevent PTFE tubes from rubbing against the top glass These lightweight PTFE tube clips are designed to help keep the tubing from wearing on the upper glass panel on enclosed Bambu Lab printers. They have been tested on the Bambu Lab X2D and are designed for standard 4 mm PTFE tubing , so they may also fit other compatible Bambu Lab models. Why I designed them As the toolhead moves around the printer, the PTFE tubes naturally twist, bend and change position. Some tube-management solutions hold multiple tubes tightly together to create a neater appearance. While this may look tidy, it can also introduce unnecessary tension, stress or twisting into the tubing as the toolhead travels. These clips are designed to support each tube individually. This helps reduce wear on the PTFE tubes from the top glass while still allowing the tubes to move as designed. Key features Helps prevent PTFE wear from rubbing on the top glass Designed for standard 4 mm PTFE tubing Tested on the Bambu Lab X2D Allows each tube to move independently Applies only light tension to the tubing Lightweight and low profile Quick snap-on installation No tools or printer modifications required Small and fast to print How many should I use? I currently use four clips , which provides good support and separation. More clips can be installed if additional support is required, but avoid using so many that the tubing becomes stiff or restricted. Recommended print settings These were successfully printed using: Layer height: 0.16 mm Walls/perimeters: 3 Bed temperature: 60°C Part cooling fan: 0% for the first 2 - 3 layers, then a maximum of 25% Brim: Not required Supports: Not required Keeping the cooling fan low helps prevent these small parts from cooling too quickly, warping or lifting from the build plate. Material recommendations PLA is suitable for normal use where the heated chamber is not being used. For printers operating with a heated chamber, use a more temperature-resistant material such as: PETG ABS ASA Another suitable heat-resistant filament PLA may soften or deform when exposed to elevated chamber temperatures for extended periods. Installation Carefully snap each clip over a PTFE tube. Position the clips along the tubing where support is required. Move the toolhead through its full range of travel. Check that each tube can still bend and move freely. Reposition or remove clips if any tension or restriction is present. Important notes These clips are intended to gently guide the PTFE tubes, not lock them rigidly in place. After installation, confirm that: The tubes still move freely The clips do not contact the cable chain The tubing is not stretched, kinked or twisted The toolhead can reach the full build area The clips remain clear of all moving components Compatibility Tested on: Bambu Lab X2D Tube size: 4 mm PTFE Other models may be compatible but have not yet been tested Support the design

description: Humidity, my worst enemy… Snapmaker sent me the U1, and unfortunately, I'm not able to get good prints with printers that have open-air spools (because of the humidity at my location). So I looked for the best way to deal with it, and none of the projects I found were good enough. The closest one used a Sunlu Filadryer S4, so that was my baseline to start this project: Snapmaker u1 + Sunlu Fliladryer S4 Setup Compact setup Air-tight (at least as much as the original S4) It has the feeders as close as possible to the spools → Easier loading and unloading This is a DIY project, so you will need some tools and materials: M3 x 6 Screws, 4 of them with nuts and washers 2 x PTFE connectors. The ones that allow the 4 mm PTFE tube to pass through Drills (3.5 mm for the screws, and one for the size of your PTFE connectors) Extra PTFE tubes (4 mm OD, 2.5 mm ID) to replace the ones that go from the original feeder location to the back of the printer. Feeder extension cable. This might be the trickiest. They can be found as GH1.25 or JST GH1.25. Be sure they are 15-pin and male-female configuration. The length depends on your setup; measure both sides from the feeder's original location to the back of the Sunlu S4. I recommend 50 cm. I'll leave some links in the comments. I don't have measurements of the process, because I did it on the go and wasn't planning to upload it anywhere. But I have some pictures taken from the video I recorded: Depending on your setup, you would want to place the S4 on the right or the left of the U1. Therefore, you need to install the feeders on the side of the S4 that faces the back (as shown in the pictures above). You need to measure the distance between the feeder inputs, and drill the holes in the S4 to install the PTFE connectors. Then, assemble the feeders in the printed holder, and place it with the holes aligned to the filament input. Mark the Holder holes, and drill the 3.5 mm holes for the screw assembly. Assemble it, place the numbers from the inside, and then the funnels (optional, but recommended) Then, place the U1 and S4 in the final position, measure, cut, and install the PTFE tubes from the printer to the feeder. Don't make them too short or they might bend; leave some extra for them to wiggle around with smooth curves. That's about it. As I said, I made it on the go, so I'm not sure if I'm forgetting something 😂
