description: Snap-On Remix for Fixed-End Spool Holders A snap-on remix of David D.'s Hanging (Pendulum) Filament Guide, a weighted arm that hangs on your spool holder and keeps light tension on the filament path from external spools, so the line can’t drift off the spool and tangle. His original closed eyelet is the right design when you can slide it onto the rod from one end, and it comes in three eyelet sizes (26, 36, and 46mm). If your spool rod is removable, go print his version. But some holders have fixed ends with flares or caps, like the Bambu X2D stock top mount, and nothing threads onto those. This version converts the 26mm eyelet to a C-clip that snaps onto the holder radially and stays put. The Engineering The opening size is not a guess. The gap is a 90 degree segment sized from bending strain math for a C-ring flexing over a 26mm shaft. Peak strain during snap-on lands around 1.4 percent, comfortably inside PETG’s working limit. Rounded entry bulbs on the tips guide the shaft in and spread the ring smoothly. The gap is also rotated 60 degrees off the arm centerline, so the load path never rests on the opening. It goes on with a firm push, a positive click, and swings freely as a pendulum. Tested on an X2D stock top holder and others (as seen in the photos) in PETG HF. Bonus: Light Spool Keeper Many fixed-end holders are graduated, widening toward the flared end. Because this clip fits snugly instead of loosely, it doubles as a spool keeper: it blocks the spool from walking outward off the end while still penduluming freely guiding your filament with ease. Material Matters Print this in PETG, ASA, or ABS. The snap fit depends on flex. PLA has roughly half the strain tolerance, so it will probably survive a couple installations, but repeated cycles with PLA will likely cause stress cracking, and matte PLA is even worse. I haven't tested PLA to failure on this, so YMMV, but I'd just use PETG or something with better strength and flex than PLA. ⚠️ IMPORTANT PRINT NOTE Use 4 or more wall loops (the profile has this set). The ring works as a spring and needs solid perimeters in the bending section, not sparse infill. Everything else stays at defaults. The plate includes mirrored left and right arms, plus the original design’s small locking pins as an optional backup if the detents ever wear. The original designer reports the detents holding fine on their own and that has been true for me as well, but they're there if you need them.

description: This is a simple magnet fit tolerance test kit for common round magnets used in 3D printed projects. Instead of guessing the perfect hole size for your magnets, print the test strip that matches the magnets you have, press your magnets into the different holes, and choose the fit that works best for your printer, slicer settings, filament, and material. The kit includes separate test pieces for: 3×2 mm magnets 4×2 mm magnets 5×2 mm magnets 6×2 mm magnets 8×2 mm magnets 10×2 mm magnets Each size is a separate part, so you do not need to print the whole kit. Just print the strip for the magnet size you actually have. Each strip includes multiple hole diameters around the nominal magnet size, with the tolerance clearly labelled above each hole. For example, the 6×2 mm strip tests hole sizes from 5.95 mm to 6.25 mm. The magnet pockets are designed for 2 mm thick magnets. The back of each pocket is intentionally thin so the magnet can be pushed back out after testing. Why use this? Magnet fit can vary a lot depending on: Printer calibration Filament type Material shrinkage Nozzle size Slicer settings Hole compensation settings Whether you want a press fit, loose fit, or glue-in fit For best results, print the test strip in the same material you plan to use for your final project. For example, if your finished part will be PETG, print the test strip in PETG. If your final part will be ABS, print the test strip in ABS. description: Tired of small, overflowing purge bins, this modular flexible tube allows you to route waste directly into any container for uninterrupted long-term printing. This is a “poop chute” or purge waste collection system that has been customized for use with the Bambu Lab H2 series printers, H2S, H2D, H2C. Here are some valuable features: Infinite Customization: It has a segmented "link" design allows you to add or remove sections to reach a waste bin at almost any height or distance from your workbench. Zero-Clog Geometry: The wide, rounded internal path of the segments prevents the "accordion" effect where purge poops occasionally snag on sharp corners or narrow bottlenecks. Workspace Flexibility: Unlike rigid chutes, the articulated tube can be snaked around power cables, enclosure legs, or other tools sitting behind your printer. Toolless Maintenance: Once the adapter is mounted, the tube segments easily snap together or apart, making it simple to clear a rare jam or adjust the routing without tools. High-Volume Ready: By bypassing small, printer-mounted bins in favor of a floor-side box, you can run massive multi-color prints without worrying about a backup at the purge exit. It includes these parts: Mounting Bracket : This part attaches to your printer and has a simple dovetail that can accept an adapter. description: One print. Twelve failure checks. Every card tells you what to inspect, what the answer means, and the three settings to change next. Now fits the A1 mini. Most calibration prints tell you that something is wrong. Print Doctor tells you what it means and what to do next — the diagnosis is printed right on the part, so you never have to go looking it up. What's new in v2 It fits your printer now. v1 was 204 × 180 mm, which meant A1 mini owners could not print it at all. v2 ships in three layouts: one full 239 × 179 mm sheet for 256 × 256 plates, plus Sheet A and Sheet B at 139 × 158 mm each, which fit a 180 × 180 plate with room to spare. Twelve tests, not ten. Three new cards: Overhang angle — four fins leaning at a labelled 30°, 45°, 55° and 65° off vertical. Find the first one whose underside breaks up: that is your printer's real overhang limit, and the number you should put in your support threshold. Clearance & fit — three print-in-place rings around capped posts at 0.15, 0.25 and 0.35 mm radial clearance. Try to spin each one. The tightest ring that still turns is the clearance you can trust in your own designs. Dimensions — a 18.00 mm square tube and a Ø14.00 mm round tube, both with a two-line wall. Measure the outside, the inside and the wall thickness with calipers to separate a flow error from an XY-compensation error. It adapts to your nozzle. Every gap, rib, wall and slot is derived from your nozzle diameter, so the tests still discriminate on a 0.6 mm or 0.2 mm nozzle instead of being tuned only for 0.4 mm. Better as a keepsake. Every card carries its number and a 4.5 mm hole, so once you snap the sheet apart the twelve cards go straight onto a binder ring and live next to the printer as a flip-through reference deck. The breakaway tabs are thinner than v1's and snap cleanly instead of tearing. Sharper geometry. The Z-seam cup is now genuinely round. In v1 it was a 48-sided polygon, and those facet lines could be mistaken for the seam artifacts the card is supposed to reveal. The cat-shaped Print Doctor nameplate, the mushroom cooling test and the elephant-foot paw all survive the rebuild. The twelve tests # Card What you do What it tells you 01 Under-extrusion Look for gaps in the single-line frame and three ribs Flow, clog, or temperature too low 02 Over-extrusion Find the smallest labelled slot still open How much excess flow is closing your gaps 03 Pressure advance Look at the ten hard corners Bulging after turns, thinning before them 04 Stringing Count the strands between four spires Retraction, temperature, wet filament 05 Weak bridging Feel the underside of the 10, 18 and 26 mm spans Longest span your cooling can hold 06 Overhang angle Find the first fin that breaks up Your real overhang limit in degrees 07 Poor cooling Look at the droop on three mushroom caps Whether the layer below is setting in time 08 Z-seam quality Look down the seam line of a smooth cup Zits, gaps, inconsistent layer starts 09 Elephant foot Look at the base flare of the paw First-layer squish and Z offset 10 Layer adhesion Bend the 0.80, 1.20 and 1.60 mm blades Whether layers split or the plastic yields 11 Clearance & fit Spin the three rings The tightest clearance you can design to 12 Dimensions Measure with calipers Flow error vs XY-compensation error The paw on card 09 prints directly on the build plate through a window in the card, so the first layer is never hidden by a card floor underneath it. Which file do I print? Your printer Print this Bambu A1 / P1S / P1P / X1C, Prusa MK4, Ender 3 (220+) print_doctor_v2_full.stl — one sheet, all 12 cards Bambu A1 mini, or any 180 × 180 plate print_doctor_v2_mini_A_cards_1-6.stl then ..._mini_B_cards_7-12.stl How to use it Slice with the profile you actually want to diagnose — not a specially tuned calibration profile. The point is to test what you print with every day. Supports off . The unsupported features are the test. Brim off if you can. A brim hides elephant foot. Print flat, exactly as supplied. Work through the cards. Each raised LOOK / FEEL / COUNT / BEND / SPIN / MEASURE line tells you what to do with that specimen. Use the three printed adjustments as your shortlist. Change one setting at a time and reprint just the card you are chasing. Snap the sheet apart, put the twelve cards on a binder ring, keep them by the printer. The printed suggestions are starting points, not laws. Material condition, hardware wear, motion settings and slicer behaviour can all produce similar-looking symptoms. Recommended print settings Material: PLA for the first diagnostic print Nozzle: 0.4 mm (the model is parametric if you run something else) Layer height: 0.20 mm — this matters, the print-in-place rings on card 11 are designed around a 0.2 mm air gap Walls: 2 Infill: 15 % Supports: Off Brim: Off where possible Orientation: Flat, as supplied Model dimensions File Footprint Max height Full sheet 239.0 × 178.7 mm 21.4 mm Mini Sheet A 138.9 × 158.2 mm 21.4 mm Mini Sheet B 138.9 × 158.2 mm 19.2 mm One connected, manifold print in every case, with optional breakaway cards. The three rings on card 11 print loose by design — that is the test. Parametric The OpenSCAD source is included and is set up for the MakerWorld Parametric Model Maker. Adjustable: sheet layout, nozzle diameter, layer height, label style (raised or flush inlay), part split for multi-colour, breakaway tab thickness, and the binder-ring hole.

description: X2D Auxiliary Fan Duct The Bambu Lab X2D auxiliary fans can direct a significant amount of cool air across the left and right edge of the build plate. For materials such as PLA, and particularly PETG, this concentrated airflow may contribute to uneven cooling, edge lifting, corner warping or reduced first-layer adhesion on some models. These deflectors redirect the auxiliary fan airflow upward and away from the print bed, helping prevent the fans from blowing directly across the edges of the print while still allowing air to circulate inside the chamber. Why I designed these I began experiencing prints lifting primarily along the edges closest to the auxiliary fans, which indicated that the concentrated airflow across the front of the build plate was contributing to uneven cooling. Although auxiliary-fan values can be adjusted within the filament and process profiles, the commanded settings do not always appear to remain in effect during printing. In some situations, the printer’s internal control logic applies its own auxiliary-fan behaviour and overrides the values defined in the slicer. This means the fan may continue operating at a higher speed than expected, even after the cooling profile has been adjusted. Because the underlying firmware-controlled behaviour is not currently exposed as a separate user-adjustable setting, it can be difficult to reliably prevent direct airflow from reaching the front edge of the print bed. These deflectors provide a mechanical solution by changing the direction of the airflow itself. Rather than attempting to reduce or disable the fan electronically, they redirect the output upward and away from the build surface while still allowing air to circulate within the chamber. Key features Redirects auxiliary fan airflow upward and away from the build plate Helps reduce concentrated cooling along the edges of the print area May help reduce edge lifting and corner warping Maintains airflow inside the printer rather than completely blocking the fans Installs without permanent modification to the printer Can be easily removed when not required Designed as separate left- and right-hand deflectors Compatibility These deflectors have currently only been tested on the Bambu Lab X2D. Should fit P2S right side Aux Fan They are designed specifically around the X2D auxiliary fan outlets and surrounding clearances. Compatibility with other Bambu Lab printers has not been confirmed. Installation Fit each deflector over its corresponding auxiliary fan outlet, ensuring it is fully seated and secure. The outlet should face upward and inward, redirecting the airflow away from the surface of the build plate. After installation: Check that both deflectors are securely fitted. Confirm that neither deflector contacts the build plate, toolhead or any moving component. Manually move the toolhead throughout the complete build area. Run the printer’s normal homing or movement checks before beginning a print. Do not begin printing until full toolhead and build-plate clearance has been confirmed. Print settings The included print profile is the profile I used successfully for these parts. Recommended starting settings: Layer height: 0.16 mm Walls/perimeters: 3 Supports: Not required Brim: Painted on edges only to prevent lifting Orientation: Print in the supplied orientation The parts should be allowed to cool before removal from the build plate to avoid distortion. Material PLA is suitable for testing and general use. PETG, ABS or ASA may provide improved temperature resistance for long-term use inside the enclosed printer, particularly when printing materials that require elevated chamber temperatures. Important notes These deflectors change the direction of the auxiliary fan airflow. They do not provide electronic control over fan speed. Cooling requirements vary depending on: Filament type Model geometry Print speed Chamber temperature Bed temperature Auxiliary fan speed These parts are intended as a practical airflow-management accessory, not as a guaranteed fix for every adhesion or warping issue. Bed cleanliness, first-layer calibration, filament condition and suitable temperature settings should still be checked.

model_name: Tilted Low-Profile TPU Assistant Mount (X2D / P2S)
description: Staffa Compatta, Inclinata e Ribassata per TPU Assistant (Compatibile con Bambu Lab X2D / P2S) Ho progettato questa staffa per la mia X2D (essendo al 100% compatibile anche con il modello P2S ) con un obiettivo principale: migliorare radicalmente l'orientamento dei tasti del TPU Assistant per renderli finalmente visibili dal davanti, ottimizzare la direzione del tubo in PTFE verso l'AMS HT ed eliminare una volta per tutte la necessità di scollegare i tubetti durante l'uso quotidiano o l'essiccazione. Le caratteristiche principali di questo design: Gestione lineare del tubo (Nessun bisogno di scollegare nulla): Molti progetti online richiedono di scollegare il tubo in PTFE dall'AMS HT quando il TPU Assistant non è in uso, ad esempio per inserire il tappo di sigillo e avviare la funzione di essiccazione dell'Hub. Questo spesso comporta il dover riporre il tubetto rimosso per non perderlo. Con questa configurazione, grazie alla distanza ridotta e all'allineamento, non è mai necessario scollegare il tubo . Il condotto rimane stabilmente al suo posto e sigillato, semplificando i passaggi: basta spingere il filamento dall'AMS HT direttamente nel TPU Assistant e si è pronti a stampare. Inclinazione ed Ergonomia dei Tasti: La staffa è posizionata più in basso e inclina il TPU Assistant verso lo sguardo di chi si trova davanti alla stampante. In questo modo la pulsantiera e i LED di stato sono facilmente visibili e comodi da raggiungere direttamente dal fronte. Geometria del percorso posteriore e specifiche tubi: Essendo una staffa ribassata, la distanza geometrica verso l'ingresso della stampante aumenta leggermente rispetto alla configurazione standard, richiedendo un percorso totale fisso di 200 mm . Nota per la community: Bambu Lab raccomanda solitamente 160 mm, ma non c'è assolutamente da preoccuparsi per il caricamento . Il sistema del TPU Assistant è infatti progettato per funzionare ufficialmente anche sulla H2D , che è una stampante molto più grande della X2D e ha un percorso interno del filamento nativamente molto più lungo. Visto che il sistema gestisce quel tragitto maggiore senza problemi, i 4 cm esterni in più introdotti su questo setup vengono digeriti dall'estrusore in totale sicurezza. Per installare il sistema avete due opzioni precise: Setup Diretto: Vi servirà uno spezzone di tubo in PTFE tagliato esattamente a 200 mm . Con Adattatore 4-in-1: Se utilizzate un connettore 4-in-1 come il mio (lungo circa 6 cm), dovrete compensare la misura tagliando il tubetto in PTFE a 140 mm (140 mm + 60 mm = 200 mm). Design Essenziale: La struttura è pensata per essere il più compatta e leggera possibile, riducendo la quantità di filamento necessaria e i tempi di stampa. 🔄 IMPORTANTE: Calibrazione post-installazione Come raccomandato dalle linee guida ufficiali Bambu Lab, dopo aver installato la nuova staffa e posizionato il tubo da 200 mm (o 140 mm con adattatore), è fondamentale lanciare la calibrazione del modulo . Questa procedura serve a far leggere al sistema la nuova lunghezza del percorso, misurando l'attrito per calibrare al millesimo la forza della spinta automatica. 👉 Potete seguire la procedura ufficiale passo-passo a questo link della Wiki Bambu Lab: Guida alla Calibrazione del TPU Assistant . 🛠️ Note di Stampa e Tolleranze Materiale di Test: Il progetto è stato sviluppato, stampato e testato in PETG . Nota sulle tolleranze: L'asola di incastro per il TPU Assistant è calibrata in modo preciso sul PETG. Se decidete di stamparlo in PLA o ABS/ASA, tenete conto che il diverso ritiro termico dei materiali potrebbe influire leggermente sulla tolleranza dell'incastro (potrebbe risultare impercettibilmente più stretto o largo). Per Inatallazione sono necessarie due viti ST 3x12 avanzate dal kit di assemblaggio del TPU Assistant Spero questa soluzione vi è utile!

description: This is a dedicated mount that uses the A1 mini's Z-axis cover to attach the BMCU 370C to the right side of the printer. Most existing mounts position the BMCU behind the printer, feeding the PTFE tube from the rear toward the front. However, if your setup has limited rear clearance, this can create an excessively tight bend in the PTFE tube. To solve this problem, this mount routes the filament from the right side of the printer toward the left, allowing the PTFE tube to follow a smoother, more natural curve even in tight spaces. After testing several designs, I found that positioning the filament path at approximately a 45° angle while placing the BMCU slightly farther from the printer provided the best tube routing. The main model is based on this design. The Long 45° Version is the main model. Three additional optional versions are also included: Short 45° Version 30° Version Straight Version Feel free to choose the version you like best. Installation Notes Before installing this mount, remove the spacer secured to the printer's Z-axis cover with three screws. The original three screws are reused to secure this mount in place. No additional hardware is required.

description: A2L and A1 Poop Bucket - Parametric Purge Waste Bin A small ask : if you print this and find it to your liking, please rate my model. Ratings contribute to model visibility. Thank you ! So, you can't find the ideal poop basket that fits your printer's exact spot on the desk ? Or you want a quick-printing basket with very low filament usage ? You've come to the right place. This is a parametric waste bin generator - design your own poop chute to exactly your specifications, for either the A1 or the A2L. When customizing, don't forget to select the correct printer type in parameters. The A1 and A2L baskets are not fully interchangeable (especially if you opt for the lip), the printers have some differences even if they look similar. This design adds what a poop basket actually needs: A deflector that catches fast-ejected blobs and drops them straight down instead of letting them ricochet onto your desk A flared lip that widens the catch opening, so blobs landing low or wide still make it in. A floor baffle - a honeycomb base that traps purge blobs so they can't rattle every time the toolhead moves. A cable guide - a chamfer under the back edge for the power cable. No other poop basket has this, and on the A2L (often installed sideways against a wall due to its size - like in my case) a special opening for routing the power cable allows you to use all the available space between the printer and the wall. The notched corner wraps the printer's foot, and two ridges snap into its slits to keep the basket from sliding around. Do you need a fast-printing (45 min.), low-filament (32g) basket ? Check out the predefined printing profile with customized baskets that print in vase mode. Fully Parametric Configure everything you need: Printer type - A1 or A2L (sets height and foot-notch automatically) Basket width and length Deflector - None, Essential, Half-Size or Full-Size Deflector height Lip , Baffle, Cable Guide - each on or off Reinforcement Ribs so you can print it in vase mode 4 times faster and with 3 times less filament (please note: deflector, lip and baffle are not suitable for vase mode printing). Preset files with ready-to-print configurations are included (standard and narrow versions), so if your setup is typical you can go straight to printing without touching a single parameter. Printing note Prints flat with no supports - every feature is self-supporting. Hook the notched corner over the printer's foot and press the ridges into the slits. Happy printing!

description: Willkommen zur DryDisc! Das Ziel war eine unauffällige, extrem robuste und professionelle Lösung, die sich nahtlos zwischen breiteren Filamentrollen einfügt. Einmal installiert, bietet diese Rolle ein Leben lang puren Nutzen. Das Silica-Gel wird beim Trocknen des Filaments im Gerät automatisch mitgetrocknet. Features Ultra-Schmal (21 mm): Nimmt kaum Platz weg und passt problemlos zwischen Standard- und breite Filamentrollen. Optimiert für 2-5 mm Silica-Gel: Die Gitteröffnungen sind exakt so dimensioniert, dass Trockenmittel-Kügelchen in dieser Größe sicher in der Rolle bleiben und gleichzeitig maximal umströmt werden. Druck- & Materialempfehlung Wichtig zur Materialwahl: Beim trocknen mit 75°C , ist normales PETG hier weich geworden! Ich empfehle dringend den Druck in PET, ABS, ASA oder PC , um eine ausreichende Formstabilität bei dieser Hitze zu gewährleisten. Sollte mit weniger Temperatur getrocknet werden, kann PETG funktionieren. Nach dem Druck das Bauteil auf der Platte auskühlen lassen, um Spannungen zu vermeiden. (nicht heiß von der Platte lösen) Benötigte Hardware Pro Rolle werden benötigt: 13x M3 x 18 mm Schrauben 13x M3 Muttern Montage-Hinweise Das Design ist mit sehr engen Toleranzen für die M3-Muttern entworfen. Das ist pure Absicht: Die Muttern sitzen extrem stramm, damit sie bei der Montage nicht herausfallen. Muttern einpressen: Falls sich die Muttern schwer einsetzen lassen, nimm eine M3-Schraube zur Hilfe. Führe die Mutter durch leichtes Hin- und Herbewegen unter etwas Druck in die Aussparung ein. model_name: Creality Space Pi X4 Desiccant Drying System
description: Hello! I’m excited to introduce my desiccant drying system specifically designed for the Creality Space Pi x4 filament dryer. I dedicated a lot of time and effort to developing this model, going through numerous iterations until I reached this version. After experimenting with a model I found in MakerWorld and encountering several issues, I decided to create my own. My goal was to design a strong, modular system that ensures unobstructed airflow. I also wanted something at incorporated a pour spout without taking up a lot of space or using a lot of filament. This filament drying system is stackable, robust, and easy to use. It’s large enough to accommodate two boxes and a frame on each side of the Space Pi x4. It measures 1500mm by 150mm by 60mm, features 2mm holes and a pour spout in one of the corners. Each box can hold a maximum of 500 grams of desiccant, but I recommend not exceeding 300 grams to expedite drying times and prevent overloading the frame. I successfully dried approximately 400 grams (200 grams per side) of wet desiccant in about 6 hours at 85 degrees Celsius, which is significantly faster compared to other solutions. Please note that to achieve the optimal drying temperature of 85 degrees Celsius, I highly recommend printing this model in ASA filament. I’ve shared my personal settings in the profile I published, which is in ASA. For faster prints, I used a .6mm nozzle, but if you prioritize quality, you can print it with a .4mm nozzle. Make sure to adjust the print settings accordingly. Turn off all cooling, lower the volumetric flow to 12 cubic millimeters per second, heat up the chamber to 65 degrees Celsius, and heat the build plate to 100 degrees Celsius. If you don’t have a heated chamber, heat soak it for at least 30 minutes before printing to minimize the risk of warping. Additionally, ensure that you use a textured PEI plate or an engineering plate. Wash it with soap and warm water, and apply a glue stick. ASA emits toxic fumes so use air filters and a proper mask when printing with ASA. Your health is too important to risk it! If this solution proves beneficial for you, I would greatly appreciate it if you could consider boosting me. Your support means a lot to me. Please also take a moment to comment, bookmark this model, and share it with others. I value all feedback, especially suggestions for model improvements. Please be aware that commercial sales of this model are strictly prohibited.

model_name: Modular AMS Riser for H2 Series Printers
description: An open-frame, highly configurable AMS riser designed around standard 2020 aluminum extrusions. Built for flexibility, expansion, and minimal material waste without requiring complete reprints when modifying your setup. KEY FEATURES Configurable & Expandable: Utilizes 2020 aluminum extrusions to allow custom attachments and easy adjustments as your setup evolves. Open & Lightweight: Minimizes filament usage and print times while maintaining structural rigidity. Forgiving Tolerances: Main frame pieces are separated from the interlocking connectors. If tolerances differ due to filament or slicer settings, only small connector pieces need quick reprinting—saving time and material. Reversible Assembly: Friction-fit tapered draft joints hold the frame together snugly without glue, allowing full disassembly if needed. Preserves all original factory (OEM) functions of the top glass lid (removable with lid closed sensor actuator). HARDWARE REQUIREMENTS Main Riser: 4x Corner Frame Sections + 4x Interlocking Keys Secure Brackets: 4x Printer Cabinet Retainer Clips AMS Mounts: 8x AMS Corner Retainers (4x Left, 4x Right) Threaded Inserts: 4x M4 Heat Set Threaded Inserts Magnet: 1x Small Magnet (4mm diameter x 1.75mm thick) 2020 Aluminum Extrusions: 8x 2020 end caps 2x Frame Side Rails (Cut to 475mm minus the thickness of your end caps) 2x AMS Support Rails (Cut to 760mm) Fasteners & Hardware: M4x8mm Socket Head Cap Screws (SHCS) M4 2020 T-Nuts 2020 90-Degree Corner Brackets Compression Spring (for Lid Sensor Switch) Optional: 2020 End Caps ASSEMBLY GUIDE Step 1: Assemble the Riser Frame Install Threaded Inserts: Heat-set one M4 threaded insert into the provided hole on each of the four main riser pieces (refer to diagrams for placement). Join the Frame: Lay out the four main riser pieces upside down on a smooth, flat surface. Insert the interlocking keys and cabinet retainer devices. Note: The interlocking components feature a slight draft taper to draw the joints tight as they seat. Make sure they are oriented correctly before pressing them together. No adhesive is required. Step 2: Attach Side Extrusions Mount the two 475mm side extrusions to the left and right sides of the main riser frame using the M4x8mm SHCS and M4 T-nuts through the pre-drilled countersunk holes. Step 3: Install AMS Crossbar Extrusions Mount the two 760mm extrusions across the frame using 2020 90-degree corner brackets. Rear Rail: Align flush with the riser assembly and tighten securely. Front Rail: Install loosely for now—you will adjust its position when seating the AMS units. Step 4: Fit AMS Units and Corner Retainers Install the 8 AMS corner retainers onto the support rails (pay attention to Left vs. Right orientation): Secure the four outer corner retainers first, ensuring they are square to one another. Attach the four inner corner retainers loosely so they can slide. Place an AMS unit onto its outer retainers, lower it into the inner retainers, and adjust until the unit rests flat without rocking. Carefully lift the AMS unit straight up and tighten the inner retainers. Repeat for the second AMS unit, then fully tighten the front crossbar rail. Step 5: Mount to Printer Remove the glass lid from the printer and set the riser frame into the top cavity. Engage the four retainer brackets so their fingers grip under the printer cabinet rim for a secure fit. Step 6: Assemble Lid Sensor Switch Install Magnet: Glue a small magnet (4mm diameter x 1.75mm thick) into the cavity on the end of the pushbutton shaft (refer to diagram). Assemble Pushbutton: Drop the two-part pushbutton assembly into the front-left hole of the riser: Place the spring inside the outer barrel. Insert the pushbutton stem, ensuring it glides smoothly. (If making a custom spring, wrap spring wire around an appropriate diameter mandrel until you achieve desired tension and bounce). Step 7: Final Set Up Reinstall the top glass lid onto the newly installed riser assembly, place your AMS units into the corner retainers, and run your lines.

Been having bridging issues with my prints so I put this together to be able to test for an ideal bridge flow ratio and speed combination to get the best results. Not a professional model maker by any stretch of the imagination, but it works for now! This test lays out 21 bridges on one plate — 3 print speeds (10 / 20 / 30 mm/s) across 7 bridge flow ratios (1.0–1.6) — so you can find the combination that gives flat, fully-fused strands with no sag. Uses only ~7 g of filament, so it's cheap to run as often as you calibrate your filaments. How to use: Print it, flip it over, and read the underside of each bridge. The cleanest, flattest strands mark your ideal bridge flow ratio for that speed. Set those values in your slicer and enjoy clean bridges. Printed on a Bambu Lab P1S. No supports, no brim needed. How to read the results: Flip the plate and look at the underside of each bridge: Best: strands are flat, straight, evenly spaced, and fully fused — no sag, no gaps. Too little flow / too fast: strands sag, droop, or break mid-span. Too much flow: strands bulge, blob, or fuse into a rough mass. Settings to modify in slicer Quality > Advanced > Bridge Flow Speed > Other Layers Speed > Bridge Feedback and comments are welcome, I have much to learn still! description: 8mm Threaded Screw Grease Applicator for Compatible BambuLab Printers Problem: I’ve looked at many designs aimed at greasing lead screws, but they all followed a similar approach: a small "fork-shaped" greaser with minimal contact surface. The result was poor—grease wasn’t evenly distributed on the screws. Solution: These designs overlooked the simplest and most effective solution: using circular geometry to spread grease evenly! How to Use the Grease Applicator: Before proceeding , make sure to have some spray degreaser (like WD-40) and/or isopropyl alcohol to clean dirt and old grease from the screws. Use the 8mm lead screw spray degreaser tool (linked at the bottom) to spray your degreaser of choice onto the screw to clean it from old grease and debris, then with a cloth, clean all the dirt away. With another cloth, use some isopropyl alcohol to clean oil residues left by the degreaser. When the screws shine, they’re ready! ;) Place the tool upright on a flat surface. Squeeze a small amount of grease into the concave space and spread it evenly—this will contact the screws. Slide the tool up and down while gently rotating it with your wrist’s movement. ⚠️ Do not apply strong force to the screw. If needed, hold the upper part of the screw with your other hand. Apply grease, leaving at least 30mm clear on both the top and bottom (the printer’s movement will distribute it evenly). Tip: It’s better to grease twice rather than have to wipe off excess. ;)

description: Print ABS, ASA or nylon on your X2D? Let's deal with that huge purge opening as a thermal leak . description: AMS HT Side Mount für Bambu Lab P2S and X2D Diese Halterung ermöglicht es, das AMS HT seitlich am oberen Rahmen des P2S und X2D zu befestigen. Dadurch kann TPU direkt über die Bypass-Öffnung des AMS HT zum Druckkopf geführt werden. Der große Vorteil dieser Positionierung ist der extrem kurze und nahezu geradlinige Filamentweg. Das reduziert den Wiederstand beim fördern des Filaments auf ein Minimum und verbessert insbesondere den Druck mit sehr weichen TPU-Filamenten, die empfindlich auf lange oder stark gekrümmte Filamentwege reagieren. Zusätzlich kann das AMS HT während des Drucks weiterhin als Filamenttrockner genutzt werden. So bleibt das TPU während des gesamten Druckvorgangs trocken, was die Druckqualität zusätzlich verbessert. Einfache Konstruktion Die Halterung besteht aus drei Steckteilen, die ohne Schrauben oder weiteres Montagematerial zusammengesteckt werden. Diese Bauweise bietet mehrere Vorteile: Sehr einfacher und zuverlässiger Druck. Durch die modulare Bauweise, kann der Halter durch austauschen des Hakens auch für andere Druckermodelle genutzt werden. Die Halterung lässt sich jederzeit wieder zerlegen und dadurch besonders platzsparend verstauen. Hinweis: Je nach verwendeten Material und Kalibrierung des Druckers und Filament, kann es sein, dass die Steckverbindung schwergängig ist. Versuche nicht die Teile mit Gewalt zusammen zu stecken! In diesen Fall ist es hilfreich die Steckverbinder mit etwas Schlafpapier nach zu arbeiten. Etwas Gleitmittel wie Balistol oder WD40 kann ebenfalls helfen. Einfache Montage Für die Montage muss lediglich der Glasdeckel des Druckers entfernt werden. Anschließend wird die Halterung einfach über den oberen Rand des Druckers gesteckt. Das AMS HT wird danach nur auf der Halterung abgestellt - ganz ohne zusätzliche Befestigung. description: FULL EXPLANATION HERE: https://www.reddit.com/r/FDMminiatures/comments/1v0rerw/introducing_the_curling_tower_a_simple_solution/ This is a “Curling Tower” - A Model designed to combat “Curling”, especially when printing Miniatures. What happened here? When 3D Printing Miniatures with an FDM Printer, we run into some unique issues. One of which is the fact that even though it takes a long time to finish the print, the time spent on each individual layer is fairly short. Ideally, by the time the current layer starts printing, the previous one should have cooled down as much as possible. Now, if you're printing something large this isn't a problem - By the time the nozzle circles back to the starting point of the next layer, the previous one will have solidified. But, as you can probably guess, this isn't always the case for miniatures. It usually doesn't affect the entire model - Most of them are still large enough that the Layers will have enough time to cool down. Where it becomes an issue is with "isolated" parts of the model - Parts that are either only partially connected to the Model, or only become fully connected throughout the print. Examples of partially connected isolated parts are but are not limited to Swords raised towards the sky, Staffs and other weapons. Examples of isolated parts that only become fully connected throughout the print, are usually legs or similar body-parts. But what exactly is Curling, and why is it such an issue? When printing these isolated parts, the time spent on each layer is very short - So short that by the time, say Layer 100 starts, Layer 99 hasn't fully solidified yet. The heat of the Nozzle as well as the new layer of filament being placed on top of the previous Layer will re-soften the material further, causing the layer to be slightly lifted upwards. If this happened only once, it wouldn't be a major issue - The lift per layer is relatively small. But if it happens over multiple layers it becomes a problem. Eventually the filament will be curled enough for the Nozzle to slam into it, at which point it will most likely break of that part and ruin the print. With print times reaching the double digits, this is - as you can imagine - moderately upsetting. So how do we fix it? There are four common solutions to curling: Since Curling is caused by filament not cooling quickly enough, the easiest way is to simply increase the speed of the cooling fans. However, since most HQ Profiles already have these maxed out, this is unlikely to help most people. However: If they are already maxed out, but you still run into the issue - Make sure that they are actually clean. The fans on my A1 were stuffed with dust, which significantly lowered the cooling effect. If it's been a while since you last cleaned the fans, or never cleaned them at all, now might be a good start. If the fans are clean and already running at 100% speed, we might need to give them a little help by lowering our printing temperature. Filament leaving the nozzle at 220° will take longer to cool down than filament leaving the nozzle at 200°. The problem here is that you can only go so low before you start creating new issues, namely Nozzle Clogs. If you are already operating in the 195-200 range, you don't have much room left. If the problem is caused because the surface of the model is too small, we could simply increase the size of the Model. By upscaling it until the "vulnerable" part of the model has enough surface area for it to be printed with regular infill as opposed Solid Infill, the likelyhood of it warping becomes substantially smaller. Of course, this solution substantially increases print time and if you're printing Wargaming Proxies where scale matters, it's not suited for you at all. Printing multiple models. Following the same logic as Solution #3, instead of going for Model Size, we aim to increase the total print volume. By introducing at least a second Model to our print and print by layer, we can give each layer a cooling-buffer. As the printer finishes the Layer on Model A, Model B will have more time to cool down and vice versa. This solution also drasticially increases print-time, and comes with the downside of not only introducing additional risks in case the print fails somewhere, but also the simple fact that not everyone wants or needs multiple models. While all those four solutions work, I wasn't satisfied with any of them. The first two are limited by Hardware which, in some cases, simply isn't enough. The other two force you to print something other than what you actually wanted to print. So, I wanted to use a compromise. The Curling Tower - It's just a simple, hollow, square tower with thin walls. The idea here is simple - You print it alongside your actual model, with some distance between the two. Once the Printer has finished a layer for the Model, it will move to the Tower, giving the Filament on the Model enough time to cool down. Now, you might be thinking - That's just Solution #4 again, printing with more than one model at the same time. And you're right - But there is a catch. Because the Curling Tower is much more basic than any miniature, there isn't a whole lot that can go wrong with it. It's "safer" to print alongside your actual print, because there can't be any failed supports, harsh overhangs or even curling. And, because it's such a simple design - it will add significantly less time to the total print duration than a second, actual miniature would. But the real difference and big advantage, is that the Tower is adjustable. Remember when I said that Curling mostly affects the isolated parts of the model? In this case, it's the leg of the Skeleton - You don't need to print the entire Tower. You can just match the height of the tower to the point where the isolated part re-connects with the model and is out of the "Danger Zone" This means that you will have all the benefits of the "Cooling Buffer" that Solution #4 gives you, at a fraction of the increase in print time and material waste. To give you some numbers: Skelly without Tower or 2nd Model to serve as a Cooling Buffer: 3h45m Skelly with a 2nd Skelly as a Cooling Buffer: 6h56m Skelly with a Curling Tower equal to the Model Height: 4h54m 4h54 Skelly with a Curling Tower adjusted to the "Danger Zone": 4h14m That's an increase of only 13% when compared to the 86% increase you'd get when printing with a 2nd model. Now, is this something that you should use for all of your prints? No, of course not - Although in theory, it should also very slightly improve Overhangs for the same reason it fixes Curling - By giving them more time to cool before the next layer is added on top. But this is primarily meant as a tool for models that have a lot of isolated parts, or if you are struggling with Curling and none of the other solutions work out for you. So next time you're running into Curling even though your fans are already maxed out - Give this one a try.

description: AMS Reliability Kit Tired of cardboard spools falling off the AMS rollers? Frustrated when nearly empty filament rolls won't feed reliably? I designed the AMS Reliability Kit to solve both problems. This system keeps spools properly aligned on the rollers, prevents them from walking side-to-side, and adds extra weight to lightweight or nearly empty spools for more consistent feeding. After implementing this system I have have experenice significantly less mid print errors errors. Features ✔ Now you can use up those almost empty filament rolls instead of throwing them away. ✔ Now you can reliably print with cardboard spools. ✔ Keeps all four spools properly centered for smoother operation. ✔ Refillable spool weight improves traction for lightweight and low-filament spools. Spool Weight has a 2nd Inner cap so you dont have to worry about your weights falling out when moving to new spools ✔ Easy to print and install. Why I Made It I designed this system because my cardboard spools were constantly falling off the AMS rollers , especially as they became lighter. After dealing with countless failed prints, I decided to create a solution that keeps every spool where it belongs and improves feeding reliability. The Full kit includes: 2× Outer Spool Guides 2× Center Spool Guides 4× Refillable Spool Weight Whether you're printing with cardboard spools, plastic spools, or almost-empty rolls , the AMS Reliability Kit helps your AMS feed filament more consistently and lets you finish every last gram of filament with confidence. Assembly Instructions Outer Spool Guides The thin, flat section of each Outer Spool Guide slides between the inner black AMS tray and the outer transparent shell. The guides are intentionally not designed to fit rigidly. This prevents unnecessary pressure that could damage or warp the AMS tray or outer shell. A small amount of movement is normal. Inner Spool Guides The Inner Spool Guides have cutouts along the bottom that pressure-fit over the original short dividers built into the AMS tray. Press each guide down only far enough to hold it securely. Do not press the guides all the way down against the spool rollers. Contact with the rollers may prevent them from rotating properly. After installation, spin the rollers by hand to confirm that they move freely. Spool Weight Fill the Spool Weight Body with a suitable dense material. I recommend using 9 mm steel ball bearings , such as these ball bearings on Amazon . Other options include: Steel nuts, washers, or small sockets Fishing weights Other compact metal objects Do not use batteries , as damaged or aging batteries can leak, corrode, or create a safety hazard. Once the body is filled, thread in the Spool Weight Seal to secure the weights inside. Do not overfill the body, the seal must seat completely into the threads. You can confirm that the seal is fully seated by installing the Spool Cap . If the cap does not sit completely against the body, remove some weight and reinstall the seal. Once the seal is installed, the outer cap can be easily removed whenever you need to transfer the weight to another spool without the weights falling out. Funnel Saver In the .3MF File I have included the “AMS 2 Pro Funnel Saver Guides” from YelTrik Designs Refer to this Model for intructions and use case. They have complemented my AMS Reliabilty Setup well. Feedback and Modification Requests Have an idea for an improvement or need a modified version? Feel free to leave a comment with any requests, questions, or concerns about the AMS Reliability Kit !

description: Flow Rate Calibration Cube | Micrometer Dieser einwandige, oben offene Kalibrierungswürfel dient zur präzisen Einstellung der Flussrate beziehungsweise des Flow Ratio eines Filaments. Die tatsächliche Wandstärke wird an mehreren Stellen mit einer Bügelmessschraube oder einem präzisen Mikrometer gemessen. Aus dem Mittelwert aller Messungen lässt sich anschließend der korrigierte Flussratenwert für das verwendete Filamentprofil berechnen. Der Würfel benötigt nur wenig Material, ist schnell gedruckt und eignet sich ideal zur Feinabstimmung neuer oder bereits vorhandener Filamentprofile. Benötigte Hilfsmittel Bügelmessschraube oder präzises Mikrometer Bambu Studio oder ein kompatibler Slicer Das zu kalibrierende Filament Aktueller Flussratenwert des Filamentprofils Eingestellte Linienbreite der Außenwand Durchführung 1. Würfel drucken Drucke den Würfel mit genau dem Filamentprofil, das kalibriert werden soll. Verändere für den anschließenden Kontrolltest möglichst keine anderen Einstellungen wie Temperatur, Geschwindigkeit oder Linienbreite. Lasse das Modell nach dem Druck vollständig abkühlen. 2. Wandstärke messen Miss jede der vier Würfelseiten an mehreren Stellen: mindestens 3 Messungen pro Seite empfohlen sind 5 Messungen pro Seite bei 5 Messungen pro Seite entstehen insgesamt 20 Messwerte Miss möglichst mittig auf den geraden Wandflächen. Vermeide dabei: die Ecken des Würfels die Z-Naht den oberen Rand die ersten Schichten sichtbar unregelmäßige Stellen Verwende bei jeder Messung einen gleichmäßigen und möglichst geringen Messdruck. Mittelwert berechnen Addiere alle gemessenen Wandstärken und teile die Summe durch die Anzahl der Messungen: Mittelwert = Summe aller Messwerte ÷ Anzahl der Messwerte Je mehr saubere Messungen verwendet werden, desto zuverlässiger ist das Ergebnis. Zielwert bestimmen Der Zielwert entspricht der in Bambu Studio eingestellten Linienbreite der Außenwand . Du findest den Wert unter: Qualität → Breite der Linien → Außenwand Beispiel: Außenwand-Linienbreite: 0,42 mm Wichtig: Verwende als Zielwert nicht automatisch den Düsendurchmesser, sondern immer die tatsächlich eingestellte Linienbreite der Außenwand. Aktuellen Flussratenwert ermitteln Öffne das verwendete Filamentprofil und notiere den dort eingestellten aktuellen Wert für die: Flussrate / Flow Ratio Beispiel: Bisheriger Flow Ratio: 0,988 Neuen Flow Ratio berechnen Verwende folgende Formel: Neuer Flow Ratio = Zielwert × bisheriger Flow Ratio ÷ gemessener Mittelwert Beispielrechnung Zielwert: 0,42 mm Bisheriger Flow Ratio: 0,988 Gemessener Mittelwert: 0,421 mm Rechnung: 0,42 × 0,988 ÷ 0,421 = 0,985653 Gerundet ergibt sich ein neuer Flow Ratio von: 0,986 Trage den neuen Wert anschließend in das Filamentprofil ein. Drucke den Würfel danach erneut und kontrolliere die Wandstärke mit einer weiteren Messung. Falls erforderlich, kann die Berechnung wiederholt werden. Excel-Formel Die Berechnung kann auch direkt in Excel oder einer anderen Tabellenkalkulation durchgeführt werden: =Zielwert*Bisheriger_Wert/Mittelwert Beispiel mit Zellbezügen: =I13*I6/D6 Dabei steht: I13 für den bisherigen Flow-Ratio-Wert I6 für den Zielwert D6 für den Mittelwert aller Messungen Ergebnis interpretieren Gemessene Wand ist dicker als der Zielwert: Der Flow Ratio wird reduziert. Gemessene Wand ist dünner als der Zielwert: Der Flow Ratio wird erhöht. Mittelwert entspricht dem Zielwert: Die Flussrate ist bereits passend eingestellt. Hinweise Die Kalibrierung sollte für jedes Filamentprofil separat durchgeführt werden. Hersteller, Material, Farbe, Drucktemperatur und weitere Einstellungen können das Ergebnis beeinflussen. Dieser Würfel dient ausschließlich zur Kalibrierung der Flussrate beziehungsweise des Flow Ratio . Er ist nicht für die Einstellung von Flow Dynamics, Pressure Advance oder K-Wert vorgesehen. Für reproduzierbare Ergebnisse sollten alle Messungen mit derselben Bügelmessschraube und mit möglichst gleichmäßigem Messdruck durchgeführt werden. Druckprofil Einwandiger, oben offener Kalibrierungswürfel Keine Stützstrukturen erforderlich Geringer Materialverbrauch Kurze Druckzeit Ideal für wiederholte Kontrollmessungen Druckzeit und Materialverbrauch können abhängig von Drucker, Filament und verwendeten Einstellungen abweichen.

Customizable Navigation Bar Holder / GPS Bar Clamp A customizable two-piece navigation bar holder for motorcycle GPS, phone, tablet and DMD-style mounts. This model is designed as a parametric OpenSCAD / MakerWorld Customizer file. You can adjust the bar diameter, clamp tolerance, block size, bolt spacing, nut pockets and corner radius directly in the MakerWorld customizer. Key Features Fully customizable bar diameter Designed for navigation bars, GPS bars and handlebar-style mounting points Bar runs through the short side of the block Two-piece clamp design: front and back part Both parts are placed print-ready with the groove facing upward M4 bolt holes Optional M4 hex nut pockets in the back part Rounded corners Adjustable clamp undersize for a tighter or looser fit Suitable for common adventure motorcycle navigation bars Common Diameter Examples Recommended starting values: BMW / adventure GPS bar: Bar_Diameter = 12.0 Clamp_Undersize = 0.30 Hardware M4 Bolt 25mm M4 nyloc nuts Some BMW navigation bars: Bar_Diameter = 16.0 Clamp_Undersize = 0.30 Hardware M4 Bolt 30mm M4 nyloc nuts Always measure your own bar with calipers before printing. Small differences matter for clamp fit. Important Assembly Note Both parts are shown in print orientation with the bar groove facing upward. For assembly: Place the back part against the navigation bar. Flip the front part over. Put the front part over the bar. Insert the M4 bolts. Tighten gradually and evenly. The two half-round grooves will clamp around the bar. Parameters Main customizer parameters: Bar_Diameter Nominal diameter of your motorcycle navigation bar. Bar_Offset_X Moves the bar groove left or right from the center of the block. This is useful when the navigation bar needs to sit slightly off-center. Default value: 0.0 mm Range: -10 mm to +10 mm Clamp_Undersize Reduces the actual groove diameter for a tighter clamp. Example: Bar_Diameter = 12.0 and Clamp_Undersize = 0.30 creates an effective 11.7 mm clamp . Block_Length Overall length of the clamp block. Block_Width Overall width of the clamp block. Half_Thickness Thickness of each half. Set to 0 for automatic thickness. Corner_Radius Controls the rounded corners. Bolt Parameters Bolt_Size Selects the bolt size used for the clamp. Options: M3, M4, M5 The model automatically adjusts the bolt hole diameter and nut pocket size based on this setting. Bolt_Clearance Adds extra clearance to the selected bolt diameter. Example : Bolt_Size = M4 Bolt_Clearance = 0.5 This creates a 4.5 mm bolt hole. Increase this value if your printer makes holes too tight. Manual_Hole_Diameter Manual override for the bolt hole diameter. Set this value to 0 to use automatic hole sizing based on Bolt_Size and Bolt_Clearance. Use this only if you want full manual control over the hole diameter. Hole_Spacing_X Horizontal spacing between the left and right bolt holes. Measured center-to-center. Hole_Spacing_Y Vertical spacing between the upper and lower bolt holes. Measured center-to-center. Back Nut Pocket Parameters Nut_Pockets Enables or disables hexagonal nut pockets in the back part. Options : true Adds hex nut pockets to the back part. false Creates normal through-holes only. Nut_Pocket_Clearance Adds extra clearance to the automatic nut pocket size. Increase this value if your nuts are too tight. Decrease this value if your nuts are too loose. Manual_Nut_Flat_To_Flat Manual override for the hex nut pocket size. Measured flat-to-flat. Set this value to 0 to use automatic sizing based on Bolt_Size and Nut_Pocket_Clearance. Manual_Nut_Depth Manual override for the hex nut pocket depth. Set this value to 0 to use automatic depth based on Bolt_Size. Increase this value if your nuts sit proud of the surface. Advanced Parameters Preview_Cutaway Creates a cutaway preview to inspect the internal groove and holes. Options: false Normal printable model. true Cutaway preview mode. description: This is a fully custom window‑mounted vent system I designed for my Bambu H2C printer. My goals were simple: Airtight Secure Permanent installation Fast magnetic connection/disconnection of the exhaust hose Weatherproof cover for when the printer isn’t running I wasn’t satisfied with the existing MakerWorld options, and my window is only 521 mm wide , so I built something specifically for my setup — but I’m sharing the Fusion file, STEP file, and laser‑cut gasket files so you can adapt it to your own window if it’s similar. This design is meant for small windows, but the parametric model makes it possible to adjust dimensions if your window differs. Features 🔒 Airtight & Secure The duct and window frame use 2 mm EVA foam gaskets , recessed 1 mm into the mating surfaces for a tight seal. With magnets pulling the duct into place, the connection feels solid and leak‑free. 🧲 Magnetic Quick‑Connect The system uses 10 mm × 2 mm neodymium round magnets : 10 magnets in the window frame 10 magnets in the duct Optional: 10 magnets in the weather cover This lets you instantly attach the exhaust hose when printing, and swap it for the weather cover when not. 🌧️ Weatherproof Cover The optional cover seals the opening when the duct is removed. I printed mine in PETG, but any outdoor‑friendly filament works. 🪟 Permanent Window Fixture The window frame stays installed permanently. The two halves connect with a tight dovetail joint . I intentionally used small tolerances for a high‑quality feel — sanding the edges slightly helps if the fit is too snug. 🧰 Customizable CAD Files Included: Fusion 360 file with editable parameters STEP file for use in any CAD program .lac laser file for cutting EVA gaskets Printable gasket groove outlines if cutting by hand If your window is wider than ~520 mm, you may need to split the extension piece — Bambu Studio makes this easy with built in tools. 🧪 Material Recommendations ASA‑CF (my choice): weather‑resistant, rigid, great for outdoor use PETG : perfectly fine for most users Any other weather resistant material that has some temperature resistance (ABS, PET-CF, etc.) Parts & Materials Printed Parts Window Frame (2 pieces, dovetail connection) Duct Outside Vent Weather Cover (optional) Gasket inserts (optional if cutting by hand) Hardware 30 ea. - 10 mm × 2 mm neodymium magnets EVA foam sheets , minimum 9" × 12" , 2 mm thick Glue for gaskets (contact cement or similar adhesive works best, super glue not recommended as it's likely too rigid) Tools Bambu H2C laser module (optional, could cut gaskets by hand) Sandpaper (for dovetail tuning) Utility knife if cutting gaskets manually Assembly Notes Ensure magnet polarity is consistent across all parts. Install magnets on the duct and optional weather cover are opposite polarity of magents in the window frame so they attract and don't oppose. Test-fit the dovetail before final installation — light sanding may be needed. Laser Cutting Notes (H2C 10W) For 2 mm EVA foam gaskets, these settings work extremely well: Power: 35% Speed: 6 Air assistant: On Pass: 1 Cut Offset: 0.00 This produces crisp edges with minimal melt. Who This Is For This design is not universal — it was built specifically for my window dimensions and style. But if your window is similar, or you’re comfortable modifying CAD files, this can get you most of the way to a perfect custom vent. If your window is very different, you may still find the duct, magnet system, and gasket approach useful as a starting point. Feel free to download my files as a starting point for your project. IMPORTANT: Before committing to a full print, I strongly recommend slicing off a small test segment of the window frame to verify the fit in your window. In your slicer, cut a short 3–5 inch section from the model (left‑to‑right, as it sits in the frame) and print that first. This quick test ensures the final part will fit properly before you invest time and material into the full print. Included Files Fusion 360 file (with parameters) STEP file STL files for all parts .lac laser file for EVA gaskets Printable gasket outlines Assembly instructions (text) Final Thoughts This vent has been rock‑solid for me — airtight, secure, and incredibly convenient. I can leave the window fixture installed permanently, snap the duct on magnetically whenever I print, and seal it with the weather cover when I’m done. If you adapt it to your own window, I’d love to see your remix.

model_name: The Ultimate Wall Mounted TPU Spool Holder!
tags: bambu|BAMBU LAB|TPU|tpu spool|tpu spool holder|tpu spool mount|wallmounted tpu|tpu wallmount|tpu holder|tpu bearing|tpu 608|spool|spool holder|spool holder bearings
description: This is the ultimate, fully customizable, wall mounted spool holder which should be suitable for the softest of filaments. It has been tested with: Bambu 95A Bambu 90A Bambu 85A Bambu TPU for AMS Siraya tech flex TPU Of course it should work with all standard filaments too. It features a total of six “tool” holders. The central two (one on each main arm) below the hub are designed to take the flap brake. The flap brake will only work with these two. The other holders are used for the friction brakes. This is the third version of my wall mount and based on the original one which was super smooth but had little control, could run backwards and overrun. I did update it with some brakes which helped but they weren’t very adjustable at all and adding a flap brake just wasn’t practical. I am still in a testing phase but even without adjusting between filaments this version has worked flawlessly so far. I hope it does for you too! Upgrading? For people who already have that old version, this version can re-use at least some parts you already have printed: The original wall brackets will work (although they will be tighter than the new ones). The PTFE tube holder is unchanged. The rear joining bracket is unchanged The wall template is unchanged, no need to redrill anything! Printing Suggestions. The 3MF file contains the settings and support methods I used for this print. Filament: Bambu PLA Metal Iridium Bambu PLA Metal Iron Grey Sparse infill 25% (15% will work just fne) Sparse infill pattern Gyroid Place brim ears on all four parts the two piece arms. In Bambu slicer the brim ears tool set to auto does a great job. You will need to set the brim type to “painted”. Materials you will need: Plugs and screws. Check the screw heads will sit in the countersunk hole and clear the dovetail on the arm. Plugs – if required – I used Fischer 4no. 6x30, 6mm drill bit Screws – 4no. 4x35 – make sure the head will sit within the recess A small amount of PTFE tube. (This is not essential, you can bypass the PTFE holder in use if you choose) Two 608 bearings – these are pretty good: https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B08ZN94S5L?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_fed_asin_title but almost any 608 bearing should be fine. Fleece fabric Tessa tape,19- 20mm ideally 51608-00001-00 Or Cable tie Velcro with the soft side as the brake 10-20mm wide Super glue. Installation and assembly: This video should help you understand how it works when assembled, I’d recommend you have sound turned on whilst I’m fitting the brake. Sorry.. VERY boring video :( https://youtube.com/shorts/ZhJ1bJGjlVE?feature=share Choosing parts: Note that I have named all the parts in the 3MF file. I will refer to them here. There are two types of spool arms. One set is only printable on a large bed printer such as the H2D. The other set should be printable on most printer beds and offers a different aesthetic if you use two colours. Photos/videos are of the two part type. Choose how many tool arms to print and of which type (more on this later!). If in doubt just print one standard tool arm “ARM TYPE1 MEDIUM”, one flap brake arm “ARM TYPE 3 Flap Brake”. Note: Arms can be inserted upside down in the front arm holder. Choose which tool to print, again, if in doubt I would suggest “Brake Tool TYPE 1” which has the ridges around and no chamfer. Choose a cover plate type (you may not want cover plates at all!) Note that the large cover plate has a bambu logo which looks nice if printed in a different colour. Choose your axle cap design round or hex – photos are of the hex type. You can choose not to print the flanges. The hub does not require either of them but you won’t get the non-reverse function of course. There is a filament guide included “Flimanent Guide OPTIONAL”. This helped to stop filament loop drops in version 1. I still have it mounted in this version (in the photos) but I haven’t used it nor needed it so far. I would suggest you don’t print it unless you have problems and think it will help. Wall mounting: I would recommend printing the template and using that to position the drill holes. Accuracy IS important. Check that your screw heads will sit within the counter sunk holes. The wall brackets have a little vertical movement in them. Screw the brackets to the wall. Assembly: The two part version is very easy to put together but make sure you trim any access filament (the brim) off the joint on both sides! You can only push the two parts together from one side. Lay the main arm flat on a table and push the small arm on until the whole thing is flush. It may require some force, it’s designed to be tight. A light tap with a hammer can help. Join the parts of the PTFE tube holder together to match the photos. Attach the PTFE tube holder to one of the arms. Take the rear bracket and insert it, bevel edges forward onto the same arm. Now take the other arm and carefully seat it on both the rear bracket and the PTFE tube carrier. Now slide the whole assembly onto the wall brackets to check alignment. It should slide on easily. Assemble the hubs. Remove any support material, use snipe nose pliers to remove the support in the axel socket. Check the supported edge looks flat with no bits of support left and test fit the flanges (if you are using them) to make sure they are flat and flush when seated. Push an axel in each hub as far as it will go. Put a spacer sleeve on next, then your bearings which should be a fairly snug fit. Finally your choice of axel cap. The cap should take quite a bit of force to get on. If it is loose you might want to add some glue. Fitting the flanges Test fit the flanges again. They should be fairly loose fitting without glue. This is by design. Remove them, run a bead of superglue all the way around the edge of the hub, stick the flanges on and leave to dry. Check they are well stuck! Almost done! The hubs should fit together without any effort. Obviously they need to come apart to insert your spools so don’t glue them! Put them together and try dropping the hub into the wall mount. It should drop in and pull out with almost no effort. If it sticks or doesn’t seat correctly there may be some support materials in the arm sockets. If there isn’t try taking the hib in and our a few times. If it doesn’t and the arms didn’t slide into the the wall brackets with ease then you may have an alignment problem. Check your drilling template against the holes in the wall. How things work and Tuning: Flap Brake (s): The function of the flap brake is primarily to stop the spool from running backwards. You will need the smaller ARM TYPE3 (they aren’t handed) and one flap brake for the side you intend to use it on. Fit the brake to the arm (it should fit fairly tightly). When correctly aligned the outer ARM hex faces should line up with the Flap Brake male end hex faces but the most important part is that the flat end of the flap must line up perfectly with the deep flat edge of the scoops on the flange plate. Once fitted the arm can be adjusted by pulling it in and out. Insert it roughly into position so that the end just sits in a scoop The designed position is when it “ticks” fairly quietly in the forward direction and stops the spool turning in the reverse direction. Tuning the flap brake: “Turn” any other brakes off! Use your hand to manually turn the spool forwards and check that there is little to no resistance and you can hear the flap ticking on the disc. Then try to gently spin with spool in reverse. It should be stopped almost immediately as the flap connects with an edge. Note - If you want you can put flap brakes on both sides of the holder. Note – The flap brakes can actually be used as friction brakes too if you push the tool arm in further – it will just be more noisy! Main friction Brakes: Generally I would recommend installing just one or two but you can use up to four. NOTE: Why four? Partly – just in case and you might only have access to one side of the holder but you may like to have one on each side to keep the spool aligned or all four installed to keep everything aligned with a light pressure on all of them. There are two brake types, one is designed for Tessa tape or Velcro style cable ties to wrap around. The other can also take tape but can be used on it’s own – you can just angle the chamfered part against the spool. Tuning the main friction brakes: You can push and pull the arms and you can also angle the tool head on the arm which should allow to you to really fine tune the amount of friction you are applying perfectly to suit the filament type. My personal preference is to use Tessa tape, it sticks on and the surface is very smooth. Tool arms: The arms are handed for left and right There are three types. Short – This makes the tool easy to remove but doesn’t provide much resistance to stop the tool head from being moved when tilted. Medium – Recommended. Some give but plenty of resistance. However it is quite hard to pull the arm out without breaking it. Long – Loads of resistance, almost impossible to remove the arm. Basically a permanent position once you push the head all the way on. Happy Soft Filament printing! Minor update 14-7-2026: The flap stop could catch on the edge of a flange when a spool is dropped in to the arms. This version adds a chamfer to the flanges to make it smoother and less likely to catch and rotate the flap stops.

The Ultimate Filament Clip! A good example of “why” there is always space for improvement. You see.. there are a lot of good designs out there, don't get me wrong, but most only solve the initial problem. In this case: Attaching the loose end! ..but there is much more to it. Many clips have to be unclipped before using the spool as they wrap around the edge, or they collide with the AMS internal guides because they attach to the outer edge. That is no bueno! So basically most designs solve “the one problem” - but silently create others. My design “should” solve them all but like I said.. “there is always space for improvement” ^^ What you get with my design: - 3 sizes (to fit all Bambu Lab spools) - Full AMS / AMS 2 & Pro compatibility - Quick & easy to print! Visual differences I noticed between Spools If indents are present: 1.65mm is most likely the one to go for. For spools without indents: Choose between 1.70 & 1.75mm Visual comparison of (my Clip) compared to (Others) and where possible collisions occur. As spools turn, they also wander from side to side and can collide with the AMS internal guides and cause jumps, jams and grinding noises. I tested multiple clips running into the same issue over and over until deciding to make my own design.. ..which you can now happily download for free :) Please: like, comment, boost, rage, hate or whatever you feel like. This is a Remix of Bambu Labs PTFE guide that was released alongside the Filament track switch. After months of usage, I started to notice some of the design flaws and things that I did not like. I downloaded the step files Bambu Lab provided in their original listing and proceeded to make my changes. The changes I made are: Reduced the PTFE guide's overall footprint to simplify it, reduce the use of filament and make it more widely compatible with AMS stacking solutions. Widened the sides of the guide to make room for the use of piece of 25mm x 10mm double sided tape (I used the Gorilla Invisible Hold Mounting Tape). Slightly increased the thickness of the guide to increase strength and rigidity, and ensure correct alignment with the AMS, AMS 2 Pro, AMS HT. Strengthened the tabs that hold the tube by increasing its thickness by .25mm. While this seems very minimal, it is very effective at preventing the tube from dropping down over time. An unexpected benefit from my changes is that you can place the guide exactly where the PTFE tube wants to be. Installations instruction: Cut a 10mm by 25mm piece of double sided tape and place them on the tabs that face the AMS, AMS 2 PRO, and AMS HT. Place the tube into the base. Remove the plastic/paper lining from the tape. Remove the PTFE tube from the AMS. Slide the PTFE tube into the guide tube. Slide the PTFE tube into the AMS. Use the PTFE tube to help you install the guide and ensure proper alignment. Aim for having the AMS and AMS 2 PRO release button to be right in the center of the guide. For the AMS HT, ensure air vent is in center of the guide. Please refer to the photos provided which are for an AMS 2 PRO and AMS HT. I do not have an AMS 1 so I am unable to provide a photo for that. If you have one, I would greatly appreciate you posting a photo in the comments and let me know if I can use your photo in my listing. I will ensure to give you credit for your contribution. Press the base firmly against the AMS, AMS 2 PRO, and AMS HT. I have tested this and have had no issues. As long as you use a good quality tape, you should not have any issues. I used the Gorilla Invisible Hold Mounting Tape because it is strong, sticky, and can be easily removed without leaving staining or debris. Please share any feedback and let me know if you run into any issues to make changes.

model_name: Ultimate Exhaust Muffler System For X2D/P2S*
description: OVERVEIW This is my incredibly over-engineered take on an exhaust fan muffler for anyone tired of the constant buzz from the rear fan on the X2D or P2S . Most designs are a trade-off between air flow or noise reduction. But I decided that wasn't good enough for me. I needed to reduce exhaust fan noise by more than 10 decibels and preserve a large amount of airflow while doing so. Now, 4 days later, I've devised a system that can do it in style. FEATURES: 18 dB noise reduction. Interference fit assembly, no glue required! Easy to install and remove ; refer to GIF. Engine-inspired design Decorative supports that also function as legitimate air cooling fins during high-temperature exhaust. Single-baffle muffler, reducing noise while preserving airflow . Screenshot from OnShape Included. Exhaust pipe can be placed under or to the left depending on personal preference. PRINTING/ASSEMBLY: Layer height: 0.16 mm recommended due to overhangs Infill: 15% Material: No restrictions. My example is printed in PLA Basic, and I expect no issues. Post-processing will be required; make sure to use a sharp craft blade, like an X-Acto knife , while removing supports due to tight tolerances. If the Exhaust Pipe is not fitting in the slots on the Air Deflector, check for remaining supports; even one layer prevents assembly. Ensure that your machine is well calibrated before printing due to complex overhangs and tight tolerances . Changing the orientation of the Exhaust Pipe while slicing WILL CAUSE A FAILURE. It must remain vertical while printing due to the structure of the muffler's internals. Press the Exhaust Pipe into the slots on the Air Deflector while pushing an Exhaust Clip into the groove on the Exhaust Pipe, then pinch the Exhaust Clip to ensure that it has been fully seated. Lastly, install the Deflector Backplate. TEST RESULTS I ran multiple tests to prove the design's functionality. Measuring at the exhaust exit, an uncovered exhaust fan can produce 80 decibels ; after installing the muffler, exhaust noise was lowered to 62 decibels . From 7 ft away, uncovered is 57, and muffled is 49. At most, this produces an 18 decibel reduction. It might not sound like much, but try it for yourself. I guarantee it's night and day. I also ran a flow test to see how quickly the fan alone could cool the chamber from 45 to 35 degrees Celsius. Without the muffler, this process took 9 minutes and 16 seconds. With the muffler, it took 9 minutes and 38 seconds. I'm not sure how conclusive a test this is; if you've got other ideas, please put them in the comments.

description: ## Bumblebee Security Camera Housing – Tapo TC71 Compatible Bring the ultimate Autobot protector to your desk or shelf! This custom-designed, Bumblebee-inspired security camera housing is built specifically to fit the **Tapo TC71** camera. ### The Story Behind the Model This is my **first-ever 3D model**! After seeing an inspiring video online, I decided to take on the challenge. I used AI to generate the initial concept image, converted it into a 3D model, and then heavily modified and engineered the design from scratch to make sure it fits the Tapo TC71 perfectly. I poured a lot of energy, time, and hours of trial and error into this project. As a beginner, I learned so much along the way (and used quite a bit of filament to get it just right!). I would be incredibly happy to hear your feedback, advice, or suggestions—good or bad—to help me improve for my next designs! --- ### Key Features * **Perfect Fit:** Tailored specifically for the Tapo TC71 camera. * **Super Stable Base:** Designed with a heavy, massive torso and legs to ensure your camera stands rock-solid on your desk without tipping over. * **Lightweight Helmet:** The helmet section is optimized to be light and perfectly sized so it doesn't strain the camera rotation. * **Two Versions Included:** Choose between the **Pin-Joint Assembly** version or the **Fixed** version. --- ### Print Settings & Assembly Tips My test models (shown in the photos) were successfully printed with the following setups: * **Yellow Version:** Printed on a **Bambu Lab A1** using the **0.24mm Draft** profile. * **Gold Version:** Printed on a **Bambu X2D** using a **Standard Layout / Settings**. To save you some headaches, here are my highly recommended tips based on my test prints: * **The Golden Rule for the First Layer:** I highly recommend starting your print at **50% speed** until the first layer is perfectly laid down and has solid bed adhesion. Once the ground is good, you can safely bump the speed back up. * **A Warning on Multi-Color Printing (AMS/AMS Lite):** I strongly advise **against** printing this model in multiple colors directly from the slicer. I tested printing just a single leg in 2 colors, and the filament waste (purge) was equivalent to the weight of an entire extra leg! It is much more efficient and cost-effective to print it in a single color and post-process/paint it afterward (which is exactly what I did with my painted version!). * **If you choose the Pin-Joint Version:** * Scale the legs up by **1mm or 1.5mm on the X, Y, and Z axes** in your slicer. * Give the pins a quick, light sanding before assembly. This will make them fit smoothly. If they go in too tight, you risk breaking the pins when trying to disassemble them. * **If you want a hassle-free print (Fixed Version):** * Print the **Fixed version**. It takes a little longer to print, but you won't need to scale anything or worry about joint tolerances. Everything is pre-sized and ready to go! --- ### Feedback is Welcome! Since I am just starting my 3D design journey, please feel free to leave a comment, post your makes, or give me a Boost if you like my work! Your support and advice mean the world to me.
